===North Africa and Middle East===
{{See also|Turkish economic crisis (2018–current)}}
Countries in [[North Africa]] were disproportionally affected by inflation. [[Tunisia]] went through a crisis triggered by soaring energy prices and unprecedented inflation of foods in 2022. Moroccan household finances also were negatively affected by [[International sanctions during the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine|imported inflation]]. Annual inflation rates in North African countries rose to 15.3 percent compared to 6.4 percent in 2021, according to the [[Central Agency for Public Mobilization and Statistics]].<ref>[https://northafricapost.com/60583-world-bank-tunisias-trade-deficit-continues-to-widen-amid-soaring-inflation.html "World Bank: Tunisia's trade deficit continues to widen amid soaring inflation"]. northafricapost.com. Retrieved 12 September 2022.</ref><ref>[https://www.reuters.com/article/morocco-inflation/moroccan-household-finances-hit-by-imported-inflation-planning-agency-idUSKBN2JS0ZO "Moroccan household finances hit by imported inflation – planning agency"] ''Reuters''.
Retrieved 12 September 2022.</ref><ref>[https://www.arabnews.com/node/2158786/amp "Egypt's inflation hits 4-year high amid surge in food prices"] ''arabnews''. Retrieved 12 September 2022.</ref>

In some North African countries, the inflation surge has encouraged hoarding practices by consumers. Price increases for basic food staples, such as coffee, were particularly high in parts of Asia and North Africa, where people spend a higher proportion of income on food and fuel than in the United States and Europe. Food producers of [[Nestlé]]'s Middle East and North Africa (MENA) unit have noticed the stock-piling of non-perishable items, as a reaction to the surging inflation. [[Nestlé|Karim Al Bitar]], head of consumer research and market intelligence at MENA, said that the company is considering making some products "more affordable" to consumers.<ref>[https://www.reuters.com/business/retail-consumer/nestle-adapts-hoarding-picks-up-asia-north-africa-2022-09-21/ "Nestle adapts as hoarding picks up in Asia, North Africa"] ''Reuters Business Unit''. Retrieved 20 September 2022.</ref>

In [[2018–2022 Turkish currency and debt crisis|Turkey]], retail prices rose 9.65% in December compared to November, for an annual rate of 34%. Some of the largest increases were for electricity, natural gas, and gasoline. The economy was further strained by a currency crisis caused by a series of rate cuts by the central bank; the Turkish lira lost 44% of its value against the dollar in 2021.<ref>{{Cite news |date=January 1, 2022 |title=Turkey hikes energy prices; Istanbul monthly inflation highest in decade |work=WTVB |url=https://wtvbam.com/2022/01/01/turkey-hikes-energy-prices-istanbul-monthly-inflation-highest-in-decade/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220101193412/https://wtvbam.com/2022/01/01/turkey-hikes-energy-prices-istanbul-monthly-inflation-highest-in-decade/ |archive-date=January 1, 2022}}</ref> By August 2022, Turkey's inflation rate was 80.21%.{{citation needed|date=May 2025}}

=== Sub-Saharan Africa ===
According to the IMF, median inflation approached 9% in August. Rising prices of food and "tradable goods like household products" have contributed most to this increase.<ref>[https://www.weforum.org/agenda/2022/10/inflation-sub-saharan-africa-economy-challenge/ "Why inflation is one of Africa's most pressing challenges – and how to tackle it"] ''World Economic Forum'' blog. Retrieved 1 November 2022.</ref>

=== North America ===

==== United States ====
{{See also|2023 United States banking crisis}}

===== 2021–2022 =====
[[File:Inflation 2018-2024 US vs. EuroZone.png|thumb|[[#United States|Post-covid inflation spike]] in the US, gray column marks start of [[COVID-19 pandemic|COVID]] in US<ref>{{Cite web |title=Harmonized Index of Consumer Prices: All Items for Euro area (19 countries) {{!}} FRED {{!}} St. Louis Fed |url=https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/?g=1vtN6 |access-date=2024-10-10 |website=fred.stlouisfed.org}}</ref> (2018–2024)]]
[[File:Housing prices inflation.webp|thumb|Housing prices inflation from Q4 2020 to Q4 2021 in the United States<br>
{{color box|#106f67}} 40% <br>
{{color box|#92cac2}} 20% <br>

{{color box|#885810}} -40%
]]In the United States, reports about post-pandemic inflation began circulating in May 2021, when the CPI was listed at 5%, the first time since just prior to the [[Great Recession in the United States|Great Recession]] of 2008.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Smialek |first=Jeanna |date=2021-06-10 |title=Prices Jumped 5% in May From Year Earlier, Stoking Debate in Washington |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/06/10/business/consumer-price-index-may-2021.html |access-date=2025-07-25 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Cox |first=Jeff |date=2021-06-10 |title=Consumer prices jump 5% in May, fastest pace since the summer of 2008 |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2021/06/10/cpi-may-2021.html |access-date=2025-07-25 |website=CNBC |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Adamczyk |first=Alicia |date=2021-06-16 |title=Inflation is continuing to rise—here's how it could affect your money |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2021/06/16/what-the-heck-is-going-on-with-inflation-heres-what-you-need-to-know.html |access-date=2025-07-25 |website=CNBC |language=en}}</ref>

By October 2021, annual inflation was reportedly 6.2%, caused largely by higher fuel prices and [[2021–2023 global supply chain crisis|global supply chain constraints]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Smialek |first=Jeanna |date=2021-11-10 |title=Fastest Inflation in 31 Years Puts More Heat on Washington |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/11/10/business/economy/consumer-price-inflation-october.html |access-date=2025-07-25 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> By December 2021, further increases for the price of gasoline, food, and housing drove annual inflation to 6.8%.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Aratani |first=Lauren |date=December 10, 2021 |title=US inflation rate rose to 6.8% in 2021, its highest since 1982 |work=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/business/2021/dec/10/us-inflation-rate-rise-2021-highest-increase-since-1982 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220103152533/https://www.theguardian.com/business/2021/dec/10/us-inflation-rate-rise-2021-highest-increase-since-1982 |archive-date=January 3, 2022}}</ref>

By March 2022, the [[Russian invasion of Ukraine]] caused food and energy prices to begin climbing in the United States and across the world.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ellyatt |first=Holly |date=2022-04-21 |title=From soaring food prices to social unrest, the fallout from the Russia-Ukraine war could be immense |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2022/04/21/from-food-to-inflation-the-russia-ukraine-war-has-a-global-impact.html |access-date=2025-07-25 |website=CNBC |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=How the energy crisis is exacerbating the food crisis – Analysis |url=https://www.iea.org/commentaries/how-the-energy-crisis-is-exacerbating-the-food-crisis |access-date=2025-07-25 |website=IEA |date=June 14, 2022 |language=en-GB}}</ref>

In response, the [[Federal Reserve]] begin imposing interest rate hikes, seven of which would occur throughout 2022. The first occurred on March 16, 2022, by 0.25 points, targeting an [[Federal funds rate|effective federal funds]] rate of 0.25% to 0.50%.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Cox |first=Jeff |date=2022-03-16 |title=Federal Reserve approves first interest rate hike in more than three years, sees six more ahead |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2022/03/16/federal-reserve-meeting.html |access-date=2025-07-25 |website=CNBC |language=en}}</ref> The second occurred on May 5, 2022, this time by 0.50 points, raising the funds rate to a target of 0.75% to 1.00%.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Cox |first=Jeff |date=2022-05-04 |title=Fed raises rates by half a percentage point — the biggest hike in two decades — to fight inflation |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2022/05/04/fed-raises-rates-by-half-a-percentage-point-the-biggest-hike-in-two-decades-to-fight-inflation.html |access-date=2025-07-25 |website=CNBC |language=en}}</ref>

By June 2022, inflation in the US peaked at 9.1%, a record not seen since 1981.<ref name="Cox" /> Higher energy costs and housing shortages were cited as major factor.<ref name="O'Donnell-2021" /><ref name="O'Donnell-2022" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Tan |first=Su-Lin |date=July 14, 2022 |title=Yellen warns inflation in the U.S. is 'unacceptably high' |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2022/07/14/yellen-warns-inflation-in-the-us-is-unacceptably-high.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220715024523/https://www.cnbc.com/2022/07/14/yellen-warns-inflation-in-the-us-is-unacceptably-high.html |archive-date=July 15, 2022 |publisher=CNBC |quote=Almost half of the increase in prices in the latest inflation numbers came from high energy costs, Yellen added.}}</ref> Amidst a 40-year high in inflation, the Fed imposed a third rate hike on June 16, 2022, this time by 0.75%.<ref>{{Cite news |date=June 15, 2022 |title=US makes biggest interest rate rise in almost 30 years |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/business-61804877 |access-date=July 22, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Cox |first=Jeff |date=2022-06-15 |title=Fed hikes its benchmark interest rate by 0.75 percentage point, the biggest increase since 1994 |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2022/06/15/fed-hikes-its-benchmark-interest-rate-by-three-quarters-of-a-point-the-biggest-increase-since-1994.html |access-date=2025-07-25 |website=CNBC |language=en}}</ref> Despite the hike, inflation continued to outpace growth in wages and spending.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Harrison |first=David |date=May 6, 2022 |title=Pay Raises Are Historically High. Inflation Is Still Eclipsing Those Gains. |language=en-US |work=[[The Wall Street Journal]] |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/inflation-eclipses-aprils-historically-strong-wage-gains-11651854549 |access-date=July 22, 2022 |issn=0099-9660}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Dougherty |first=Danny |date=July 17, 2022 |title=Inflation Has Outpaced Wage Growth. Now It's Cutting Into Spending. |language=en-US |work=[[The Wall Street Journal]] |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/inflation-has-outpaced-wage-growth-now-its-cutting-into-spending-11658050200 |access-date=July 22, 2022 |issn=0099-9660}}</ref> According to the [[Economic Policy Institute]], the [[Minimum wage in the United States|minimum wage]] was worth less than any time since 1956 due to inflation.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Konish |first=Lorie |date=July 15, 2022 |title=High inflation leads federal minimum wage to reach lowest value since 1956, report finds |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2022/07/15/inflation-leads-federal-minimum-wage-to-reach-lowest-value-since-1956.html |access-date=July 22, 2022 |website=CNBC |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=The value of the federal minimum wage is at its lowest point in 66 years |url=https://www.epi.org/blog/the-value-of-the-federal-minimum-wage-is-at-its-lowest-point-in-66-years/ |access-date=July 22, 2022 |website=Economic Policy Institute |language=en-US}}</ref> Nevertheless, the hikes were seen as faster and sooner than the response by the European Central Bank, so while the euro fell, the dollar remained relatively strong, helping it to be the more valuable currency for the first time in 20 years.<ref name="BBC News">{{Cite news |date=July 13, 2022 |title=Euro falls below dollar for first time in 20 years |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/business-62153251 |access-date=July 22, 2022}}</ref><ref name="bbc.com">{{Cite news |date=July 21, 2022 |title=Eurozone raises interest rates for first time in 11 years |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/business-62240730 |access-date=July 22, 2022}}</ref>

The fourth rate hike occurred on July 27, 2022, by 0.75 points, bringing the funds rate to a range between 2.25% and 2.5%.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Federal Reserve issues FOMC statement |url=https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20220727a.htm |access-date=August 3, 2022 |website=Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=July 27, 2022 |title=US makes huge interest rate rise to tame soaring prices |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/business-62310354 |access-date=August 3, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |title=Fed to Inflict More Pain on Economy as It Readies Big Rate Hike |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2022-07-24/fed-to-inflict-more-pain-on-economy-as-it-readies-big-rate-hike |access-date=August 3, 2022 |newspaper=Bloomberg |date=July 24, 2022}}</ref> On July 28, data from the [[Bureau of Economic Analysis|BEA]] showed that the economy shrunk for the second quarter in a row, which aligned with a general definition of a [[recession]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Gross Domestic Product, Second Quarter 2022 (Advance Estimate) |url=https://www.bea.gov/news/2022/gross-domestic-product-second-quarter-2022-advance-estimate |access-date=August 3, 2022 |website=Bureau of Economic Analysis}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=July 28, 2022 |title=US economy shrinks again sparking recession fears |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/business-62310355 |access-date=August 3, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=May 5, 2008 |title=The risk of redefining recession |url=https://money.cnn.com/2008/05/05/news/economy/recession/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080513013719/http://money.cnn.com/2008/05/05/news/economy/recession/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=May 13, 2008 |access-date=August 3, 2022}}</ref> [[Bureau of Labor Statistics|BLS]] data showed that inflation eased in July to 8.5%<ref>{{Cite news |date=August 10, 2022 |title=US inflation eases in July as petrol prices drop |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/business-62482143 |access-date=August 14, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=August 10, 2022 |title=US Inflation Runs Cooler Than Forecast, Easing Pressure on Fed |language=en |work=Bloomberg.com |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2022-08-10/us-inflation-decelerates-more-than-forecast-on-gas-price-drop |access-date=August 14, 2022}}</ref> from the 40-year peak reached in June at 9.1%.<ref>{{Cite news |date=July 13, 2022 |title=US prices rising at fastest rate for 40 years |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/business-62148662 |access-date=August 14, 2022}}</ref> Annual inflation again eased to 8.3% in August 2022, however grocery prices continued to rise.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Boehm |first=Eric |date=September 13, 2022 |title=Rising Grocery Prices Pushed Annual Inflation to 8.3 Percent in August|url=https://reason.com/2022/09/13/rising-grocery-prices-pushed-annual-inflation-to-8-3-percent-in-august/}}</ref>

Inflation remained at 8.2% in September 2022.<ref>{{Cite web |title=U.S. inflation pressures further intensified in September |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2022/10/13/us-inflation-pressures-intensified-september-00061628 |access-date=2025-07-25 |website=POLITICO |date=October 13, 2022 }}</ref> On September 22, 2022, the Fed increased the interest for a fifth time in the year reaching a 14-year high, delivering another 0.75 points to bring rates to 3.00–3.25%.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2022-09-21 |title=Fed rate hike: US interest rates hit 14-year high in inflation battle |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/business-62973376 |access-date=2022-09-26}}</ref>

On November 3, 2022, the Fed increased rates for a sixth time, again by 0.75 points, targeting another fed funds rate range of 3.75% to 4.00%.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-11-02 |title=Bedeviled by high inflation, Federal Reserve hikes interest rate by 0.75% again |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/business/economy/interest-rate-hike-november-2022-how-much-federal-reserve-rcna54863 |access-date=2025-07-25 |website=NBC News |language=en}}</ref>  While year-over-year inflation rate was 7.1%, lower than it had in December 2021, this was still much higher than average.<ref>{{Cite news |date=December 13, 2022 |title=Inflation Cools to 7.1 Percent, but Still Has a Long Way To Fall |url=https://reason.com/2022/12/13/inflation-cools-to-7-1-percent-but-still-has-a-long-way-to-fall/}}</ref>

A seventh and final rate hike for the year occurred on December 15, 2022, where the Fed increased rates by 0.50 points, bringing the benchmark interest rate to just under 4.5%.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Horsley |first=Scott |date=2022-12-14 |title=The Fed continues its crackdown on inflation, pushing up interest rates again |url=https://www.npr.org/2022/12/14/1142757646/fed-federal-reserve-interest-rates-december-inflation-benchmark |access-date=2025-07-25 |work=NPR |language=en}}</ref>

A 2022 analysis by the [[Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City]] ascertained the role America is playing in the current inflationary trend worldwide. Before 2019, the U.S. was seen as a last resort for consumer spending during a [[global recession]], but after 2020, U.S. exports have contributed to foreign inflation. At the same time, energy prices had gone up as well as the value of the U.S. dollar, which both increased monetary pressures on nations that mostly rely on energy imports. In effect, the strength of the U.S. dollar and [[International sanctions during the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine|sanctions on energy commodities]] have contributed to global inflation in 2022.<ref>[https://www.kansascityfed.org/research/economic-bulletin/price-pressures-for-us-exporters-and-a-strong-dollar-have-increased-inflation-in-foreign-countries/ "Price Pressures for U.S. Exporters and a Strong Dollar Have Increased Inflation in Foreign Countries"] ''kansascityfed.org Economic Bulletin International Inflation''. Retrieved 12 September 2022.</ref>

Inflation is believed to have played a major role in a decline in the [[2021 opinion polling on the Joe Biden administration|approval rating of President Joe Biden]], who took office in January 2021, being net negative starting in October of that year.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Enten |first=Harry |date=December 21, 2021 |title=Biden's economic ratings are worse than Carter's |url=https://www.cnn.com/2021/12/21/politics/joe-biden-jimmy-carter-economic-ratings/index.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211225065557/https://www.cnn.com/2021/12/21/politics/joe-biden-jimmy-carter-economic-ratings/index.html |archive-date=December 25, 2021 |work=CNN}}</ref> Many [[Republican Party (United States)|Republicans]] blamed stimulus spending by Biden and fellow [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrats]] for fueling the surge; while some economists have argued that the government's [[Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021|COVID stimulus during 2020 under Trump]], as well as the Federal reserve's inactions thereafter, and [[American Rescue Plan Act of 2021|more stimulus under Biden]], started the 2021 inflation spike.{{r | NYT_2023-03-23 }}<ref>{{Cite news |last=Guida |first=Victoria |date=December 9, 2021 |title=Another eye-popping inflation reading is ahead. Next year could look very different. |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2021/12/09/biden-inflation-next-year-523984 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211226205425/https://www.politico.com/news/2021/12/09/biden-inflation-next-year-523984 |archive-date=December 26, 2021 |work=Politico}}</ref>

===== 2023–2024 =====
After peaking at 9.1% in June 2022, the United States inflation rate declined steadily into 2023, representing overall [[disinflation]]. Analysis conducted by [[NerdWallet]] {{not a typo|on}} October 2023 data found that prices for 92 of the 338 goods and services measured in CPI had declined from one year earlier, representing [[deflation]] for those items.{{sfn|Helhoski|2023}} The [[Farm Bureau]] annual survey found the average cost of a Thanksgiving dinner would be down 4.5% from 2022.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Schneider |first1=Harold |date=November 15, 2023 |title=More peas please? Thanksgiving meal costs Americans less this year |url=https://www.reuters.com/markets/us/more-peas-please-thanksgiving-meal-costs-americans-less-this-year-2023-11-15/ |publisher=Reuters}}</ref>

In March 2023, Federal Reserve chairman [[Jerome Powell]] said that the primary drivers of inflation at the time were supply chain problems, consumers' change to purchases of goods rather than services, and the tight labor market.<ref name="NYT_2023-03-23">{{cite news |last1=Tankersley |first1=Jim |date=March 23, 2023 |title=Republicans Say Spending Is Fueling Inflation. The Fed Chair Disagrees. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/03/23/us/politics/republicans-inflation-federal-reserve-powell.html |work=The New York Times |quote="You have to look at the fiscal impulse from spending," Mr. Powell said on Wednesday, referring to a measure of how much tax and spending policies are adding or subtracting to economic growth. "Fiscal impulse is actually not what's driving inflation right now. It was at the beginning perhaps, but that's not the story right now." Instead, Mr. Powell — along with Mr. Biden and his advisers — says rapid price growth is primarily being driven by factors like snarled supply chains, an oil shock following Russia's invasion of Ukraine and a shift among American consumers from spending money on services like travel and dining out to goods like furniture. Mr. Powell has also said the low unemployment rate was playing a role: "Some part of the high inflation that we're experiencing is very likely related to an extremely tight labor market," he told a House committee earlier this month. ... Economists generally agree that those stimulus efforts — carried out by the Fed, by Mr. Biden and in trillions of dollars of pandemic spending signed by Mr. Trump in 2020 — helped push the inflation rate to its highest level in 40 years last year. But researchers disagree on how large that effect was, and over how to divide the blame between federal government stimulus and Fed stimulus.}}</ref>

An analysis conducted in May 2023 by ''[[Politico]]'' found that in the United States, wage growth for the bottom 10th percentile of the wage scale beat inflation by a strong 5.7% from 2020 through 2022. For the middle 50th percentile, real wages were down by 1%, while they were down 5% for the top 90th percentile.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Guida |first1=Victoria |date=May 29, 2023 |title=Historic gains: Low-income workers scored in the Covid economy |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2023/05/29/low-income-wages-employment-00097135 |work=Politico}}</ref>

On July 26, 2023, the FED raised the interest rate to 5.5%, the highest since 2001;<ref>{{Cite news |date=2023-07-26 |title=Fed raises interest rates to highest in 22 years |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/business-66316710 |access-date=2023-08-04 |work=BBC News |language=en-GB}}</ref> in October, the 10-year Treasury yield rose to 5%, a 16-year high,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Li |first=Yun |date=2023-10-19 |title=10-year Treasury yield rises to 5%, the highest level for the key rate in 16 years |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2023/10/19/us-treasurys-ahead-of-fed-chair-powell-speech.html |access-date=2023-11-08 |website=CNBC |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Timiraos |first=Nick |title=Higher Bond Yields Could End the Fed's Historic Rate Rises |url=https://www.wsj.com/economy/central-banking/higher-bond-yields-could-end-the-feds-historic-rate-rises-f54b65d3 |access-date=2023-11-08 |website=WSJ |language=en-US}}</ref> while the 30-year fixed mortgage rate rose to 8%, a 23-year high.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Olick |first=Diana |date=2023-10-18 |title=The 30-year fixed mortgage rate just hit 8% for the first time since 2000 as Treasury yields soar |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2023/10/18/30-year-fixed-mortgage-rate-just-hit-8percent-for-the-first-time-since-2000.html |access-date=2023-11-08 |website=CNBC |language=en}}</ref> 2023 was the worst year for US home sales since 1995.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2024-01-19 |title=US home sales see worst year since 1995 |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/business-68035274 |access-date=2024-02-20 |language=en-GB}}</ref> Despite gloom numbers, the US defied recession fears with 3.3% growth in the fourth quarter.<ref>{{Cite web |title=US economy defies recession fears with 3.3% growth in fourth quarter |url=https://www.ft.com/content/05c88898-7573-426f-b656-5c76e3a51bfc |access-date=2024-02-22 |website=www.ft.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=2024-01-26 |title=US Economy Outstrips China, Adds a Korea Worth of GDP |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/newsletters/2024-01-26/global-economy-latest-us-and-china-battle-for-top-economy |access-date=2024-02-22 |work=Bloomberg.com |language=en}}</ref>

A report issued in August 2023 found no evidence linking President [[Joe Biden]]'s [[Inflation Reduction Act|Inflation Reduction Act of 2022]] to increased or decreased inflation.<ref>{{cite news |author1=Josh Boak |author2=Paul Wiseman |date=August 13, 2023 |title=Yes, inflation is down. No, the Inflation Reduction Act doesn't deserve the credit |url=https://apnews.com/article/biden-inflation-reduction-climate-anniversary-9950f7e814ac71e89eee3f452ab17f71. |publisher=Associated Press}}</ref> Gernot Wagner argued that the benefits of the Act would likely not be felt before the 2024 election, but that the act is a great long-term strategy to decouple from volatile energy markets that drive inflation.<ref name="Wagner-2022" /><ref name="Wagner-2024" />

At the end of 2023, the [[United States Census Bureau|U.S. Census Bureau]] found that if housing inflation were taken out, inflation would have been 1.8% instead of 3.2%.<ref name="Boak-2024" /> [[Climate change and insurance in the United States|Climate-change also exacerbated home insurance premiums in the U.S.]], which rose 33% between 2020 and 2023.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Becker |first=William S. |date=2024-07-22 |title=Opinion: Climate inflation is eating your paycheck — and it's only going to get worse |url=https://thehill.com/opinion/energy-environment/4782252-climate-inflation-economic-impact/ |access-date=2024-07-24 |website=The Hill |language=en-US}}</ref>

In April 2024, the annual inflation rate in the United States was 3.5% for the twelve months ending in March, compared to 7% in 2021 and 6.5% in 2022.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2008-07-23 |title=Current US Inflation Rates: 2000–2024 |url=https://www.usinflationcalculator.com/inflation/current-inflation-rates/ |access-date=2024-04-15 |website=www.usinflationcalculator.com |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Consumer Price Index Summary – 2024 M03 Results |url=https://www.bls.gov/news.release/cpi.nr0.htm |access-date=2024-04-15 |website=www.bls.gov |language=en-us}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-04-10 |title=Higher gas and rents keep US inflation elevated, likely delaying Fed rate cuts |url=https://apnews.com/article/inflation-prices-rates-economy-federal-reserve-biden-f02b969d1b44a7ccb0385be03f766de0 |access-date=2024-04-15 |website=AP News |language=en}}</ref>

An April 2024 ''Wall Street Journal'' poll across seven political [[swing states]] in the United States found that 74% of respondents thought inflation had worsened over the preceding year, though the inflation rate had declined by nearly half from one year earlier. On net, respondents in every state said the economy had improved in their state over the past two years, though they believed the national economy had worsened.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Ip |first1=Greg |date=April 4, 2024 |title=What's Wrong With the Economy? It's You, Not the Data |url=https://www.wsj.com/economy/consumers/whats-wrong-with-the-economy-its-you-not-the-data-cfa911e6 |work=The Wall Street Journal}}</ref> Numerous surveys showed that respondents considered inflation the single most important indicator of economic performance and that consumers were more likely to perceive inflation as price levels rather than the pace of price increases.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Galston |first1=William |date=March 25, 2024 |title=Inflation and the gap between economic performance and economic perceptions |url=https://www.brookings.edu/articles/inflation-and-the-gap-between-economic-performance-and-economic-perceptions/ |publisher=Brookings Institution}}</ref> The Federal Reserve February 2024 Survey of Consumer Expectations found that consumers had a median expectation of a 3.0% inflation rate in the coming year, and 2.7% over a three-year time horizon.<ref>{{cite news |date=March 11, 2024 |title=Inflation Expectations Increase at the Medium and Longer-Term Horizons |url=https://www.newyorkfed.org/newsevents/news/research/2024/20240311 |publisher=Federal Reserve Bank of New York}}</ref>

The inflation surge and aggressive Federal Reserve response caused widespread concern among economists and market analysts that a U.S. [[recession]] would imminently result. As the Federal Reserve sharply increased the [[fed funds rate]] to combat the inflation surge, the longest and deepest Treasury [[inverted yield curve]] in history began in July 2022. Many analysts consider an inverted yield curve to be a harbinger of recession. No recession had materialized by July 2024, economic growth remained steady, and a Reuters survey of economists that month found they expected the economy to continue growing for the next two years. An earlier survey of bond market strategists found a majority no longer believed an inverted curve to be a reliable recession predictor.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Peck |first1=Emily |title=Why everyone was so wrong about the 2023 economy |url=https://www.axios.com/2023/12/22/2023-economy-predictions-wrong-recession |work=[[Axios (website)|Axios]] |date=December 22, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Barbuscia |first1=Davide |title=US yield curve nears flip with jury out on recession signal |url=https://www.reuters.com/markets/rates-bonds/us-yield-curve-nears-flip-with-jury-out-recession-signal-2024-07-29/#:~:text=%22Right%20now%2C%20as%20the%20yield,previous%20inversion%20record%20from%201978. |publisher=Reuters |date=July 29, 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=10-Year Treasury Constant Maturity Minus 2-Year Treasury Constant Maturity |url=https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/T10Y2Y |publisher=[[Federal Reserve Economic Data]]}}</ref>

July 2024 data showed that the inflation rate had dropped to 2.9%, the lowest since March 2021, with used car prices returning to normal following the [[2020–2023 global chip shortage]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Subramanian |first=Pras |date=2024-08-14 |title=Used car prices fall again in July, down nearly 20% from pandemic highs |url=https://finance.yahoo.com/news/used-car-prices-fall-again-in-july-down-nearly-20-from-pandemic-highs-162244164.html |access-date=2024-08-15 |publisher=Yahoo! Finance}}</ref> Increases in rent,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Narea |first=Nicole |date=2024-08-14 |title=The inflation crisis appears to be over. What happens next? |url=https://www.vox.com/business-and-finance/367103/inflation-report-cpi-ppi-us-economy-fed-rate-cut |access-date=2024-08-14 |website=Vox |language=en-US}}</ref> childcare<ref>{{cite web |last=Wong |first=Venessa |date=2024-08-14 |title=Child-care costs keep rising faster than overall prices |url=https://www.marketwatch.com/livecoverage/cpi-report-for-july-inflation-expected-to-rise-again-after-last-month-s-surprise-fall/card/child-care-costs-keep-rising-faster-than-overall-prices-4wnNJD91W3xygHPTPbbU |access-date=2024-08-15 |publisher=[[MarketWatch]]}}</ref> and electricity{{sfn|Estes|2024}} still outpaced inflation at around 5%. According to think-tank Energy Innovations, electricity prices may continue rising due to incentives for [[investor-owned utilities in the United States]] to overspend on capital projects for [[Electric power transmission|transmission lines]] and [[distribution lines]] instead of on [[Distributed generation|distributed]] and renewable [[electricity generation]] which reduces the amount spent on transmission networks that climate change has made more expensive to build and maintain.{{sfn|Estes|2024}} An August 2024 survey of inflation expectations showed consumers predicting 2.3% average inflation over the next three years, the lowest figure since the survey was created in 2013.<ref name="Rugabear-2024" />

Inflation was reportedly voters' primary issue in the November [[2024 United States presidential election|2024 U.S. presidential election]], given the common association by voters between the health of the economy with the incumbent administration, and was therefore speculated by some to be the main reason behind then former President [[Donald Trump]]'s victory.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Lopez |first=German |date=2024-11-08 |title=How Inflation Shaped Voting |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/11/08/briefing/how-inflation-shaped-voting.html |access-date=2025-07-25 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Brenan|first=Megan |date=2024-10-09 |title=Economy Most Important Issue to 2024 Presidential Vote |url=https://news.gallup.com/poll/651719/economy-important-issue-2024-presidential-vote.aspx |access-date=2025-07-25 |website=Gallup.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Horsley |first=Scott |date=2024-11-12 |title=Why high prices toppled Democrats — and other governments around the world |url=https://www.npr.org/2024/11/12/nx-s1-5186615/high-prices-inflation-economy-election-voters |access-date=2025-07-25 |work=NPR |language=en}}</ref>

===== 2025–present =====
However, following the 2024 election, then President-elect Trump began escalating tariff threats on China and Mexico, causing some to fear exacerbated inflation during the start of his presidency.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Swanson |first=Ana |date=2024-11-26 |title=Tariff Threats Show Trump's Commitment to Upending Global Trade |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/11/26/us/politics/trump-tariffs-global-trade.html |access-date=2025-07-25 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=President-Elect Trump Announces Tariff Plans for Largest U.S. Trading Partners {{!}} Insights {{!}} Holland & Knight |url=https://www.hklaw.com/en/insights/publications/2024/12/president-elect-trump-announces-tariff-plans |access-date=2025-07-25 |website=www.hklaw.com |language=en}}</ref> By January 10, 2025, long-term inflation expectations rose to 3.3 percent from 3.0 percent in December 2024, the highest level since June 2008, according to a University of Michigan survey.<ref>{{cite news |title=US consumer inflation expectations soar in January on tariff fears |url=https://www.reuters.com/markets/us/us-consumer-inflation-expectations-soar-january-tariff-fears-2025-01-10/ |work=Reuters |date=10 January 2025}}</ref>

In February 2025, following the start of the [[Second presidency of Donald Trump|second Trump Administration]], consumer inflation in the United States reportedly dropped to 2.8% on a year-over-year basis, but this data was still above the Federal Reserve's target rate of 2% and was projected to climb following Trump's implementation of tariffs.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Mutikani |first=Lucia |date=March 12, 2025 |title=US consumer inflation slows in February; tariffs expected to boost prices |url=https://www.reuters.com/markets/us/us-consumer-price-growth-slows-february-2025-03-12/ |access-date=March 17, 2025 |website=Reuters}}</ref> An April 2025 CPI report showed annual inflation had slowed to 2.3%, however this figure again had not yet taken into account the full impact of the Trump Administration's tariffs on the economy, [[Liberation Day tariffs|which were imposed at the start of the month]], as many were given a 90-day pause pending further trade deals.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Consumer prices up 2.3 percent from April 2024 to April 2025 |url=https://www.bls.gov/opub/ted/2025/consumer-prices-up-2-3-percent-from-april-2024-to-april-2025.htm |access-date=2025-07-25 |website=Bureau of Labor Statistics |language=en-us}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Carlson |first=Seth |title=April 2025 inflation rate lower than expected: What this means for investors |url=https://www.chase.com/personal/investments/learning-and-insights/article/cpi-report-april-2025 |access-date=2025-07-25 |website=www.chase.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

In May 2025, the national average for gasoline across the United States reached a four-year low of $3.08 per gallon, down 50 cents from 2024, and $1.52 from 2022 during the height of the inflation surge.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Egan |first=Matt |date=2025-05-20 |title=Gas prices are set for their cheapest Memorial Day since 2021 {{!}} CNN Business |url=https://www.cnn.com/2025/05/20/business/gas-prices-memorial-day-trump-inflation |access-date=2025-07-25 |website=CNN |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-05-22 |title=Memorial Day weekend gas prices could be cheapest since 2021 – CBS News |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/2025-memorial-day-weekend-gas-prices/ |access-date=2025-07-25 |website=www.cbsnews.com |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Timotija |first=Filip |date=2025-05-20 |title=Memorial Day weekend gas prices expected to be cheapest in years |url=https://thehill.com/homenews/state-watch/5310454-gas-prices-cheapest-summer-years/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250521103805/https://thehill.com/homenews/state-watch/5310454-gas-prices-cheapest-summer-years/ |archive-date=2025-05-21 |access-date=2025-07-25 |work=The Hill |language=en-US}}</ref>

By July 2025, annual inflation increased to 2.7%, corresponding with earlier warnings from economists that the U.S. tariffs will soon be passed along to consumers enough to be reflected in the Bureau of Labor and Statistics' CPI reports.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Cox |first=Jeff |date=2025-07-15 |title=Inflation picks up again in June, rising at 2.7% annual rate |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2025/07/15/cpi-inflation-report-june-2025.html |access-date=2025-07-25 |website=CNBC |language=en}}</ref><ref name="www.cbsnews.com-2025"/>

The cause for the 2021–2023 inflation surge in the United States has generally been believed to be a combination of factors, including the increasing of [[money supply]] from the fiscal stimulus provided in 2020 and 2021, supply chain constraints following the reopening of the United States economy in mid-2021, and energy price shocks resulting from the Russo-Ukraine war in 2022.<ref>{{Cite web |title=What caused the high inflation during the COVID-19 period? : Monthly Labor Review : U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics |url=https://www.bls.gov/opub/mlr/2023/beyond-bls/what-caused-the-high-inflation-during-the-covid-19-period.htm |access-date=2025-07-25 |website=Bureau of Labor Statistics |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Vinocur |first=Gabriel DeLuca |date=2025-02-03 |title=Fact Check: Would stopping government overspending 'end' post-COVID inflation? {{!}} Econofact |url=https://econofact.org/factbrief/fact-check-would-stopping-government-overspending-end-post-covid-inflation |access-date=2025-07-25 |website=econofact.org |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-12-12 |title=A "Grumpy Economist" Weighs in on Inflation's Causes — And Its Cures |url=https://www.gsb.stanford.edu/insights/grumpy-economist-weighs-inflations-causes-its-cures |access-date=2025-07-25 |website=Stanford Graduate School of Business |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-09-19 |title=The drivers of post-pandemic inflation |url=https://cepr.org/voxeu/columns/drivers-post-pandemic-inflation |access-date=2025-07-25 |website=CEPR |language=en}}</ref>

In September 2026, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time since 2023, a decision shaped by a combination of domestic economic resilience and elevated energy prices stemming from the Iran war.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2026-09-25 |title=Soaring bond yields ‘not even close’ to cooling red-hot US economy, investors say |url=https://www.ft.com/content/bcf0715b-4292-428e-80ec-e6702d430aa4?syn-25a6b1a6=1 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260926122617/https://www.ft.com/content/bcf0715b-4292-428e-80ec-e6702d430aa4?syn-25a6b1a6=1 |archive-date=2026-09-26 |access-date=2026-09-26 |language=en-GB}}</ref>

==== Canada ====

since 1991 |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/business/canada-inflation-january-1.6353464 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220216135214/https://www.cbc.ca/news/business/canada-inflation-january-1.6353464 |archive-date=February 16, 2022 |publisher=Canadian Broadcasting Corporation}}</ref> and further increasing to 6.7% two months later.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Evans |first=Pete |date=April 20, 2022 |title=Canada's inflation rate jumps to new 31-year high of 6.7% |work=[[Bloomberg News]] |publisher=[[Bloomberg L.P.]]}}</ref> before jumping to 7.7% in May, the highest ever since 1983.<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 22, 2022 |title=Consumer Price Index, May 2022 ==== Mexico ====
In July 2022, Mexico's [[INEGI]] reported a year-on-year increase in consumer prices of 8.15%, against a [[Bank of Mexico|Central Bank]] target of 2–4%.<ref>{{cite news |last=De Haldevang |first=Max |date=August 11, 2022 |title=Mexico Raises Key Interest Rate to Highest Ever as Inflation Accelerates |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2022-08-11/banxico-raises-key-rate-to-highest-ever-as-inflation-accelerates |publisher=Bloomberg}}</ref>

=== South America ===
{{See also|La Década Perdida|Argentine monetary crisis}}
In Brazil, inflation hit its highest rate since 2003 — prices rose 10.74% in November 2021 compared to November 2020. Economists predicted that inflation has peaked and that the economy may be headed for recession, in part due to aggressive interest rate increases by the central bank.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Rosati |first=Andrew |date=December 10, 2021 |title=Brazil's Inflation Likely Peaked After Hitting 18-Year High |work=Bloomberg |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2021-12-10/brazil-s-consumer-prices-rise-less-than-forecast-in-november |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220101184610/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2021-12-10/brazil-s-consumer-prices-rise-less-than-forecast-in-november |archive-date=January 1, 2022}}</ref>

According to Austing Rating data, Brazil ended 2022 with the sixth lowest G20 inflation rate. Inflation recorded in Brazil in 2022 was below the United States for the first time in 15 years, in addition to being lower than that of the United Kingdom and the 6th lowest in the G20 (group of the 19 largest and most important economies in the world and the European Union).<ref>{{Cite web |last=Shoes |first=Eloisa |date=2023-01-19 |title=Inflação do Brasil está entre as menores do Mundo em 2022 |url=https://investidoresbrasil.com.br/inflacao-do-brasil-esta-entre-as-menores-do-mundo-em-2022/ |access-date=2023-02-16 |website=Investidores Brasil – Juntos Podemos Mais |language=pt-BR}}</ref>

In Argentina, a country with a chronic [[Economy of Argentina#Inflation|inflation problem]], the interest rate was hiked to 69.5% in August, as inflation has further deteriorated hitting a 20-year high at 70%, and is forecasted to top 90% by the end of the year.<ref>{{Cite news |date=August 12, 2022 |title=Argentina rate hiked to 69.5% as inflation hits 20-year high |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/business-62514970 |access-date=August 19, 2022}}</ref> Inflation hit past 100% in February 2023 for the first time since 1991.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2023-03-15 |title=Argentina inflation soars past 100% mark |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-latin-america-64960385 |access-date=2023-03-15}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last1=Bianco |first1=Miguel Lo |last2=Martini |first2=Claudia |date=2023-03-14 |title=Argentina inflation tops 100% for first time since 1991 |language=en |work=Reuters |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/argentines-struggle-shadow-100-inflation-2023-03-14/ |access-date=2023-03-15}}</ref> Argentina's December 2023 annual inflation was the highest in the world at 211.4%.<ref>{{Cite web |agency=AP |date=2024-01-12 |title=Argentina's annual inflation soars to 211.4%, the highest in the world |url=https://english.elpais.com/economy-and-business/2024-01-11/argentinas-annual-inflation-soars-to-2114-the-highest-in-32-years.html |access-date=2024-02-06 |website=EL PAÍS English |language=en-us}}</ref>

Chile had low inflation for several years thanks to the monetary policy of its autonomous central bank. However, in 2022 there was a record intranual inflation of 14.1%, the highest in the last 30 years. There is a consensus among economists that Chilean inflation is mainly caused by endogenous factors, especially the aggressive expansionary policies during the COVID-19 pandemic and the massive withdrawals from pension funds. Economists have also predicted a possible recession by 2023 due to high interest rates to combat inflation.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Inflación anual de Chile es la más alta en 30 años |url=https://www.cnnchile.com/economia/inflacion-anual-chile-30-anos_20220909/ |access-date=2022-09-26 |website=CNN Chile |language=es}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-09-09 |title=La mayor en 30 años: Expertos analizan compleja persistencia inflacionaria y las acciones del Banco Central para controlarla |url=https://www.emol.com/noticias/Economia/2022/09/09/1072368/economistas-politica-monetaria-inflacion.html |access-date=2022-09-26 |website=Emol |language=es}}</ref>

=== Europe ===
{{See also|2021–present United Kingdom cost-of-living crisis}}
In the Netherlands, the average 2021 inflation rate was the highest since 2003.<ref name="NOS-2022">{{Cite web |date=January 11, 2022 |title=Torenhoge inflatie in december, cijfer over heel 2021 naar 2,7 procent |url=https://nos.nl/artikel/2412657-torenhoge-inflatie-in-december-cijfer-over-heel-2021-naar-2-7-procent |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220111061119/http://nos.nl/artikel/2412657-torenhoge-inflatie-in-december-cijfer-over-heel-2021-naar-2-7-procent |archive-date=January 11, 2022 |publisher=[[Nederlandse Omroep Stichting|NOS]] |language=nl}}</ref> With energy prices having increased by 75%, December saw the highest inflation rate in decades.<ref name="NOS-2022" /> In 2023, the Netherlands fell into recession from April to June.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Netherlands dips into recession after strong COVID rebound |publisher=DW |date=August 16, 2023 |url=https://www.dw.com/en/netherlands-dips-into-recession-after-strong-covid-rebound/a-66551394 |access-date=2023-08-30 |website=dw.com |language=en}}</ref>

In the UK, inflation reached a 40-year high of 10.1% in July 2022, driven by food prices, and further increase is anticipated in October [[2021 United Kingdom natural gas supplier crisis|when higher energy bills are expected to hit]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=August 17, 2022 |title=UK inflation: Food costs push price rises to new 40-year high |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/business-62562025 |access-date=August 19, 2022}}</ref> In September, the Bank of England warned the UK may already be in recession<ref>{{Cite news |date=2022-09-22 |title=UK may already be in recession – Bank of England |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/business-62991376 |access-date=2022-09-27}}</ref> and in December, the interest rate was raised by the ninth time in the year to 3.5%, the highest level for 14 years.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2022-12-15 |title=UK interest rates raised to highest level for 14 years |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/business-63977963 |access-date=2023-01-05}}</ref>

UK food and drink prices rose by 19.2% in the year to March 2023, a 45-year high.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2023-04-19 |title=Inflation falls but food prices climb to 45-year high |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-northern-ireland-65317256 |access-date=2023-04-25}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Consumer price inflation, UK – Office for National Statistics |url=https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/inflationandpriceindices/bulletins/consumerpriceinflation/march2023 |access-date=2023-04-25 |website=www.ons.gov.uk}}</ref> On 3 August the BoE raised the interest rate to 5.25%, the highest since 2008.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2023-08-02 |title=Interest rates: No cut until 'solid evidence' price rises slowing – Bank boss |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/business-66384289 |access-date=2023-08-04}}</ref> The UK entered a [[technical recession]] in the final six months of 2023.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2024-02-15 |title=UK economy fell into recession after people cut spending |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/business-68285833 |access-date=2024-04-05 |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-03-28 |title=Revised figures confirm UK ended 2023 in recession |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/live/business-68680004 |access-date=2024-04-05 |website=BBC News |language=en-gb}}</ref>

Germany's inflation rate reached 11.7% in October 2022, the highest level since 1951.<ref name="Hannon-2022">{{cite news |last1=Hannon |first1=Paul |date=October 31, 2022 |title=Eurozone Inflation Rate Rises to 10.7% as Recession Looms |work=The Wall Street Journal |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/eurozone-inflation-rate-rises-to-10-7-as-recession-looms-11667210401}}</ref> In 2023, Germany fell into recession from January to March due to persistent inflation.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2023-05-25 |title=Germany falls into recession as inflation hits economy |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/business-65707206 |access-date=2023-05-27}}</ref>

In [[France]], inflation reached 5.8% in May, the highest in more than three decades.<ref>{{cite web|title=Projections macroéconomiques – Juin 2022|url=https://publications.banque-france.fr/projections-macroeconomiques-juin-2022|website=Banque de France|language=fr|date=2022-06-21|access-date=2022-10-25}}</ref>

An estimated 70,000 people protested against the Czech government as a result of rising energy prices.<ref>{{cite web |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=2022-09-04 |title=Tens of thousands protest in Prague against Czech government, EU and NATO |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/tens-thousands-protest-prague-against-czech-government-eu-nato-2022-09-03/ |access-date=2022-09-30 |website=Reuters}}</ref>

|language=en}}</ref><ref name="Hannon-2022" />

=== Asia ===
In April 2022, the [[Philippines]] recorded 6.1% inflation, its highest since October 2018. The [[Philippine Statistics Authority]] forecasted that the number would most likely be higher in the following months. President [[Bongbong Marcos]] claimed that the record inflation rate was "not that high".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Cuyco |first=Jan |date=July 6, 2022 |title=That high: What you need to know about inflation in the Philippines |url=https://interaksyon.philstar.com/trends-spotlights/2022/07/06/221496/inflation-philippines-explainer/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220713193921/https://interaksyon.philstar.com/trends-spotlights/2022/07/06/221496/inflation-philippines-explainer/ |archive-date=July 13, 2022 |website=Interaksyon |language=en-US}}</ref> On January 5, 2023, the Philippines rapidly increased to a record-breaking 8.1% inflation from December 2022.<ref>{{Cite web |date=January 5, 2023 |title=Summary Inflation Report Consumer Price Index (2018=100): December 2022 |url=https://psa.gov.ph/statistics/survey/price/summary-inflation-report-consumer-price-index-2018100-december-2022 |website=Philippine Statistics Authority |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |first=Ronnel W. |last=Domingo |date=January 5, 2023 |title=Philippine inflation rose further to 8.1% in December |url=https://business.inquirer.net/380969/philippine-inflation-rose-again-at-8-1-in-december |newspaper=Philippine Daily Inquirer |language=en}}</ref>

In October 2022, the [[Japanese yen]] touched a 32-year low against the U.S. dollar, mainly because of the strength of the latter.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2022-10-14 |title=Japanese yen touches 32-year low against US dollar |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/business-63252034 |access-date=2022-11-04}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Yen hits fresh 32-year low of 151 against U.S. dollar |url=https://asia.nikkei.com/Business/Markets/Currencies/Yen-hits-fresh-32-year-low-of-151-against-U.S.-dollar |access-date=2022-11-04 |website=Nikkei Asia |language=en-GB}}</ref> In November, the Japanese core inflation rate reached a 41-year high of 3.7%.<ref>{{cite news |title=Cost of living: Japan's inflation hits a 41-year high |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/business-64072866 |publisher=BBC |date=December 23, 2022|author1=Monica Miller|author2=Mariko Oi}}</ref>

=== Oceania ===
Inflation in [[New Zealand]] exceeded forecasts in July 2022, reaching 7.3%, which is the highest since 1990.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2022-07-17/new-zealand-inflation-accelerates-more-than-expected-to-7-3 |title=New Zealand Inflation Outpaces Forecasts at Fresh 32-Year High |last=Brockett |first=Matthew |date=July 17, 2022 |publisher=Bloomberg |access-date=July 18, 2022 }}</ref> Economists at [[Australia and New Zealand Banking Group|ANZ]] reportedly said they expected faster interest rate increases to counteract inflationary pressures.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2022-07-18/treasurer-jim-chalmers-warns-on-rates-budget-nz-inflation-surges/101247330 |title=Federal Treasurer Jim Chalmers warns on budget outlook, New Zealand inflation surge hints at even bigger interest rate rises |last=Janda |first=Michael |date=July 17, 2022 |publisher=[[ABC News (Australia)|ABC News]] |access-date=July 18, 2022 }}</ref>

In [[Fiji]], inflation rose to 4.7% in April 2022 compared to −2.4% in 2021.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Fijivillage |title=Annual headline inflation rises to 4.7% in April |url=https://www.fijivillage.com/news/Annual-headline-inflation-rises-to-47-in-April-54xrf8/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220526092408/https://www.fijivillage.com/news/Annual-headline-inflation-rises-to-47-in-April-54xrf8/ |archive-date=May 26, 2022 |website=www.fijivillage.com |language=en}}</ref> Food prices rose by 6.9% in April 2022, fuel increased by 25.2%, [[kerosene]] by 28.5% and gas by 27.7%.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Fijivillage |title=Food prices rose by 6.9% in April |url=https://www.fijivillage.com/news/Food-prices-rose-by-69-in-April-4x58fr/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220611092036/https://www.fijivillage.com/news/Food-prices-rose-by-69-in-April-4x58fr/ |archive-date=June 11, 2022 |website=www.fijivillage.com |language=en}}</ref>

In November 2023, Australia lifted the interest rate to 4.35%, a 12-year high.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Cole |first=Wayne |date=2023-11-07 |title=Australia's central bank raises rates to 12-year high, tempers hawkish stance |language=en |work=Reuters |url=https://www.reuters.com/markets/rates-bonds/australias-central-bank-raises-rates-12-year-high-tempers-hawkish-stance-2023-11-07/ |access-date=2023-11-08}}</ref>

== Electoral impacts ==
[[File:U.S. Presidential Election Swing by County from 2020 to 2024.svg|300px|thumb|In the [[2024 United States presidential election|2024 U.S. presidential election]], all 50 states and DC swung rightward, as did around 90% of counties.<ref name="Red Shift">{{Cite news |last1=Bloch |first1=Matthew |last2=Collins |first2=Keith |last3=Gebeloff |first3=Robert |last4=Hernandez |first4=Marco |last5=Khurana |first5=Malika |last6=Levitt |first6=Zach |date=November 6, 2024 |title=Election Results Show a Red Shift Across the U.S. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2024/11/06/us/politics/presidential-election-2024-red-shift.html |access-date=November 10, 2024 |work=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>]]
In 2024, for the first time ever, every governing party facing election in a developed country lost vote share, and many experienced their worst electoral performances in decades.<ref>{{Cite web|url= https://www.semafor.com/article/11/08/2024/the-democrats-join-a-long-list-of-global-parties-wrecked-by-post-pandemic-backlash|title=The Democrats join a long list of global parties wrecked by post-pandemic backlash|first1=Brad|last1=Glasser|quote=Four years after the pandemic, governing dysfunction is the story of almost every democracy on the planet, with few examples defying the trend. On nearly every continent, opposition movements have charged ahead in polls, unseated incumbents or lodged in-some-cases historic election gains against a global backdrop of inflation and agitation.|website=Semafor|date=November 8, 2024}}</ref> These governing parties had a variety of ideological leanings, in many different countries.<ref name="graveyard">{{Cite news |last=Burn-Murdoch |first=John |date=2024-11-07 |title=Democrats join 2024's graveyard of incumbents |url=https://www.ft.com/content/e8ac09ea-c300-4249-af7d-109003afb893 |access-date=2024-12-05 |work=Financial Times |quote=That different politicians, different parties, different policies and different rhetoric deployed in different countries have all met similar fortunes suggests that a large part of Tuesday's American result was locked in regardless of the messenger or the message. The wide variety of places and people who swung towards Trump also suggests an outcome that was more inevitable than contingent.}}</ref>

This was widely attributed to the worldwide impact of inflation, as economic sentiment across the world dropped. The electoral declines occurred after inflation had peaked and started decreasing, meaning that electorates assigned blame with [[Hindsight bias|the benefit of hindsight]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lippert |first=Laura Clancy and Jordan |date=2024-06-07 |title=Economic ratings across 34 countries are more negative than positive |url=https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2024/06/07/economic-ratings-across-34-countries-are-more-negative-than-positive/ |access-date=2024-12-05 |website=Pew Research Center |language=en-US}}</ref>

The United States [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]] lost the [[2024 United States presidential election|2024 presidential election]] and 3% in vote share, while losing the [[Popular vote (United States presidential election)|popular vote]] for the first time since [[2004 United States presidential election|2004]] and winning the same vote share of 48.3% in both elections. The election was very close due to [[Political polarization in the United States|political polarization]], with the Democratic Party losing the popular vote by 1.5% and the [[tipping-point state]] by 1.7%. Despite the popular vote margin of victory being the closest since [[2000 United States presidential election|2000]], the swings to the right were nearly everywhere.<ref name="graveyard"/> All 50 states and [[District of Columbia|D.C.]] shifted rightward by varying margins, the first time they all swung in the same direction since [[1976 United States presidential election|1976]].<ref name="swing wide">{{Cite web |url=https://abcnews.go.com/538/americas-swing-2024-wide-deep/story?id=116639076 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241210221226/https://abcnews.go.com/538/americas-swing-2024-wide-deep/story?id=116639076 |url-status=dead |archive-date=December 10, 2024 |title=America's swing to the right in 2024 was wide, if not always deep |date=December 10, 2024 |access-date=December 11, 2024 |first=Geoffrey |last=Skelley |publisher=ABC News|quote=From one presidential election to the next, more states usually swing toward the party that gains ground compared with how it performed four years earlier. However, it's rare for every state to move in the same direction, even in elections where one candidate wins decisively. ... But in 2024, all 50 states and D.C. swung to the right to varying degrees based on their margins versus the 2020 race. This marked the first presidential election since 1976 in which all 51 components of the Electoral College moved in the same direction relative to how they voted four years earlier.}}</ref> Around 90% of [[List of counties by U.S. state and territory|U.S. counties]] swung rightward, and not a single county flipped Democratic, the first time since [[1932 United States presidential election|1932]] that a party failed to flip a single county.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://econotimes.com/Kamala-Harris-Breaks-a-90-Year-Record-Not-a-Single-County-FlippedWhat-Went-Wrong-in-2024-1695747|title=Kamala Harris Breaks a 90-Year Record: 'Not a Single County Flipped!'—What Went Wrong in 2024?|date=December 2, 2024|access-date=December 11, 2024|website=EconoTimes}}</ref> The Democratic Party also won the highest-income voters while losing the presidential election. Specifically, Democratic nominee [[Kamala Harris]]'s strongest income demographic consisted of voters making over $200,000 a year.<ref name="Poorer voters">{{Cite news |last1=Suss |first1=Joel |last2=Xiao |first2=Eva |last3=Burn-Murdoch |first3=John |last4=Murray |first4=Clara |last5=Vincent |first5=Jonathan |date=2024-11-09 |title=Poorer voters flocked to Trump — and other data points from the election |url=https://www.ft.com/content/6de668c7-64e9-4196-b2c5-9ceca966fe3f |access-date=2024-11-12 |work=Financial Times}}</ref>

The United Kingdom's [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative Party]] experienced the worst defeat in their history, losing 19.9% in vote share and receiving just 23.7% of the vote in the [[2024 United Kingdom general election|2024 general election]], winning fewer seats than even their landslide defeat in [[1906 United Kingdom general election|1906]]. This was the [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]]'s first victory in 19 years, with the Labour vote share of 33.7% making it the [[2024 United Kingdom general election#Summary of seats returned|least proportional]] general election in British history according to the [[Gallagher index]].<ref name="graveyard"/><ref>{{Cite news |title=Britain swings to the center-left in a historic U.K. election landslide |url=https://www.npr.org/2024/07/05/g-s1-8456/uk-labour-party-win-keir-starmer |access-date=2025-02-04 |work=NPR |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |title=Britain's general election was its least representative ever |url=https://www.economist.com/britain/2024/07/11/britains-general-election-was-its-least-representative-ever |access-date=2025-02-10 |newspaper=The Economist |issn=0013-0613}}</ref>

In some countries, previously minor parties won their first electoral majorities and defeated long-time dominant parties. In the [[2024 Botswana general election]], the [[Botswana Democratic Party]] lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since [[Botswana]]'s independence in 1966, ending 58 years of being the country's dominant party. The [[Umbrella for Democratic Change]] won its first parliamentary majority in Botswana.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Ndebele |first=Lenin |date=31 October 2024 |title=Initial counting suggests Botswana may just get a new ruling party after 58 years |url=https://www.news24.com/news24/africa/news/initial-counting-suggests-botswana-may-just-get-a-new-ruling-party-after-58-years-20241031 |work=News24}}</ref> In the [[2024 Sri Lankan presidential election]] and [[2024 Sri Lankan parliamentary election]], the [[National People's Power]] won in landslides after having previously been a [[minor party]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sri Lanka: Left-leaning leader's coalition secures landslide victory |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/crr9n2w0lyzo |access-date=15 November 2024 |website=www.bbc.com |date=November 15, 2024 |language=en-GB}}</ref>

In countries where the incumbent party remained in power, they often lost their majorities in their respective parliaments. This included Japan, where the [[Liberal Democratic Party (Japan)|Liberal Democratic Party]] (LDP), who have governed the country nearly continuously since 1955, suffered its worst loss since [[2009 Japanese general election|2009]], as voters grappled with rising housing costs and inflation.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Japan's ruling party loses its majority in blow to new PM |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c8xpev42g78o |access-date=2024-12-05 |website=www.bbc.com |date=October 28, 2024 |language=en-GB}}</ref> India's [[Bharatiya Janata Party]] (BJP) lost the [[parliamentary majority]] that it had held since [[2014 Indian general election|2014]], with voters citing inflation as a top issue.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ioanes |first=Ellen |date=2024-06-07 |title=Modi won the Indian election. So why does it seem like he lost? |url=https://www.vox.com/world-politics/354352/modi-india-election-gandhi-bjp-uttar-pradesh-inauguration-hindutva |access-date=2024-12-05 |website=Vox |language=en-US}}</ref> In [[South Africa]], the ruling [[African National Congress]] (ANC) lost the parliamentary majority that it had held since the [[1994 South African general election|inaugural post-apartheid election in 1994]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.enca.com/news-top-stories/2024-elections-enca-projects-anc-will-take-45-national-vote|title=2024 ELECTIONS: eNCA Project ANC Will Take 45% Of National Vote|publisher=eNCA|date=30 May 2024|accessdate=30 May 2024|archive-date=30 May 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240530123735/https://www.enca.com/news-top-stories/2024-elections-enca-projects-anc-will-take-45-national-vote|url-status=live}}</ref>

In South Korea, the [[2024 South Korean legislative election|2024 parliamentary midterm elections]] resulted in incumbent president [[Yoon Suk Yeol]]'s party suffering an electoral defeat, which weakened his political power.<ref name="Diplomat">{{cite web |last1=Shin |first1=Mitch |date=2024-04-11 |title=In South Korea, President Yoon's Lame Duck Era Officially Begins |url=https://thediplomat.com/2024/04/in-south-korea-president-yoons-lame-duck-era-officially-begins/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240416130903/https://thediplomat.com/2024/04/in-south-korea-president-yoons-lame-duck-era-officially-begins/ |archive-date=16 April 2024 |access-date=17 April 2024 |publisher=The Diplomat}}</ref><ref name="Japan Times">{{cite web |date=11 April 2024 |title=Election rout makes Yoon's 'lame duck' fears reality |url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2024/04/11/asia-pacific/politics/election-rout-yoon-lame-duck/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240411094953/https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2024/04/11/asia-pacific/politics/election-rout-yoon-lame-duck/ |archive-date=11 April 2024 |access-date=17 April 2024 |website=[[The Japan Times]] |publisher=Jiji Press}}</ref>   On 3 December 2024, Yoon [[2024 South Korean martial law crisis|declared martial law]] in South Korea, the first time it had been declared since the military dictatorship of [[Chun Doo-hwan]] in 1980, accusing members of the [[National Assembly (South Korea)|National Assembly]] of supporting North Korea; however, Yoon lifted it after the National Assembly passed an emergency motion nullifying the declaration several hours after Yoon's speech.<ref>{{cite news |title=South Korea cabinet lifts martial law |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/live/cn38321180et?post=asset%3A69e3ba8d-55f4-443e-9531-84ad91772741#post |access-date=3 December 2024 |work=BBC News |date=3 December 2024}}</ref> Yoon was [[Impeachment of Yoon Suk Yeol|successfully impeached]] and suspended from his presidential powers on 14 December 2024.<ref>{{Cite web |date=14 December 2024 |title=South Korea's parliament votes to impeach President Yoon Suk Yeol over his martial law order |first1=Hyung-jin |last1=Kim |last2=Kim |first2=Tong-hyung|url=https://apnews.com/article/south-korea-martial-law-yoon-impeach-6432768aafc8b55be26215667e3c19d0 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241215192446/https://apnews.com/article/south-korea-martial-law-yoon-impeach-6432768aafc8b55be26215667e3c19d0 |archive-date=15 December 2024 |access-date=16 December 2023 |website=AP News |language=en}}</ref>

This trend continued into early 2025. In the [[2025 German federal election]], the three parties of the formerly governing "[[Traffic light coalition]]" all lost support. In particular, the centre-left [[Social Democratic Party of Germany|Social Democratic Party]] (SPD) lost over 9% and dropped to third rank with just 16.4% of the vote, their worst result since [[1887 German federal election|1887]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=24 February 2025 |title=Five key takeaways from the German election |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx29wlje6dno |access-date=2 March 2025 |website=BBC News |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250301214927/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx29wlje6dno |archive-date=1 March 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>

The '''Central Bank of Brazil''' ('''BCB'''; {{langx|pt|Banco Central do Brasil}}, {{IPA|pt-br|ˈbɐ̃ku sẽˈtɾaw du bɾaˈziw|pron}}) is the [[central bank]] of [[Brazil]]. It is the country's chief monetary authority and is responsible for maintaining the stability of the national currency's purchasing power. The bank was established on 31 December 1964.

The Central Bank of Brazil is not affiliated with any ministry and, like other central banks, exercises monetary authority in the country. It was created through the merger of three institutions: the [[:pt:Superintendência da Moeda e do Crédito|Superintendência da Moeda e do Crédito]] (SUMOC), the [[Banco do Brasil|Bank of Brazil]] (BB), and the [[:pt:Tesouro Nacional|National Treasury]]. One of the main instruments of Brazil's [[monetary policy]] is the bank's benchmark overnight interest rate, known as the [[SELIC]] rate, which is set by the bank's [[Monetary Policy Committee (Brazil)|Monetary Policy Committee]] (Copom).<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.bcb.gov.br/en/#!/n/COMMITTEE |title=Banco Central do Brasil |website=bcb.gov.br |access-date=23 June 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230524104757/https://www.bcb.gov.br/en#!/n/COMMITTEE |archive-date=24 May 2023 |url-status=dead}}</ref> The bank is also active in promoting [[financial inclusion]] and is a leading member of the Alliance for Financial Inclusion.

It was one of the original 17 regulatory institutions to make national commitments to financial inclusion under [[the Maya Declaration]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/maya-declaration-urges-financial-inclusion-for-worlds-unbanked-populations-130887928.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111004080445/http://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/maya-declaration-urges-financial-inclusion-for-worlds-unbanked-populations-130887928.html |archive-date=4 October 2011 |title=Maya Declaration Urges Financial Inclusion for World's Unbanked Populations |publisher=PR Newswire |access-date=19 November 2025}}</ref> Since 25 February 2021, the bank has been institutionally independent from the [[Federal government of Brazil|federal government]].<ref>{{cite web |date=25 February 2021 |title=Autonomia do Banco Central é sancionada |url=https://www.bcb.gov.br/detalhenoticia/517/noticia |website=Banco Central do Brasil |language=pt-br |access-date=30 June 2022}}</ref>

==Independence of the Central Bank==
On 3 November 2020, the bill of the Independence of Central Bank passed the [[Federal Senate (Brazil)|Senate]], by 56 votes to 12.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://portal.sinal.org.br/publicacoes/autonomia-do-bc-senado-aprova-plp-19-2019-e-materia-segue-para-a-camara/ |title=Autonomia do BC: Senado aprova PLP 19/2019 e matéria segue para a Câmara &#124; SINAL – Sindicato Nacional dos Funcionários do Banco Central}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.migalhas.com.br/quentes/335864/senado-aprova-projeto-de-lei-que-da-autonomia-ao-banco-central |title=Senado aprova projeto de lei que dá autonomia ao Banco Central – Migalhas |date=4 November 2020}}</ref>

And on 10 February 2021, in the [[Chamber of Deputies (Brazil)|Chamber of Deputies]] was approved by 339 votes in favor and 114 against without changes, going to President [[Jair Bolsonaro]]'s sanction, generating the Federal Complementary Law No. 179 of 24 February 2021.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://valor.globo.com/politica/noticia/2021/02/10/camara-aprova-projeto-de-autonomia-do-banco-central-por-339-votos-a-114.ghtml |title=Câmara aprova projeto de autonomia do Banco Central por 339 votos a 114|date=10 February 2021 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.poder360.com.br/economia/camara-aprova-texto-base-da-autonomia-do-banco-central/ |title=Câmara aprova texto-base da autonomia do Banco Central |date=10 February 2021}}</ref>

With the Federal Complementary Law No. 179 of 24 February 2021, it became autonomous, in addition to gaining a new organizational structure.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://g1.globo.com/politica/noticia/2021/02/24/bolsonaro-sanciona-lei-que-estabelece-a-autonomia-do-banco-central-veja-detalhes.ghtml |title=Bolsonaro sanciona lei que estabelece a autonomia do Banco Central; veja detalhes|date=24 February 2021 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://agenciabrasil.ebc.com.br/politica/noticia/2021-02/bolsonaro-sanciona-lei-que-da-autonomia-ao-banco-central |title=Bolsonaro sanciona projeto que dá autonomia ao Banco Central |date=24 February 2021}}</ref>
