==Uncertainties==
A few of the uncertainties involved in monetary policy decision making are described by the federal reserve:<ref>{{harvnb|BoG|2005|pp=18–21}}</ref>
*While these policy choices seem reasonably straightforward, monetary policy makers routinely face certain notable uncertainties. First, the actual position of the economy and growth in aggregate demand at any time are only partially known, as key information on spending, production, and prices becomes available only with a lag. Therefore, policy makers must rely on estimates of these economic variables when assessing the appropriate course of policy, aware that they could act on the basis of misleading information. Second, exactly how a given adjustment in the federal funds rate will affect growth in aggregate demand—in terms of both the overall magnitude and the timing of its impact—is never certain.  Economic models can provide rules of thumb for how the economy will respond, but these rules of thumb are subject to statistical error. Third, the growth in aggregate supply, often called the growth in potential output, cannot be measured with certainty.
*In practice, as previously noted, monetary policy makers do not have up-to-the-minute information on the state of the economy and prices. Useful information is limited not only by lags in the collection and availability of key data but also by later revisions, which can alter the picture considerably. Therefore, although monetary policy makers will eventually be able to offset the effects that adverse demand shocks have on the economy, it will be some time before the shock is fully recognized and—given the lag between a policy action and the effect of the action on aggregate demand—an even longer time before it is countered. Add to this the uncertainty about how the economy will respond to an easing or tightening of policy of a given magnitude, and it is not hard to see how the economy and prices can depart from a desired path for a period of time.
*The statutory goals of maximum employment and stable prices are easier to achieve if the public understands those goals and believes that the Federal Reserve will take effective measures to achieve them.
*Although the goals of monetary policy are clearly spelled out in law, the means to achieve those goals are not. Changes in the FOMC's target federal funds rate take some time to affect the economy and prices, and it is often far from obvious whether a selected level of the federal funds rate will achieve those goals.

==Opinions of the Federal Reserve==
[[File:Great Depression money supply contraction.webp|thumb|Total money supply contracted -10.28% in [[October 1929]] when [[Roy A. Young]] was [[Chair of the Federal Reserve|Chairman of the Federal Reserve]] and continued to contract for the next few years during the [[Great Depression in the United States|Great Depression]] and [[Presidency of Herbert Hoover|Herbert Hoover's presidency]]]]
The Federal Reserve is lauded by some economists, while being the target of scathing criticism by other economists, legislators, and sometimes members of the general public. The former Chairman of the Federal Reserve Board, [[Ben Bernanke]], is one of the leading academic critics of the Federal Reserve's policies during the [[Great Depression]].<ref>Joseph Mason, Ali Anari, and James Kolari, [http://eh.net/Clio/Conferences/ASSA/Jan_00/mason.pdf "The Stock of Closed Bank Deposits, Duration of Credit Channel Effects, and the Persistence of the U.S. Great Depression"] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110609124224/http://eh.net/Clio/Conferences/ASSA/Jan_00/mason.pdf |date=June 9, 2011 }}: "Since Ben Bernanke's (1983) seminal paper entitled "Nonmonetary Effects of the Financial Crisis in the Propagation of the Great Depression"...</ref>

===Achievements===
One of the functions of a central bank is to facilitate the transfer of funds through the economy, and the Federal Reserve System is largely responsible for the efficiency in the banking sector.  There have also been specific instances which put the Federal Reserve in the spotlight of public attention.  For instance, after the stock market crash in 1987, the actions of the Fed are generally believed to have aided in recovery.  Also, the Federal Reserve is credited for easing tensions in the business sector with the reassurances given following the 9/11 terrorist attacks on the United States.<ref>{{Cite web
  |title= Financial Instability and the Federal Reserve as a Liquidity Provider
  |url=http://stlouisfed.org/news/speeches/2005/7_06_05.html
  |access-date=2008-01-06 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20061011061618/http://stlouisfed.org/news/speeches/2005/7_06_05.html |archive-date = October 11, 2006}}</ref>

===Criticisms===
The Federal Reserve has been the target of [[Criticism of the Federal Reserve|various criticisms]], involving: accountability, effectiveness, opacity, inadequate banking regulation, and potential [[market distortion]]. Federal Reserve policy has also been criticized for directly and indirectly benefiting large banks instead of consumers. For example, regarding the [[Federal Reserve]]'s response to the [[2008 financial crisis]], Nobel laureate [[Joseph Stiglitz]] explained how the U.S. [[Federal Reserve]] was implementing another monetary policy—creating currency—as a method to combat the [[liquidity trap]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Stiglitz|first=Joseph|title=New $600B Fed Stimulus Fuels Fears of US Currency War|url=http://www.democracynow.org/2010/11/5/new_600b_fed_stimulus_fuels_fears|access-date=5 November 2010|newspaper=Democracy Now|date=5 November 2010}}</ref>

By creating $600 billion and inserting this directly into banks the Federal Reserve intended to spur banks to finance more domestic loans and refinance mortgages.  However, banks instead were spending the money in more profitable areas by investing internationally in emerging markets. Banks were also investing in foreign currencies which Stiglitz and others point out may lead to [[currency war]]s while China redirects its currency holdings away from the United States.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Wheatley|first1=Jonathan|title=Brazil in 'currency war' alert|url=https://www.ft.com/content/33ff9624-ca48-11df-a860-00144feab49a |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20221210/http://www.ft.com/cms/s/0/33ff9624-ca48-11df-a860-00144feab49a.html |archive-date=2022-12-10 |url-access=subscription|access-date=5 November 2010|newspaper=Financial Times|date=5 November 2010|first2=Peter|last2=Garnham}}</ref>

====Auditing====
The Federal Reserve is subject to different requirements for transparency and audits than other government agencies, which its supporters claim is another element of the Fed's independence. Although the Federal Reserve has been required by law to publish [[financial audit|independently audited]] [[financial statements]] since 1999, the Federal Reserve is not audited in the same way as other government agencies. Some confusion can arise because there are many types of audits, including: investigative or fraud audits; and financial audits, which are audits of accounting statements; there are also compliance, operational, and information system audits.

The Federal Reserve's annual financial statements are audited by an outside auditor. Similar to other government agencies, the Federal Reserve maintains an Office of the Inspector General, whose mandate includes conducting and supervising "independent and objective audits, investigations, inspections, evaluations, and other reviews of Board programs and operations".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://oig.federalreserve.gov/default.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090411113042/http://www.federalreserve.gov/oig/oig_mission.htm|url-status=dead|title=OIG: Office of Inspector General|archive-date=April 11, 2009|website=oig.federalreserve.gov}}</ref>  The Inspector General's audits and reviews are available on the Federal Reserve's website.<ref>[http://www.federalreserve.gov/oig/oig_rpt_2007.htm FRB: OIG – Complete List of OIG Reports]. 2007 {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131002035210/http://www.federalreserve.gov/oig/oig_rpt_2007.htm |date=October 2, 2013 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web
  |title=The Federal Reserve Board (Senate – March 26, 1996)
  |url=http://www.calneva.com/money/refrnc3.htm
  |access-date=2008-01-06 }}</ref>

The [[Government Accountability Office]] (GAO) has the power to conduct audits, subject to certain areas of operations that are excluded from GAO audits; other areas may be audited at specific Congressional request, and have included bank supervision, government securities activities, and payment system activities.<ref name=comptroller>{{cite web|url=http://archive.gao.gov/t2pbat5/150187.pdf |title=Archived copy |access-date=2008-02-02 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303173214/http://archive.gao.gov/t2pbat5/150187.pdf |archive-date=2016-03-03 }} Charles Bowsher, "Federal Reserve System Audits: Restrictions on GAO's Access", Statement by Charles Bowsher, Comptroller General of the United States, October 27, 1993.</ref><ref name="psmale">{{Cite web
 |first=Pauline 
 |last=Smale 
 |title=Structure and Functions of The Federal Reserve System 
 |url=http://www.fas.org/sgp/crs/misc/RS20826.pdf 
 |publisher=Congressional Research Service 
 |page=6 
 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080529145606/http://www.fas.org/sgp/crs/misc/RS20826.pdf 
 |archive-date=2008-05-29 
 |access-date=2008-02-01 
 |url-status=bot: unknown 
}}</ref> The GAO is specifically restricted any authority over [[Open market operations|monetary policy transactions]];<ref name="comptroller" /> the New York Times reported in 1989 that "such transactions are now shielded from outside audit, although the Fed influences interest rates through the purchase of hundreds of billions of dollars in Treasury securities."<ref>{{cite news|title=Moves On in Congress to Lift Secrecy at the Federal Reserve |first=Louis |last=Uchitelle |newspaper=The New York Times |url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=950DEED71539F937A1575BC0A96F948260&sec=&spon=&pagewanted=all |archive-date=2012-07-12 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120712163749/http://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=950DEED71539F937A1575BC0A96F948260&sec=&spon=&pagewanted=all |access-date=2008-01-06 |date=1989-08-24 |url-status=dead }}</ref> As mentioned above, it was in 1999 that the law governing the Federal Reserve was amended to formalize the already-existing annual practice of ordering independent audits of financial statements for the Federal Reserve Banks and the Board;<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.federalreserve.gov/GeneralInfo/fract/sect11b.htm |title=Archived copy |access-date=2008-02-02 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120218122655/http://www.federalreserve.gov/GeneralInfo/fract/sect11b.htm |archive-date=2012-02-18 }} Federal Reserve Act, Section 11b ([12 USC 248b.]).</ref>  the GAO's restrictions on auditing monetary policy continued, however.<ref name="psmale" />

Congressional oversight on monetary policy operations, foreign transactions, and the
FOMC operations is exercised through the requirement for reports and through semi-annual monetary policy hearings.<ref name="psmale"/> Scholars have conceded that the hearings did not prove an effective means of increasing oversight of the Federal Reserve, perhaps because "Congresspersons prefer to bash an autonomous and secretive Fed for economic misfortune rather than to share the responsibility for that misfortune with a fully accountable Central Bank", although the Federal Reserve has also consistently lobbied to maintain its independence and freedom of operation.<ref>{{Cite book
  |first=Thomas M.
  |last=Havrilesky
  |title=The Pressures on American Monetary Policy
  |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=q2CIYuflBUgC&pg=PA113  |publisher= Springer
  |year=1995
  |page=113
  |access-date=2008-02-01
  |isbn=978-0-7923-9561-4 }}</ref>

====Fulfillment of wider economic goals====
By law, the goals of the Fed's monetary policy are: high employment, [[sustainable growth]], and stable prices.<ref>{{Cite web
  |title=Monetary Policy
  |publisher=Federal Reserve Bank of New York
  |url=http://www.newyorkfed.org/education/fed/monpol.html
  |access-date=2008-01-06 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20071208235807/http://www.newyorkfed.org/education/fed/monpol.html |archive-date = December 8, 2007}}</ref>

Critics say that monetary policy in the United States has not achieved consistent success in meeting the goals that have been delegated to the Federal Reserve System by Congress. Congress began to review more options with regard to macroeconomic influence beginning in 1946 (after World War II), with the Federal Reserve receiving specific mandates in 1977 (after the country suffered a period of [[Stagflation#Stagflation of the 1970s|stagflation]]).

Throughout the period of the Federal Reserve following the mandates, the relative weight given to each of these goals has changed, depending on political developments.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Suominen |first=Kati |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Cvm2nOi_LVQC&dq=Federal+Reserve+dual+mandate+%22political%22+goal&pg=PA222 |title=Peerless and Periled: The Paradox of American Leadership in The World Economic Order |date=2012-06-20 |publisher=Stanford University Press |isbn=978-0-8047-8490-0 |language=en}}</ref> In particular, the theories of [[Keynesianism]] and [[monetarism]] have had great influence on both the theory and implementation of monetary policy, and the "prevailing wisdom" or consensus view of the economic and financial communities has changed over the years.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id%3DDktBcxprXaEC |title=A History of the Federal Reserve, Volume 1: 1913-1951 - Allan H. Meltzer - Google Books |access-date=2016-05-18 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121114095154/http://books.google.com/books?id=DktBcxprXaEC |archive-date=2012-11-14 }} Allan H. Metzler, A History of the Federal Reserve.</ref>

* Elastic currency (magnitude of the money multiplier): the success of monetary policy is dependent on the ability to strongly influence the supply of money available to the citizens. If a currency is highly "elastic" (that is, has a higher money multiplier, corresponding to a tendency of the financial system to create more broad money for a given quantity of base money), plans to expand the money supply and accommodate growth are easier to implement. Low elasticity was one of many factors that contributed to the depth of the [[Great Depression]]: as banks cut lending, the money multiplier fell, and at the same time the Federal Reserve constricted the monetary base.  The depression of the late 1920s is generally regarded as being the worst in the country's history, and the Federal Reserve has been criticized for monetary policy which worsened the depression.<ref>{{Cite web
  |first=Ben S.
  |last=Bernanke
  |title=Money, Gold, and the Great Depression
  |publisher=Federal Reserve Board
  |url=http://www.federalreserve.gov/boarddocs/speeches/2004/200403022/default.htm
 |access-date=2008-01-06 }}</ref>  Partly to alleviate problems related to the depression, the United States transitioned from a gold standard and now uses a fiat currency; elasticity is believed to have been increased greatly.<ref>{{Cite web
  |title=The Evolution of Banking in a Market Economy
  |url=http://www.federalreserve.gov/boardDocs/speeches/1997/19970412.htm
 |access-date=2008-02-06 }}</ref>

* High employment – Unemployment has experienced significant increases on occasion, despite the efforts of the Federal Reserve.<ref>{{Cite web
  |title=Business Cycle Expansions and Contractions
  |publisher=National Bureau of Economic Research, Inc.
  |url=https://www.nber.org/cycles/
 |access-date=2008-02-06 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20071012231548/https://www.nber.org/cycles/ <!-- Bot retrieved archive --> |archive-date = 2007-10-12}}</ref>  These periods include the [[early 1990s recession]] caused by the [[savings and loan crisis]], the bursting of the [[dot-com bubble]] and the 2006 bursting of the [[United States housing bubble|housing bubble]] and the [[subprime mortgage crisis]]. In some cases, the Federal Reserve intentionally sacrificed employment levels in order to rein in spiralling inflation, as was the case for the [[Early 1980s recession]], which was induced to alleviate a [[Stagflation#Explaining the 1970s stagflation|stagflation]] problem.
[[Image:Dollar value chart.png|thumb|350px|The value of $1 over time, in 1776 dollars.<ref>[http://www.measuringworth.com/ppowerus/ Purchasing Power of Money in the United States from 1774 to 2006] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160719190438/http://www.measuringworth.com/ppowerus/ |date=July 19, 2016 }} from measuringworth.com</ref>]]

* Stable prices – While some economists would regard any consistent inflation as a sign of unstable prices,<ref>{{Cite web
 |title       = Low Inflation or No Inflation
 |url         = http://www.brookings.edu/papers/1996/08useconomics_akerlof.aspx
 |access-date  = 2008-01-06
 |url-status     = dead
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20071103012632/http://www3.brookings.edu/papers/1996/08useconomics_akerlof.aspx
 |archive-date = 2007-11-03
}}</ref> policymakers could be satisfied with 1 or 2%;<ref>{{cite news
 |first=Richard G.
 |last=Anderson 
 |title=Inflation's Economic Cost: How Large? How Certain? 
 |work=Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis – Regional Economist 
 |year=2006 
}}</ref> the consensus of "price stability" constituting long-run inflation of 1–2% is, however, a relatively recent development, and a change that has occurred at other central banks throughout the world. Inflation has averaged a 4.2% increase ''annually'' following the mandates applied in 1977; historic inflation since the establishment of the Federal Reserve in 1913 has averaged 3.4%.<ref>{{Cite web
  |title= Consumer Price Index, 1913–
  |publisher=Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis
  |url=http://minneapolisfed.org/research/data/us/calc/hist1913.cfm
  |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070812022655/https://www.minneapolisfed.org/research/data/us/calc/hist1913.cfm
  |archive-date=2007-08-12 |access-date=2008-01-06 }}</ref>  In contrast, some research indicates that average [[inflation]] for the 250 years before the system was near zero percent, though there were likely sharper upward and downward spikes in that timeframe as compared with more recent times.<ref>{{Cite web
  |first=Robert
  |last=Sahr
  |title=Inflation Conversion Factors for Dollars 1665 to Estimated 2017
  |url=http://oregonstate.edu/cla/polisci/faculty-research/sahr/sahr.htm
  |access-date=2008-01-06
  |url-status=dead
  |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071230220607/http://oregonstate.edu/cla/polisci/faculty-research/sahr/sahr.htm
  |archive-date=2007-12-30
}}</ref>  Central banks in some other countries, notably the German [[Bundesbank]], had considerably better records of achieving price stability drawing on experience from the two episodes of [[hyperinflation]] and economic collapse under the country's [[Reichsbank|previous central bank]].

<blockquote>Inflation worldwide has fallen significantly since former Federal Reserve Chairman Paul Volcker began his tenure in 1979, a period which has been called the Great Moderation; some commentators attribute this to improved monetary policy worldwide, particularly in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.<ref>John Taylor, [http://research.stlouisfed.org/publications/review/98/11/9811jt.pdf "Monetary Policy and the Long Boom"] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161011085729/http://research.stlouisfed.org/publications/review/98/11/9811jt.pdf |date=October 11, 2016 }}, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis Review, November–December 1998.</ref><ref>Peter M. Summers, [http://www.kc.frb.org/Publicat/Econrev/PDF/3q05summ.pdf "What Caused the Great Moderation? Some Cross-Country Evidence"] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131031181135/http://www.kc.frb.org/Publicat/Econrev/PDF/3q05summ.pdf |date=October 31, 2013 }}, Kansas City Federal Reserve Bank: "The most common explanations for increased output stability include better monetary policy."</ref> BusinessWeek notes that inflation has been relatively low since mid-1980s<ref>{{Cite web|title= Investor TIPS for Fighting Inflation  |last= Ghosh  |first=Palash R  |url=http://www.businessweek.com/investor/content/jun2006/pi20060621_214282.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060628124714/http://www.businessweek.com/investor/content/jun2006/pi20060621_214282.htm |url-status=dead |archive-date=June 28, 2006 |quote=The annual inflation rate has been relatively low since the mid-1980s}}</ref> and it was during this time that Volcker wrote (in 1995), "It is a sobering fact that the prominence of central banks [such as the Federal Reserve] in this century has coincided with a general tendency towards more inflation, not less. By and large, if the overriding objective is price stability, we did better with the nineteenth-century gold standard and passive central banks, with currency boards, or even with 'free banking.'."</blockquote>

* [[Sustainable growth]] – The growth of the economy may not be sustainable as the ability for households to save money has been on an overall decline<ref>{{Cite web
 |title        = Personal Saving Rate
 |publisher    = U.S. Department of Commerce, Bureau of Economic Analysis
 |url          = https://www.bea.gov/briefrm/saving.htm
 |access-date   = 2008-01-06
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20071217193831/http://www.bea.gov/briefrm/saving.htm
 |archive-date = 2007-12-17
 |url-status     = dead
}}</ref> and [[household debt]] is consistently rising.<ref>{{Cite web |first=Michael W |last=Hodges |title=Grandfather Economic Report series |url=http://mwhodges.home.att.net/nat-debt/debt-nat-a.htm#household |access-date=2008-01-06 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080117081301/http://mwhodges.home.att.net/nat-debt/debt-nat-a.htm#household |archive-date=2008-01-17 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

====Causes of The Great Depression====
{{Main|Causes of the Great Depression}}

[[File:Money_supply_during_the_great_depression_era.png|thumb|right| Money supply decreased significantly between [[Black Tuesday]] and the [[Emergency Banking Act|Bank Holiday in March 1933]] when there were massive [[bank runs]] ]]
[[Monetarism|Monetarists]] believe that the Great Depression started as an ordinary recession, but that significant policy mistakes by monetary authorities (especially the [[Federal Reserve]]) caused a shrinking of the money supply, which greatly exacerbated the economic situation, causing a recession to descend into the Great Depression.

====Public confusion====

The concepts involved in monetary policy may be widely misunderstood in the general public, as evidenced by the volume of literature on topics such as "Federal Reserve conspiracy" and "Federal Reserve fraud".<ref>{{Cite web
  |first=Elizabeth Dunne
  |last=Schmitt
  |quote=Professor of Economics
  |title=Myths vs. Realties for the United States Federal Reserve System
  |url=http://www.oswego.edu/~edunne/fedmyths.html
  |access-date=2008-01-09
  |url-status=dead
  |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080928041720/http://www.oswego.edu/~edunne/fedmyths.html
  |archive-date=2008-09-28
}}</ref>

The Federal Reserve has established a library of information on their websites, however, many experts have spoken about the general level of public confusion that still exists on the subject of the economy; this lack of understanding of macroeconomic questions and monetary policy, however, exists in other countries as well. Critics of the Fed widely regard the system as being "opaque", and one of the Fed's most vehement opponents of his time, Congressman [[Louis T. McFadden]], even went so far as to say that "Every effort has been made by the Federal Reserve Board to conceal its powers. ... "<ref>{{Cite web
  |title=An Astounding Exposure
  |url=http://home.hiwaay.net/~becraft/mcfadden.html
  |access-date=2008-01-06 }}</ref>{{Unreliable source?|date=January 2008}}

There are, on the other hand, many economists who support the need for an independent central banking authority, and some have established websites that aim to clear up confusion about the economy and the Federal Reserve's operations.  The Federal Reserve website itself publishes various information and instructional materials for a variety of audiences.

====Criticism of government interference====
Some economists, especially those belonging to the [[heterodox economics|heterodox]] [[Austrian School]], criticize the idea of even establishing monetary policy, believing that it distorts investment. [[Friedrich Hayek]] won the [[Nobel Prize]] for his elaboration of the [[Austrian business cycle theory]].

Briefly, the theory holds that an artificial injection of credit, from a source such as a central bank like the Federal Reserve, sends false signals to entrepreneurs to engage in long-term investments due to a favorably low interest rate. However, the surge of investments undertaken represents an artificial boom, or bubble, because the low interest rate was achieved by an artificial expansion of the money supply and not by savings. Hence, the pool of real savings and resources have not increased and do not justify the investments undertaken.

These investments, which are more appropriately called "malinvestments", are realized to be unsustainable when the artificial credit spigot is shut off and interest rates rise. The malinvestments and unsustainable projects are liquidated, which is the recession. The theory demonstrates that the problem is the artificial boom which causes the malinvestments in the first place, made possible by an artificial injection of credit not from savings.

According to Austrian economics, without government intervention, interest rates will always be an equilibrium between the time-preferences of borrowers and savers, and this equilibrium is simply distorted by government intervention. This distortion, in their view, is the cause of the [[business cycle]]. Some Austrian economists—but by no means all—also support [[full reserve banking]], a hypothetical financial/banking system where banks may not lend deposits. Others may advocate [[free banking]], whereby the government abstains from any interference in what individuals may choose to use as money or the extent to which banks create money through the deposit and lending cycle.

====Reserve requirement====
The Federal Reserve regulates banking, and one regulation under its direct control is the reserve requirement which dictates how much money banks must keep in reserves, as compared to its demand deposits. Banks use their observation that the majority of deposits are not requested by the account holders at the same time.

Until March 2020 the Federal Reserve required that banks keep 10% of their deposits on hand, but in March 2020 the reserve requirement was reduced to zero.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.newyorkfed.org/aboutthefed/fedpoint/fed46.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20121202223143/http://www.newyorkfed.org/aboutthefed/fedpoint/fed46.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=2012-12-02 |title=Board of the Governors of the Federal Reserve System |quote=In April 2007, the reserve requirement was 10% on transaction deposits and 0% on time deposits }}</ref><ref name="RR">{{cite web |title=Policy Tools &mdash; Reserve Requirements |publisher=Federal Reserve |date=February 3, 2021 |url= http://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/reservereq.htm |access-date=2021-03-16}}</ref>  Some countries have no nationally mandated [[reserve requirement]]s—banks use their own resources to determine what to hold in reserve, however their lending is typically constrained by other regulations.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://ideas.repec.org/p/bca/bocawp/97-8.html |title=Implementation of Monetary Policy in a Regime with Zero Reserve Requirements |year=1997 |access-date=2013-09-15 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304110816/https://ideas.repec.org/p/bca/bocawp/97-8.html |archive-date=2016-03-04 |last1=Clinton |first1=Kevin |journal=Staff Working Papers }} Kevin Clinton, Bank of Canada: "Implementation of Monetary Policy in a Regime with Zero Reserve Requirements", Bank of Canada Working Paper 97–8, 1997. "A number of countries now have no requirement, such as Australia, Belgium, Canada, Sweden and the United Kingdom."</ref> Other factors being equal, [[Fractional-reserve banking|lower reserve percentages]] increases the possibility of [[Bank run]]s, such as the widespread runs of [[Great Depression|1931]]. Low reserve requirements also allow for larger expansions of the money supply by actions of commercial banks—currently the private banking system has created much of the broad money supply of US dollars through lending activity.

Monetary policy reform calling for [[Full-reserve banking|100% reserves]] has been advocated by economists such as: [[Irving Fisher]],<ref>{{Cite book |title=100% Money |publisher=Pickering & Chatto Ltd. |first=Irving |last=Fisher |isbn=978-1-85196-236-5 |year=1997}}</ref> [[Frank Knight]],<ref>{{Cite book |title=Ecological Economics: Principles and Applications |publisher=Island Press |first1=Herman E |last1=Daly |first2=Joshua |last2=Farley |page=250 |isbn=1-55963-312-3 |year=2004}}</ref> many [[ecological economics|ecological economists]] along with economists of the [[Chicago school (economics)|Chicago School]] and [[Austrian School]]. Despite calls for reform, the nearly universal practice of fractional-reserve banking has remained in the United States.
{{See also|Monetary reform in the United States}}

====Monetary policy and debt====

In 2005, the Federal Reserve held approximately 9% of the [[United States public debt|national debt]]<ref>{{Cite web|title=Who are the largest holders of U.S. public debt? |publisher=Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco |url=http://www.frbsf.org/education/activities/drecon/answerxml.cfm%3Fselectedurl%3D/2005/0507.html |access-date=2008-01-06 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111102114535/http://www.frbsf.org/education/activities/drecon/answerxml.cfm?selectedurl=%2F2005%2F0507.html |archive-date=November 2, 2011 }}</ref> as assets against the liability of printed money. In previous periods, the Federal Reserve has used other debt instruments, such as debt securities issued by private corporations. During periods when the national debt of the United States has declined significantly (such as happened in fiscal years 1999 and 2000), monetary policy and financial markets experts have studied the practical implications of having "too little" government debt: both the Federal Reserve and financial markets use the price information, [[yield curve]] and the so-called [[risk free rate]] extensively.<ref>Thomas Palley, [http://www.thomaspalley.com/docs/articles/macro_policy/rethinking_surplusses.pdf "The Case Against Budget Surpluses] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160413210601/http://www.thomaspalley.com/docs/articles/macro_policy/rethinking_surplusses.pdf |date=April 13, 2016 }}," Challenge, Nov. - Dec., 2001, 13 - 27: "...the interest rate payable on government debt establishes the pure risk free interest rate that provides a benchmark for the entire system."</ref>

Experts are hopeful that other assets could take the place of National Debt as the base asset to back Federal Reserve notes, and [[Alan Greenspan]], long the head of the Federal Reserve, has been quoted as saying, "I am confident that U.S. financial markets, which are the most innovative and efficient in the world, can readily adapt to a paydown of Treasury debt by creating private alternatives with many of the attributes that market participants value in Treasury securities."<ref>{{Cite web
 |title=What will happen to the Fed if the national debt is paid off? 
 |publisher=Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco 
 |url=http://www.frbsf.org/education/activities/drecon/answerxml.cfm%3Fselectedurl%3D/2001/0103.html 
 |access-date=2008-01-06 
 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080526015349/http://www.frbsf.org/education/activities/drecon/answerxml.cfm?selectedurl=%2F2001%2F0103.html 
 |archive-date=2008-05-26 
 |url-status=dead 
}}</ref> In principle, the government could still issue debt securities in significant quantities while having no net debt, and significant quantities of government debt securities are also held by other government agencies.

Although the U.S. government receives income overall from [[seigniorage]], there are costs associated with maintaining the money supply.<ref name="daly" /><ref>Joseph H. Haslag, 1998. [http://www.dallasfed.org/research/er/1998/er9803b.pdf "Seigniorage revenue and monetary policy: some preliminary evidence] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061006235434/http://www.dallasfed.org/research/er/1998/er9803b.pdf |date=October 6, 2006 }}," Economic and Financial Policy Review, Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas, issue Q III, pages 10-20.</ref> Leading [[Ecological economics|ecological economist]] and [[Steady-state economy#Herman Daly's concept of a steady-state economy|steady-state theorist]]  [[Herman Daly]], claims that "over 95% of our [broad] money supply [in the United States] is created by the private banking system (demand deposits) and bears interest as a condition of its existence",<ref name="daly" /> a conclusion drawn from the Federal Reserve's ultimate dependence on increased activity in fractional reserve lending when it exercises open market operations.<ref>{{Cite book
  |title=Ecological Economics and Sustainable Development, Selected Essays of
 |publisher=Edward Elgar Publishing
 |first=Herman E
 |last=Daly
 |year=2007
 |isbn=978-1-84720-101-0
}}</ref> Economist Eric Miller criticizes Daly's logic because money is created in the banking system in response to demand for the money.<ref>{{Cite journal
 |first=Eric
 |last=Miller
 |title=A Treatise on the Ecological Economics of Money
 |date =  August 27, 2004 |publisher=York University
 |pages=72
 |url=http://www.cansee.org/wp/2004emiller_EcologicalEconomicsMoney.pdf
 |access-date=2008-01-26
 |quote=The growth of fractional-reserve fiat money is better understood as a response to the financing needs of economic activities, not the cause of those activities.
 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070715114603/http://www.cansee.org/wp/2004emiller_EcologicalEconomicsMoney.pdf |archive-date = July 15, 2007}}</ref>

Thus, use of expansionary open market operations typically generates more debt in the private sector of society (in the form of additional bank deposits).<ref>{{Cite journal   |first1=Guillermo A   |last1=Calvo   |first2=Carmen M   |last2=Reinhart   |title=When Capital Inflows Come to a Sudden Stop: Consequences and Policy Options   |publisher=International Monetary Fund   |page=20   |url=http://www.bsos.umd.edu/econ/ciecpp6.pdf   |access-date=2008-02-04   |url-status=dead   |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080529145608/http://www.bsos.umd.edu/econ/ciecpp6.pdf   |archive-date=2008-05-29 }}</ref>  The private banking system charges interest to borrowers as a cost to borrow the money.<ref name="casestudy" /><ref name="mmm" /><ref>{{Cite book
|first1=C.
|last1=McConnell
|first2 = S.
|last2 = Brue
|title=Microeconomics: Principles, Problems, and Policies
|year=2005
|publisher=McGraw-Hill Professional
|pages=303
|isbn=0-07-287561-5
|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hlwqualKNjEC
|access-date=2008-02-06
}}.</ref> The interest costs are borne by those that have borrowed,<ref name="casestudy" /><ref name="mmm" /> and without this borrowing, open market operations would be unsuccessful in maintaining the broad money supply,<ref name="hlsimons" /> though alternative implementations of monetary policy could be used. Depositors of funds in the banking system are paid interest on their savings (or provided other services, such as checking account privileges or physical security for their "cash"), as compensation for "lending" their funds to the bank.

Increases (or contractions) of the money supply corresponds to growth (or contraction) in interest-bearing debt in the country.<ref name="casestudy" /><ref name="hlsimons" /><ref name="daly" />

====Criticism of private sector involvement====
Historically and to the present day, various social and political movements (such as [[social credit]]) have criticized the involvement of the private sector in "creating money", claiming that only the government should have the power to "make money". Some proponents also support full reserve banking or other non-orthodox approaches to monetary policy. Various terminology may be used, including "debt money", which may have emotive or political connotations. The consensus changed after the [[2008 financial crisis]] when a number of mainstream economists embraced that banks create money when they make loans.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Braun |first1=Benjamin |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZpGZEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22mainstream+economists%22+%22create+money%22+global+financial+crisis&pg=PT9 |title=Capital Claims: Power and Global Finance |last2=Koddenbrock |first2=Kai |date=2022-12-23 |publisher=Taylor & Francis |isbn=978-1-000-80199-6 |language=en}}</ref>
