======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Debt monetization
======================================================================

{{short description|Government finance}}
{{Use American English|date=August 2020}}
'''Debt monetization''' or '''monetary financing''' is the practice of a government borrowing money from the [[central bank]] to finance public spending instead of selling bonds to private investors or raising taxes. The central banks who buy [[government debt]], are essentially creating new money in the process to do so. This practice is often informally and pejoratively called '''printing money<ref name="m643">{{cite book|last=Mishkin|first=Frederic S.|title=The Economics of Money, Banking, and Financial Markets|publisher=Addison Wesley|year=2003|isbn=978-0-321-10683-4|edition=7th|page=643}}</ref>''' or (net) [[money creation]]. It is prohibited in many countries, because it is considered dangerous due to the risk of creating runaway inflation.

== Forms of monetary financing ==
Monetary financing can take various forms depending on the motivating policies and purposes. The [[central bank]] can directly purchase [[government debt]] that would otherwise have been offered to public sector investors in the [[Bond market|financial markets]], or the government can simply be allowed to have a negative treasury balance. In either case, [[money creation|new money is created]] and government debt to private parties does not increase.<ref name="bloomberg">{{cite web|last=Holland|first=Ben|date=2020|title=How Long-Feared 'Monetary Finance' Becomes Mainstream|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2020-05-05/how-long-feared-monetary-finance-becomes-mainstream-quicktake|publisher=[[Bloomberg L.P.]]}}</ref> 
{| class="wikitable"
|+Taxonomy of monetary financing
!
!Direct
!Indirect or ex-post
|-
|'''Non-reimbursable'''
(permanent)
|Direct monetary financing without [[Asset|corresponding asset]] on the [[Balance sheet|balance-sheet]]

|}

=== Direct forms of monetary financing ===
In its most direct form, monetary financing would theoretically take the form of an irreversible direct transfer of money from the [[central bank]] to the government. However, in practice monetary financing is most usually done in a way that is reversible, for example by offering costless direct credit lines or overdrafts to the government. The Bank of England can do this for example through its "ways and means" facility.<ref>{{Cite web|title=HM Treasury and Bank of England announce temporary extension to Ways and Means facility|url=http://www.bankofengland.co.uk/news/2020/april/hmt-and-boe-announce-temporary-extension-to-ways-and-means-facility|access-date=2021-03-27|website=www.bankofengland.co.uk|language=en}}</ref> In these cases, a government does have a liability towards its central bank.

A second form of direct monetary financing is the purchase of government debt securities on issue (i.e. on the primary market). In this case, the central bank can in theory resell the acquired treasury bills.

Those forms of monetary financing were practised in many countries during the decades following the Second World War, for example in France<ref>Vincent Duchaussoy, Eric Monnet, [https://www.economie.gouv.fr/files/ww1_duchaussoy_monnet.pdf La Banque de France et le financement direct et indirect du Trésor pendant la Première Guerre mondiale : un modèle français ?]</ref> and Canada.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Ryan-Collins|first=Josh|date=December 2017|title=Breaking the taboo: a history of monetary financing in Canada, 1930-1975|journal=The British Journal of Sociology|volume=68|issue=4|pages=643–669|doi=10.1111/1468-4446.12278|issn=1468-4446|pmid=28783229|s2cid=22386890 }}</ref>

=== Indirect forms of monetary financing ===
[[Quantitative easing]] as practised by the major central banks is not strictly speaking a form of monetary financing, due to the fact that these monetary stimulus policies are carried out indirectly (on the secondary market), and that these operations are reversible (the CB can resell the bonds to the private sector) and therefore not permanent as monetary financing. Moreover, the intention of the central bank is different: the QE programmes are not justified to finance governments, but to push down long rates in order to stimulate money creation through bank credit. The increase in the government deficit that these policies allow is presented as an unintended side effect. This is at least the legal view: for example the European Court of Justice has ruled that the programme does not violate the prohibition of monetary financing as laid down in the European Treaties.

However, it is often said that the frontiers are blurry between QE and monetary financing. Indeed, the economic effect of QE can be considered similar or even equivalent to monetary financing. Insofar as ECB QE effectively reduces the cost of indebtedness of Eurozone countries by lowering market rates, and as central banks pass on to governments the profits made on these public debt obligations, the benefit of QE policy is significant for governments. Some observers thus believe that the distinction between QE and monetary financing is hypocritical or at best very blurry.

Moreover, quantitative easing could become an ex-post monetisation of debt if the debt securities held by the central bank were to be cancelled or converted into perpetual debt, as is sometimes proposed.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2021-02-08|title=Cancel the public debt held by the ECB and 'take back control' of our destiny|url=https://www.euractiv.com/section/economy-jobs/opinion/cancel-the-public-debt-held-by-the-ecb-and-take-back-control-of-our-destiny/|access-date=2021-03-27|website=www.euractiv.com|language=en-GB}}</ref> According to the ECB, an ex-post debt cancellation of public debt securities held under QE would clearly constitute an illegal situation of monetary financing.<ref>"The simple answer is: no, we cannot do that, because the Treaties don’t allow sovereign debt cancellation. But, regardless of the legal aspects, cancelling debt would not be a good idea in general, and the debate is a digression. We are seeing that governments are able to issue a lot of debt and to do it at low interest rates in a sustainable way." https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/inter/date/2021/html/ecb.in210131_1~650f5ce5f7.en.html</ref>

== Legal prohibitions against monetary financing ==
Because the process implies coordination between the government and the central bank, debt monetization is seen as contrary to the doctrine of central bank independence. Most developed countries instituted this independence, "keep[ing] politicians [...] away from the printing presses", in order to avoid the possibility of the government, in order to increase its popularity or to achieve short-term political benefits, creating new money and risking the kind of [[runaway inflation]] [[Hyperinflation in the Weimar Republic|seen]] in the German [[Weimar Republic]]<ref>{{Cite web|last=Heimberger|first=Philipp|title=Fiscal austerity and the rise of the Nazis|url=https://heimbergecon.substack.com/p/fiscal-austerity-and-the-rise-of|access-date=2021-03-27|website=heimbergecon.substack.com|date=22 March 2021 }}</ref> or [[Hyperinflation in Venezuela|more recently in Venezuela]].<ref name=bloomberg/>

In the [[Eurozone]], Article 123 of the [[Lisbon Treaty]] explicitly prohibits the [[European Central Bank]] from financing public institutions and state governments.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2016-04-27|title=Independence|url=https://www.ecb.europa.eu/ecb/orga/independence/html/index.en.html|access-date=2021-03-31|website=European Central Bank|language=en}}</ref>

In the United States, The [[Banking Act of 1935]] prohibited the central bank from directly purchasing Treasury securities, and permitted their purchase and sale only "in the open market". In 1942, during [[United States home front during World War II|wartime]], Congress amended the Banking Act's provisions to allow purchases of government debt by the federal banks, with the total amount they'd hold "not [to] exceed $5&nbsp;billion." After the war, the exemption was renewed, with time limitations, until it was allowed to expire in June 1981.<ref name="garbade">{{cite web|last=Garbade|first=Kenneth D.|date=August 2014|title=Direct Purchases of U.S. Treasury Securities by Federal Reserve Banks|url=https://www.newyorkfed.org/medialibrary/media/research/staff_reports/sr684.pdf|website=FRBNY Staff Reports no. 684|publisher=[[Federal Reserve Bank of New York]]|quote=}}</ref>

In Japan, where debt monetization is on paper prohibited,<ref>{{cite news|date=28 April 2020|title=Editorial: Bank of Japan's scrapping of state bond purchase ceiling carries risks|work=[[The Mainichi]]|url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20200428/p2a/00m/0bu/011000c}}</ref> the nation's [[Bank of Japan|central bank]] "routinely" purchases approximately 70% of state debt issued each month,<ref>{{cite web|last=Evans-Pritchard|first=Ambrose|author-link=Ambrose Evans-Pritchard|date=10 August 2013|title=Japan's Debt Has Officially Passed ¥1,000,000,000,000,000 — No Problem|url=http://www.businessinsider.com/japans-1-trillion-yen-of-debt-2013-8|access-date=8 March 2018|website=[[The Daily Telegraph]]|quote=}}</ref> and owns, {{as of|October 2018|lc=yes}}, approximately 440&nbsp;[[trillion (short scale)|trillion]] [[Yen|JP¥]] or over 40% of all outstanding government bonds.<ref>[https://www.boj.or.jp/en/statistics/boj/other/mei/index.htm/ Gov't Bonds], [[Bank of Japan]]</ref> The central bank purchased the bonds through the banks instead of directly, and books them as temporary holding, allowing the parties involved to argue that no debt monetization actually occurred.<ref name="businessweek">{{cite magazine|author1=Ben Holland|author2=Liz McCormick|author3=John Ainger|date=15 May 2020|title=Pandemic Bills Are So Big That Only Money-Printing Can Pay Them|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2020-05-15/pandemic-bills-are-so-big-that-only-money-printing-can-pay-them|magazine=[[Bloomberg Businessweek]]}}</ref>

The [[People's Bank of China]] (PBOC), is forbidden by the PBOC Law of 1995 to give overdrafts to government bodies, or buy government bonds directly from the government, or underwrite any other government debt securities.<ref>{{citation
|url = http://www.gov.cn/gongbao/content/2004/content_63110.htm
|title = Gazette of the State Council of the People's Republic of China
|date=1 February 2004
|issue=7
|publisher=Government of the People's Republic of China
|language=zh
|access-date=1 January 2022
}}</ref>

[[File:Jakarta Indonesia Central-Bank-of-Indonesia-02.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Bank Indonesia]] (''pictured'') agreed to directly purchase about US$27.4&nbsp;billion of government debt in July 2020]]

== Policy debate ==

=== Debt monetization and inflation ===<!-- I temporarily copy pasted this from the confused "Monetization" page. I'm aware this needs re-working a lot and intend to do that in the future. ~~~~ -->

When government deficits are financed through debt monetization the outcome is an increase in the [[monetary base]], shifting the aggregate-demand curve to the right leading to a rise in the price level (unless the money supply is infinitely [[Elasticity (economics)|elastic]]).<ref name="ReferenceA">The Economics of Money, Banking, and the Financial Markets 7ed, Mishkin</ref><ref>[https://www.economist.com/blogs/freeexchange/2013/01/economics-platinum-coin-option The economics of the platinum coin option] ''[[The Economist]]'' 9 January 2013</ref> When governments intentionally do this, they devalue existing stockpiles of fixed income cash flows of anyone who is holding assets based in that currency.  This does not reduce the value of floating or hard assets, and has an uncertain (and potentially beneficial) impact on some equities.  It benefits debtors at the expense of creditors and will result in an increase in the nominal price of real estate.  This wealth transfer is clearly not a [[Pareto distribution|Pareto]] improvement but can act as a stimulus to economic growth and employment in an economy overburdened by private debt.{{Citation needed|date=August 2011}}  It is in essence a "tax" and a simultaneous redistribution to debtors as the overall value of creditors' fixed income assets drop (and as the debt burden to debtors correspondingly decreases).

If the beneficiaries of this transfer are more likely to spend their gains (due to lower income and asset levels) this can stimulate demand and increase liquidity.  It also decreases the value of the currency - potentially stimulating exports and decreasing imports - improving the [[balance of trade]].  Foreign owners of local currency and debt also lose money. Fixed income creditors experience decreased wealth due to a loss in spending power. This is known as "[[inflation tax]]" (or "inflationary debt relief").  Conversely, tight monetary policy which favors creditors over debtors even at the expense of reduced economic growth can also be considered a wealth transfer to holders of fixed assets from people with debt or with mostly human capital to trade (a "deflation tax").

A deficit can be the source of sustained inflation only if it is persistent rather than temporary, and if the government finances it by creating money (through monetizing the debt), rather than leaving bonds in the hands of the public.<ref name="ReferenceA" />

On the other hand, economists (e.g. [[Adair Turner, Baron Turner of Ecchinswell|Adair Turner]], [[Jordi Galí|Jordi Gali]], [[Paul De Grauwe|Paul de Grauwe]]) are in favor of monetary financing as an emergency measure.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Galí|first=Jordi|date=2020-03-17|title=Helicopter money: The time is now|url=https://voxeu.org/article/helicopter-money-time-now|access-date=2021-03-31|website=VoxEU.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Turner|first=Adair|date=2020-04-20|title=Monetary Finance Is Here {{!}} by Adair Turner|url=https://www.project-syndicate.org/commentary/monetary-finance-of-covid19-fiscal-deficits-by-adair-turner-2020-04|access-date=2021-03-31|website=Project Syndicate|language=en}}</ref> During an exceptional circumstances, such as the [[economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic|situation created by the COVID-19 pandemic]], the benefits of avoiding a severe depression outweighs the need to maintain monetary discipline.<ref>{{Cite web|last1=Grauwe|first1=Paul De|last2=Diessner|first2=Sebastian|date=2020-06-18|title=What price to pay for monetary financing of budget deficits in the euro area|url=https://voxeu.org/article/what-price-pay-monetary-financing-budget-deficits-euro-area|access-date=2021-03-31|website=VoxEU.org}}</ref> In addition, the policy responses to the 2007–2009 [[Great Recession]] showed that money can be injected into economies in crisis without causing inflation.<ref name="bloomberg" /> An economy in recession is a "deflating" enterprise and as the quantity of money in circulation declines, economic activity naturally recedes, reinforcing collapse. Economists would say that contraction is "sticky," on the downside. Thus, deflation was a far bigger threat than inflation during the pandemic.<ref name="businessweek" />

=== COVID-19 pandemic response ===
National responses to the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] include increasing public spending to support affected households and businesses. The resulting deficits are increasingly financed by debt that are eventually purchased by the central bank. The business publication ''Bloomberg'' estimates that the [[Federal Reserve|United States Federal Reserve]] will buy $3.5&nbsp;trillion worth of bonds in 2020, mostly U.S. government bonds.{{Citation needed|date=July 2025}}

The [[Bank of England]] allowed an [[overdraft]] in the government account.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-04-09|title=Bank of England to finance UK government Covid-19 crisis spending|url=http://www.theguardian.com/business/2020/apr/09/bank-of-england-to-finance-uk-government-covid-19-crisis-spending|access-date=2021-03-31|website=The Guardian|language=en}}</ref>

In July 2020, [[Bank Indonesia]] agreed to purchase approximately 398&nbsp;trillion [[Indonesian rupiah|rupiah]] (US$27.4&nbsp;billion) and return all the interest to the government. In addition, the central bank would cover part of the interest payments on an additional 123.46&nbsp;trillion rupiah of bonds. The central bank governor [[Perry Warjiyo]] billed the decision as a one-time policy.<ref>{{cite news|author1=Grace Sihombing|author2=Tassia Sipahutar|date=6 July 2020|title=Bank Indonesia Agrees to Buy Government Debt to Fund Budget|work=Bloomberg L. P.|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2020-07-06/bank-indonesia-agrees-to-buy-government-debt-to-help-fund-budget}}</ref>

The economist [[Paul McCulley]] commented that despite the lack of an explicit declaration, the various policies represented the breakdown of the "church-and-state separation" between monetary and fiscal policy.<ref name="businessweek" />

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Denmark and the euro
======================================================================

{{Short description|none}}
{{Use British English|date = April 2022}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=March 2020}}
{{Euro accession map}}

[[Denmark]] uses the [[Danish krone]] as its official currency. While it is a [[member state of the European Union]], it has not joined the [[eurozone]] or adopted the [[euro]]. The country negotiated the right to [[Opt-outs in the European Union|opt out]] from participation under the [[Maastricht Treaty]] of 1992. In 2000, the government [[2000 Danish euro referendum|held a referendum on introducing the euro]], which was defeated with 53.2% voting no and 46.8% voting yes. The Danish krone is part of the [[European Exchange Rate Mechanism|ERM II]] mechanism, so its exchange rate is tied to within a 2.25% range of the euro.

Several [[List of political parties in Denmark|Danish political parties]] favour adopting the euro, and a second referendum has been proposed several times since 2000. However, some important parties such as the [[Danish People's Party]], [[Socialist People's Party (Denmark)|Socialist People's Party]], and [[Red–Green Alliance (Denmark)|Red–Green Alliance]] do not support joining the currency. Public opinion surveys have shown fluctuating support for the single currency, with the majority in favour for a few years before the [[2008 financial crisis]], with support falling further due to the [[euro area crisis]] in 2011.<ref>{{cite news |title=Danskerne siger nej tak til euroen |url=http://www.business.dk/oekonomi/danskerne-siger-nej-tak-til-euroen |access-date=29 September 2011 |newspaper=Business.dk|date=27 September 2011 |language=da}}</ref>

[[International finance]] scholars generally consider [[currency peg]]s to be fragile; however, Denmark has been able to maintain the krone's peg to the euro consistently since its introduction in 1999.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Eichengreen |first=Barry |date=2023 |title=The Danish problem |journal=Economia Politica |language=en |volume=40 |issue=3 |pages=781–794 |doi=10.1007/s40888-023-00313-y |issn=1973-820X|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cnb.cz/en/about_cnb/cnblog/cnBlog-Denmarks-monetary-policy-Permanently-halfway-to-the-euro/|title=cnBlog – Denmark's monetary policy: Permanently halfway to the euro?|author=Molnár Vojtěch|publisher=Czech National Bank|date=13 March 2024|access-date=15 March 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240315110850/https://www.cnb.cz/en/about_cnb/cnblog/cnBlog-Denmarks-monetary-policy-Permanently-halfway-to-the-euro/|archive-date=15 March 2024|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Current status ==

=== Opt-outs ===
The Danish government held a referendum in 1992 to approve ratification of the [[Maastricht Treaty]], as required by the [[Constitution of Denmark|Danish constitution]] for any transfers of sovereignty which are not approved by 5/6 of parliament ''([[Folketing]])''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://grundloven.dk/|title=Danmarks Riges Grundlov|website=grundloven.dk|access-date=24 March 2020}}</ref> The coalition government of Denmark in 1992 consisted of the [[Conservative People's Party (Denmark)|Conservatives]] and [[Venstre (Denmark)|Agrarian Liberals]], which together with the Social Democrats in opposition held approximately 80% of the seats in parliament leading them to believe that the referendum would be easily approved.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Siune|first=Karen|date=March 1993|title=The Danes said NO to the Maastricht Treaty. The Danish EC Referendum of June 1992|journal=Scandinavian Political Studies|volume=16|issue=1|pages=93–103|doi=10.1111/j.1467-9477.1993.tb00031.x|issn=0080-6757}}</ref> However, the [[1992 Danish Maastricht Treaty referendum|referendum]] resulted in 50.7% of the population voting against the ratification of the Maastricht Treaty, while only 49.3% voted in favour.

Ratification of the [[Maastricht Treaty]] required unanimous approval by all the member states in the [[European Union]]. The Danish "no", therefore, posed a significant issue for further integration.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Barker |first1=Alex |date=23 January 2013 |title=Opinion, Brussels blog - How do you revise the EU treaties? |website=Financial Times |url=https://www.ft.com/content/8cd660aa-a4e4-310e-acd6-cb572de94da2 |access-date=24 March 2020}}</ref> Denmark was not the only country issuing a referendum for the ratification of the [[Maastricht Treaty]]. In [[France]], the public supported the treaty by only a small margin, while the [[Irish people|Irish]] also voted in favour of the Treaty. The Danish "no" and the French ''"[[petit oui]]"'' are known in scholarly circles as the erosion of the permissive consensus regarding public support for [[European integration]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Euroscepticism: Party politics, national identity and European integration|date=2004|publisher=Rodopi|author1=Harmsen, Robert |author2=Spiering, Menno|isbn=1-4237-9199-1|location=Amsterdam|oclc=70910464}}</ref>

The solution to the lack of public support for further European integration in Denmark is known as "the National Compromise". 7 out of 8 parties in the Danish parliament came together in support a proposal to request [[Danish opt-outs from the European Union|4 opt-outs]]: Union citizenship, Common Security and Defence, Justice and Home Affairs and participation in the last phase of the European Monetary Union. At the European Council summit on 11–12 December 1992 in [[Edinburgh]], the European leaders agreed to these four opt-outs.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Svensson|first=Palle|date=March 1994|title=The Danish Yes to Maastricht and Edinburgh. The EC Referendum of May 1993|journal=Scandinavian Political Studies|volume=17|issue=1|pages=69–82|doi=10.1111/j.1467-9477.1994.tb00050.x|issn=0080-6757}}</ref> This led to the Maastricht Treaty being [[1993 Danish Maastricht Treaty referendum|accepted in a second referendum]] on 18 May 1993.

=== Exchange Rate Mechanism II ===
While Denmark chose not join the eurozone due to its opt-out, it participates in the Exchange Rate Mechanism II ([[ERM II]]), a fixed exchange rate regime in which the Danish currency and other participating countries' currency are pegged to the euro.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://ec.europa.eu/info/business-economy-euro/euro-area/introducing-euro/adoption-fixed-euro-conversion-rate/erm-ii-eus-exchange-rate-mechanism_en|title=ERM II – the EU's Exchange Rate Mechanism|website=European Commission – European Commission|access-date=24 March 2020}}</ref>

The [[Danish krone|krone]] has been part of the [[ERM II]] mechanism since 1 January 1999, when it replaced the original [[European Exchange Rate Mechanism|ERM]]. This policy marks continuation of a similar peg from 1982 to 1999 with the [[Deutsche Mark]]. Following Bulgaria's adoption of the euro on 1 January 2026, Denmark is the only [[Member state of the European Union|European Union]] member state participating in the ERM II.

Denmark is required to ensure that the kroner trades within 2.25% either side of a specified rate of 1 euro equal to 7.46038 kroner (making the lower rate 7.29252 and the upper rate 7.62824).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/pr/date/2004/html/pr040628.en.html|title=Euro central rates and compulsory intervention rates in ERM II|website=European Central Bank|date=28 June 2004|access-date=24 March 2020}}</ref> However, in practice the exchange rate has kept within 0.5% of the defined rate, even less than the set limits.{{Citation needed|date=June 2026}} If the Krone goes beyond the limits, the [[Danmarks Nationalbank]] is mandated to intervene and bring it back within the fluctuation band, with the [[European Central Bank]] obliged to intervene if the Danish central bank is unable to do so.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book|author1=Hougaard, Jensen |author2=Svend, Erik|title=Fastkurspolitik, ØMU og valutaspekulation|date=2000|publisher=Economic Policy Research Unit, Institute of Economics, University of Copenhagen|oclc=784980209}}</ref> Two approaches are used to adjust the money supply and exchange rate. The first tool is intervention through the purchase and selling currencies to adjust the available money level. The second tool is an adjustment of the interest rates.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nationalbanken.dk/en/about_danmarks_nationalbank/frequently_asked_questions/Pages/Denmarks-fixed-exchange-rate-policy.aspx|title=Denmark's fixed exchange rate policy|website=nationalbanken.dk|access-date=24 March 2020}}</ref>

The [[European Central Bank]] conducts monetary policy independently of the national governments in the [[eurozone]], resulting in loss of independence in [[Monetary policy|monitary policy]] in favour of price stability.<ref name=":1" /> The ECB is committed to maintaining 2% inflation in the middle to long run.<ref name=":4">{{Cite book|title=Pengepolitik i Danmark|date=2009|publisher=Danmarks Nationalbank|isbn=978-87-87251-70-9|edition=3. udgave|location=København|oclc=837748184}}</ref> The decrease in fluctuations of currency reduces uncertainty for traders.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last=PÉTURSSON|first=THÓRARINN G|year=2000|title=Exchange rate or inflation targeting in monetary policy?|url=https://www.cb.is/library/Skraarsafn---EN/FromOldWeb/Acrobat-(PDF)/mb001_6.pdf|journal=Monetary Bulletin 2000/1}}</ref>

Denmark has had a fixed exchange rate since the end of the [[Second World War]] and has participated in several monetary cooperation systems. Therefore, participating in ERM II was not a change in this sense, and the lost autonomy in monetary policy and associated inability to respond to domestic economic shocks with monetary policy tools, had existed since the creation of the [[Bretton Woods system]].<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal|last=MARCUSSEN|first=MARTIN|date=March 2005|title=Denmark and european monetary integration: Out but far from over|journal=Journal of European Integration|volume=27|issue=1|pages=43–63|doi=10.1080/07036330400029918|s2cid=154927996|issn=0703-6337}}</ref>

== History ==

=== Early monetary unions in Denmark (1873–1914) ===
On 5 May 1873 Denmark with Sweden fixed their currencies against gold and formed the [[Scandinavian Monetary Union]], with Norway joining in 1875. Prior to this date, Denmark used the [[Danish rigsdaler]] divided into 96 rigsbank skilling. The union had the currency pegged to gold at the rate of 2.48 kroner per gram of gold, or 0.4032 grams per krone. An equal valued ''krone'' of the monetary union replaced the three legacy currencies at the rate of ''1 krone'' = ½ [[Danish rigsdaler]] = ¼ [[Norwegian speciedaler]] = 1 [[Swedish riksdaler]]. The new currency became a legal tender and was accepted in all three countries. This monetary union lasted until 1914 when [[World War I]] brought an end to it.

===European Monetary System and pre-euro monetary co-operation===
The collapse of the [[Bretton Woods system]] destabilised European markets, and monetary integration among the member states of the [[European Economic Community]] (now European Union).<ref name=":6">{{Cite web|url=https://www.cvce.eu/en/collections/unit-content/-/unit/02bb76df-d066-4c08-a58a-d4686a3e68ff/38cf7d33-69b8-4550-a648-67f433ac14a1|title=The European currency snake – Historical events in the European integration process (1945–2014) – CVCE Website|website=cvce.eu|access-date=24 March 2020}}</ref> Under the Bretton Woods system, the [[United States dollar|dollar]] was pegged to the gold standard.<ref name=":7">{{Cite journal|last=Oxenford|first=Matthew|date=September 2016|title=The Evolution of US and European Monetary Policy after Bretton Woods: A historical Overview and Lession for the Future|url=https://www.chathamhouse.org/sites/default/files/publications/research/2016-09-07-monetary-policy-oxenford.pdf|journal=Chatham House}}</ref> Following the collapse of the Bretton Woods system, the [[European Currency Snake]] system came into force on 24 April 1972 with Denmark joining on 1 May 1972. Shortly after, the [[Danish krone|Danish Crown]] came under speculative attacks, and was forced to abandon the system, but the joined again a few months later.<ref name=":6" /><ref name=":8">{{Cite book|last=Kaelberer, Matthias |title=Money and power in Europe : the political economy of European monetary cooperation|date=2001|publisher=State University of New York Press|isbn=0-7914-4996-3|location=Albany|oclc=44769076}}</ref>

The [[European Monetary System]] was established in 1979 to maintain stability in EEC countries with Denmark being one of the 8 participating countries.<ref name=":9">{{Cite web|url=https://www.europarl.europa.eu/factsheets/en/sheet/79/history-of-economic-and-monetary-union|title=History of economic and monetary union {{!}} Fact Sheets on the European Union {{!}} European Parliament|publisher=European Parliament|access-date=24 March 2020}}</ref> The [[European Monetary System|EMS]] created an [[European Exchange Rate Mechanism|Exchange Rate Mechanism]] with fixed bands for currencies of participating countries. The Danish economy experienced recession in 1980, forcing the government to introduce several economic reforms.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Times |first=R. w Apple Jr Special To the New York |date=1980-08-29 |title=Danes, Hit by Recession, Clash on Arms Spending; 'The Zero Solution' Importance of Danish Role Opposition Speaks Out The Dispute Is a Symbol |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1980/08/29/archives/danes-hit-by-recession-clash-on-arms-spending-the-zero-solution.html |access-date=2026-06-22 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> The most significant reform was the decision to opt for a fixed exchange rate policy in 1982 and stopping currency devaluation by pegging it against the [[Deutsche Mark|German D-mark]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Abildgren, Kim.|title=Monetary history of Denmark, 1990–2005|date=2010|publisher=Danmarks Nationalbank|isbn=978-87-87251-84-6|oclc=701865891}}</ref>

As the Danish people did not vote in favour of the 1992 Treaty, it did not adopt the euro, However, in 1998 Denmark agreed to participate in Exchange Rate Mechanism II with a narrow fluctuation band of ± 2.25% (instead of the ± 15%, which is the standard fluctuation band in the mechanism).<ref name=":2" /> The agreement was negotiated and finalised in the [[Economic and Financial Affairs Council|ECOFIN]] Council 25–27 September 1998.<ref name=":4" /> The difference between [[European Exchange Rate Mechanism|ERM]] and ERM II is that the currencies participating in ERM II are no longer linked to bilateral parities with other participating currencies as they were in the original [[European Exchange Rate Mechanism|ERM]] system, but rather they are pegged to the euro instead.<ref name=":5" />

=== Euro referendum (2000) ===
{{Main|Danish euro referendum, 2000}}

A [[2000 Danish euro referendum|referendum]] was held on 28 September 2000, proposing that Denmark join the eurozone on 1 January 2002. While most political parties, media organisations and economic actors in Denmark campaigned in favour of adopting the euro, the referendum was rejected. Turnout was 87.6%, with 46.8% voting in favour of adopting the euro and 53.2% voting against.<ref name="Results">{{cite web |url=http://www.eu-oplysningen.dk/dkeu/dk/afstemninger/afstemning/2000/ |title=Folkeafstemning om euroen den 28. september 2000 |date=8 August 2006 |publisher=Folketinget |language=da |access-date=23 December 2008 }}</ref> Some analysts believe that the significant weakening of the euro against the US dollar preceding the referendum directly contributed to its rejection.

=== Possible second euro referendum ===
{{main|Danish European Union opt-outs referendum}}
[[File:Denmark-euro-3.jpg|thumb|Double [[Danish krone|krone]] and [[euro]] prices in [[Magasin du Nord|Magasin]] (2009)]]

On 22 November 2007, the newly re-elected Danish government declared its intention to hold a new referendum on the abolition of the four opt-outs, including the opt-out from the euro, by 2011.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/eu/story/0,,2215481,00.html |title=Danes to hold referendum on relationship with EU |date=22 November 2007 |access-date=22 November 2007 |work=The Guardian | location=London | first=Allegra | last=Stratton}}</ref> It was unclear if people would vote on each exemption separately, or if people would vote on all of them together.<ref>{{cite web |author=Dagens Huvudledare |url=http://www.dn.se/DNet/jsp/polopoly.jsp?d=573&a=718468 |title=Danmark går före |work=Dagens Nyheter |date=24 November 2007 |language=sv |access-date=23 December 2008 |archive-date=17 December 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081217164646/http://www.dn.se/DNet/jsp/polopoly.jsp?d=573 |url-status=dead }}</ref> However, the uncertainty, both in terms of the stability of the euro and the establishment of new political structures at the EU level, resulting first from the [[2008 financial crisis]] and then subsequently from the related [[euro area crisis]], led the government to postpone the referendum to after the end of its legislative term. When a [[2011 Danish parliamentary election|new government came to power in September 2011]], it decided to not hold a referendum.<ref>{{cite news|last=Brand|first=Constant|title=Denmark scraps border-control plans|url=http://www.europeanvoice.com/article/2011/october/denmark-scraps-border-control-plans/72315.aspx|access-date=18 October 2011|newspaper=European Voice|date=13 October 2011}}</ref>

As part of the [[2014 European Parliament election|European elections in 2014]], it was argued collectively by the group of [[pro-Europeanism|pro-European]] Danish parties ([[Venstre (Denmark)|Venstre]], [[Konservative Folkeparti|Konservative]], [[Social Democrats (Denmark)|Social Democrats]] and [[Radikale Venstre]]), that a euro referendum would not be held until the "development dust had settled" from the establishment of multiple initiatives in response to the [[euro area crisis]].{{citation needed|date=July 2015|reason=The noted joint political position was spoken during an election campaign debate broadcasted by DR2 in May 2014, which is not disputed as a fact. But to comply with Wikipedia Policy, we need to find and add a linkable source.}} When a [[2015 Danish parliamentary election|new Venstre-led government came to power in June 2015]], its manifesto did not include any plan for holding a referendum on euro adoption.<ref name="Government manifest 2015">{{cite web|url=http://www.venstre.dk/_Resources/Persistent/63002ee09c17ea437981728a5d7f2402e4c472d9/Regeringsgrundlag-2015.pdf|title=Regeringsgrundlag juni 2015: Sammen for Fremtiden (Government manifest June 2015: Together for the Future)|language=da|publisher=Venstre|date=27 June 2015|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150701021935/http://www.venstre.dk/_Resources/Persistent/63002ee09c17ea437981728a5d7f2402e4c472d9/Regeringsgrundlag-2015.pdf|archive-date=1 July 2015}}</ref> During the [[2022 Danish European Union opt-out referendum|referendum to abolish the defence opt-out in 2022]], the prime minister of Denmark, [[Mette Frederiksen]], promised not to hold an additional euro referendum during her tenure as prime minister.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ecfr.eu/article/denmarks-zeitenwende/|title=Denmark's Zeitenwende|date=7 June 2022|access-date=25 February 2024|publisher=[[European Council on Foreign Relations]]}}</ref> No plans for holding a euro referendum were included in the government manifest of 2022.<ref name="DanishGovernment2022">{{cite web|url=https://fm.dk/media/26729/ansvar-for-danmark_det-politiske-grundlag-for-danmarks-regering_december-2022.pdf|title=Regeringsgrundlag December 2022: Ansvar for Danmark (Government manifest December 2022: Responsibility for Denmark)|language=da|publisher=Danish Ministry of Finance|date=14 December 2022}}</ref>

There has been some speculation that the result of a Danish referendum would affect the [[Sweden and the euro|Swedish debate on the euro]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.dn.se/DNet/jsp/polopoly.jsp?d=148&a=718135 |title=Utspelet kan höja temperaturen i den iskalla svenska EU-debatten |date=22 November 2007 |author=Henrik Brors |work=Dagens Nyheter |language=sv |access-date=23 December 2008 |archive-date=17 December 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081217005951/http://www.dn.se/DNet/jsp/polopoly.jsp?d=148 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

=== Usage today ===
The euro can be used at some locations in Denmark, usually in places catering to tourists, such as museums, airports and shops with large numbers of international visitors. However, change is usually given in kroner. Double krone-euro prices are used on all ferries going between Denmark and Germany.

On 10 January 2020, the [[500 euro note]] was phased out in Denmark as part of the fight against [[money laundering]] and [[terrorism financing]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Brink |first1=Carsten |title=500-eurosedlen udfases |url=https://finansdanmark.dk/nyheder/2019/500-eurosedlen-udfases/ |website=finansdanmark.dk |publisher=[[Finance Denmark]] |access-date=15 May 2020 |language=da}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Bekendtgørelse af lov om forebyggende foranstaltninger mod hvidvask og finansiering af terrorisme (hvidvaskloven) |url=https://www.retsinformation.dk/eli/lta/2020/380#P6a |website=retsinformation.dk |access-date=15 May 2020 |language=da}}</ref> At the time, the banknote was worth 3,737 Danish kroner (DKK), more than three times the highest denomination of the domestic currency, [[Danish thousand-kroner bill|the thousand-kroner banknote]].<ref>{{cite web |title=500 EUR in DKK on 10 January 2020 |url=https://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=500+EUR+in+DKK+on+10+January+2020 |website=wolframalpha.com |publisher=[[WolframAlpha]] |access-date=15 May 2020}}</ref> The [[European Central Bank]] had stopped issuing the banknote in 2019, but was critical of the law. In an opinion published in February 2019, it was argued that it conflicted with the principle of "[[sincere cooperation]]" set out in Article IV of the [[Treaty on European Union]], and noted that no ban was planned for other high-value units of currency, such as the highest [[Banknotes of the Swiss franc|Swiss franc banknote]],<ref>{{cite web |last1=Schwartzkopff |first1=Frances |title=Denmark Ignores ECB to Ban 500-Euro Note in Dirty Money Battle |url=https://www.bloombergquint.com/onweb/denmark-ignores-ecb-to-ban-500-euro-note-in-dirty-money-battle |website=bloombergquint.com |date=4 April 2019 |publisher=[[BloombergQuint]] |access-date=15 May 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Opinion on banning the use of euro 500 denomination banknotes and on certain amendments to anti-money laundering legislation |url=https://www.ecb.europa.eu/ecb/legal/pdf/en_opinion_con-2019-05_dk_on_banning_the_use_of_euro_500_denomination_banknotes_and_on_certain_amendments_to_anti-money_.pdf |website=ecb.europa.eu |publisher=[[European Central Bank]] |access-date=15 May 2020 |date=12 February 2019}}</ref> worth more than 6,500 DKK at the time.<ref>{{cite web |title=1,000 CHF in DKK in February 2019 |url=https://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=1000+CHF+in+DKK+in+February+2019 |access-date=15 May 2020 |website=wolframalpha.com |publisher=[[WolframAlpha]]}}</ref>

== Impact of potential euro adoption ==
If Denmark were to adopt the euro, the monetary policy would be transferred from the [[Danmarks Nationalbank]] to the [[European System of Central Banks|ESCB]], limiting its ability to have an independent monetary policy. However, a study of the history of the Danish monetary policy shows that, "while Denmark does not share a single currency, its central bank has always tracked changes made by the ESCB".<ref name="Danish road to the euro">{{cite web |url=http://www.konferencja.edu.pl/ref8/pdf/en/Fic-Warszawa.pdf |title=How long is the Danish road to the euro? |date= n.d.|access-date=3 November 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111009101143/http://www.konferencja.edu.pl/ref8/pdf/en/Fic-Warszawa.pdf |archive-date=9 October 2011 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

While outside the euro, Denmark does not have any representation in the ESCB direction. Non-participation in the eurozone has been criticised by the former Prime Minister [[Anders Fogh Rasmussen]], who stated that: "De facto, Denmark participates in the euro zone but without having a seat at the table where decisions are made, and that's a political problem".<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.bloomberg.com/apps/news?pid=20601085&sid=a7HNDE8bkkUE&refer=europe | work=Bloomberg | title=Rasmussen Says He Isn't Candidate for EU Presidency (Update1) | date=31 March 2008}}</ref> The ESCB has no obligation to defend the Danish krone exchange rate, which is the responsibility of the Danmarks Nationalbank and Danish government. In a crisis, a small country's national bank can defend the exchange rate only to a limited extent.

The expected practical advantages of euro include lower transaction costs, transparency of foreign markets for Danish consumers, and possibly a lowering of interest rates.<ref name="Danish road to the euro"/>

During the [[euro area crisis]], European leaders established the [[European Financial Stability Facility]], a [[special purpose vehicle]] to maintain financial stability in the eurozone by providing financial assistance to member states in difficulty.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Chief bail-out officer |url=https://www.economist.com/finance-and-economics/2010/07/01/chief-bail-out-officer |access-date=2026-06-22 |work=The Economist |issn=0013-0613}}</ref> It has two parts, the first establishing a €60 billion stabilisation fund ([[European Financial Stabilisation Mechanism]])<ref>{{Cite web |title=Spain seeks to reassure EU leaders {{!}} European Voice |url=http://www.europeanvoice.com/article/2010/06/spain-seeks-to-reassure-eu-leaders/68293.aspx |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140107184753/http://www.europeanvoice.com/article/2010/06/spain-seeks-to-reassure-eu-leaders/68293.aspx |archive-date=2014-01-07 |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=www.europeanvoice.com |language=en}}</ref> with contributions from European countries on a [[pro-rata]] basis, regardless of their membership in the eurozone.<ref>{{Cite news | title=Debt crisis Q&A: How the EU bailout will work| url=https://www.theguardian.com/business/2010/may/10/eu-rescue-package-q-a |  work=[[The Guardian]] | date=10 May 2010 | access-date=12 May 2010 | location=London | first=Elena | last=Moya}}</ref> The second part consisted €440 billion worth [[government-backed loan]]s to improve market confidence. All eurozone economies will participate in funding this mechanism, while other EU members can choose whether to participate. Unlike Sweden and Poland, Denmark has refused to help fund this portion of the EFSF.<ref>{{cite web | title = France attacks UK over attitude to bail-out fund| url = http://euobserver.com/9/30060 | work = EUobserver | date = 11 May 2010 | access-date = 12 May 2010 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title = EU's lånepakke kan koste Danmark ni milliarder kroner | url = http://politiken.dk/politik/article968137.ece | work = Politiken | date = 10 May 2010 | access-date = 12 May 2010 | language = da | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20100513072228/http://politiken.dk/politik/article968137.ece | archive-date = 13 May 2010 | url-status=dead | df = dmy-all }}</ref>

== Public opinion ==
{{Update|section|date=November 2024}}
[[File:Euro opinion danmark.PNG|thumb|right|Euro opinion in [[Denmark]] since August 2006 by Børsen.<br />green – support of adopting the euro<br />red – against adopting the euro<br />blue – undecided{{Update inline|reason=Chart has not been updated in 10 years|date=February 2021}}]]
[[File:DKK-EUR 1999-.svg|thumb|right|DKK-EUR exchange rate since 1999]]

There have been numerous opinion polls on whether Denmark should abolish the krone and join the eurozone, with varied wordings of the questions. Polls generally favoured euro adoption from 2002 to 2010; however, they showed a rapid decline in support during the [[euro area crisis]],<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/2011-09-27/debt-crisis-pushes-danish-euro-opposition-to-record-poll-shows.html|title=Debt Crisis Pushes Danish Euro Opposition to Record, Poll Shows |publisher=[[Bloomberg News|Bloomberg]]|date=27 September 2011|access-date=22 January 2013}}</ref> reaching a low in May 2012 with 26% in favour versus 67% against, and 7% being doubtful.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://img.borsen.dk/img/cms/tuksi4/media/cmsmedia/2246_content_2_2859.pdf|title=Greens Analyseinstitut|publisher=Børsen (Greens Analyseinstitut)|date=7 May 2012|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130120193927/http://img.borsen.dk/img/cms/tuksi4/media/cmsmedia/2246_content_2_2859.pdf|archive-date=20 January 2013|df=dmy-all}}</ref> In March 2018, 29% of respondents from Denmark in a [[Eurobarometer]] opinion poll stated that they were in favour of the EMU and the euro, while 65% were against.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://europa.eu/eurobarometer/surveys/detail/2180|title=Standard Eurobarometer 89 - Spring 2018 - Factsheets Denmark|publisher=Eurobarometer|date=June 2018|access-date=18 December 2018 }}</ref> The same poll conducted in May 2024 signaled a gradual rise in support for the euro from the previous level recorded in 2012 and 2018; with 34% now in favour, 58% against, and 8% undecided.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://europa.eu/eurobarometer/surveys/detail/3216|title=Standard Eurobarometer 101 - Spring 2024 - Data annex|work=Data annex: QB3.1 What is your opinion on each of the following statements? Please tell for each statement, whether you are for it or against it. A European economic and monetary union with one single currency, the euro?|publisher=Eurobarometer|date=May 2024|access-date=22 June 2024}}</ref>

{{#chart:Public support for adoption of the euro.chart}}

== Danish autonomous territories ==
The [[Faroe Islands]] currently use the [[Faroese króna]], a localised version of the Danish krone, but legally the same currency. It is normally not accepted by shops in the mainland Denmark, or foreign exchange bureaus, however they can be exchanged 1:1 in Danish banks. [[Greenland]] uses ordinary Danish kroner, but has considered introducing its own currency, the [[Greenlandic krone]], similar Faroese króna.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.statsrevisor.dk/Samling/20061/lovforslag/L42/som_fremsat.htm |title=Parliament of Denmark, 2006–2007 session, law no. 42 |access-date=15 October 2008 |archive-date=16 May 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090516034309/http://www.statsrevisor.dk/Samling/20061/lovforslag/L42/som_fremsat.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref> Both territories continue to use Danish coins.

It remains unclear if Greenland and the Faroe Islands would adopt the euro should Denmark choose to do so. Both are parts of the [[Kingdom of Denmark]], but remain outside the EU. They usually do not take part in EU related referendums.

== Possible euro coin design ==

Before Denmark's 2000 referendum on the issue, [[Danmarks Nationalbank]] and the [[Royal Mint of Denmark|Royal Mint]] were asked by the Ministry of Economics to propose possible designs for the future Danish euro coins. The suggested design was based on the designs of the Danish 10- and 20-krone coins, with Queen [[Margrethe II]] on the front, and the 25- and 50-øre coins, switching their back motif (a crown) to the front of the euro coins.<ref>{{Cite web |date=21 December 2014 |title=Illustration af danske euromønter / EU-Oplysningen |url=http://www.eu-oplysningen.dk/emner/euro/Afstemning/DKmoenter/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141221210908/http://www.eu-oplysningen.dk/emner/euro/Afstemning/DKmoenter/ |archive-date=21 December 2014}}</ref> However, Denmark did not adopt the euro during the reign of Margrethe II, so an updated design, revolving around her son King [[Frederik X]], would be possible, should Denmark adopt the euro during his reign.
