The '''economy of Singapore''' is a [[Developed country|highly developed]] [[mixed economy|mixed]] [[market economy]] with [[dirigiste]] characteristics.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |url= https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/singapore/ |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210109141540/https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/singapore |url-status= dead |archive-date= 9 January 2021 |title= The World Factbook |date= 6 August 2012 |author= Central Intelligence Agency |publisher= cia.gov |access-date= 13 August 2012}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url= http://www.mti.gov.sg/MTIInsights/Pages/Free%20Market%20System.aspx|title= Free Market System|author= Ministry of Trade and Industry Singapore|publisher= mti.gov.sg|access-date= 11 December 2018|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20151007040335/https://www.mti.gov.sg/MTIInsights/Pages/Free%20Market%20System.aspx|archive-date= 7 October 2015}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Huff |first=W.G. |date=1995-12-01 |title=What is the Singapore model of economic development? |journal=Cambridge Journal of Economics |doi=10.1093/oxfordjournals.cje.a035339 |issn=1464-3545}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Nolan |first=Peter |date=1990 |title=Assessing economic growth in the Asian NICs |url=http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/00472339080000031 |journal=Journal of Contemporary Asia |language=en |volume=20 |issue=1 |pages=41–63 |doi=10.1080/00472339080000031 |issn=0047-2336|url-access=subscription}}</ref> [[Singapore]]'s economy has been consistently ranked as the most open, competitive and pro-business in the world.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://members.weforum.org/pdf/GETR10/GETR10-Overall-Rankings.pdf|title=Global Enabling Trade Report|author=World Economic Forum|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120729221945/https://members.weforum.org/pdf/GETR10/GETR10-Overall-Rankings.pdf|archive-date=29 July 2012}}</ref> It is also perceived as the [[Corruption in Singapore|3rd least corrupt]] in the world.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.transparency.org/files/content/pages/CPI_2018_Executive_Summary_EN.pdf |title= Corruption Perceptions Index 2018 Executive Summary p. 8 |publisher= [[Transparency International]] |website= transparency.org |access-date= 27 April 2019 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20190421141719/https://www.transparency.org/files/content/pages/CPI_2018_Executive_Summary_EN.pdf |archive-date= 21 April 2019 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url= http://www.doingbusiness.org/reports/global-reports/doing-business-2012|title= World Bank Doing Business Report 2012|publisher= World Bank|access-date= 27 May 2013|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20130524040825/http://doingbusiness.org/reports/global-reports/doing-business-2012|archive-date= 24 May 2013|url-status= live}}</ref> Singapore has low [[tax rate|tax-rate]]s<ref>{{cite web|title= Country Rankings|url= http://www.heritage.org/index/Ranking.aspx|work= 2013 Index of Economic Freedom|publisher= The Heritage Foundation|access-date= 18 April 2013|year= 2013|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20090720010300/http://www.heritage.org/index/ranking.aspx|archive-date= 20 July 2009|url-status= unfit}}</ref> and the [[List of countries by GDP (PPP) per capita|highest per-capita GDP]] in the world in terms of purchasing power parity (PPP). The [[Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation]] (APEC) is headquartered in Singapore.

Alongside the [[business]]-friendly reputation for global and local [[Privately held company|privately held companies]] and [[Public company|public companies]], various national [[state-owned enterprise]]s play a role in Singapore's economy.  The [[sovereign wealth fund]] [[Temasek Holdings]] holds majority stakes in several of the nation's largest [[:wikt:bellwether|bellwether]] companies, such as [[Singapore Airlines]], [[Singtel]], [[ST Engineering]] and [[Mediacorp]].  With regard to [[foreign direct investment]] (FDI), the Singaporean economy is a major [[List of countries by FDI abroad|FDI outflow-financier]] in the world.  In addition, throughout its history, Singapore has benefited from the [[List of countries by received FDI|large inward flows of FDI]] from global [[investor]]s, [[financial institution]]s and [[multinational corporation]]s (MNCs) due to its attractive investment climate along with a stable political environment throughout its modern years.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.unctad-docs.org/files/UNCTAD-WIR2012-Chapter-I-en.pdf |title=World Investment Report, Chapter 1: Global Investment Trends |access-date=1 June 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121021182524/http://www.unctad-docs.org/files/UNCTAD-WIR2012-Chapter-I-en.pdf |archive-date=21 October 2012 |website=unctad-docs.org |publisher=United Nations Conference on Trade and Development}}</ref>

== Overview ==
Singapore relies on an extended concept of intermediary trade to [[entrepôt]] trade,<ref>{{cite web |author=Clare Lockhart |date=31 January 2014 |title=Singapore: The Evolution of an Entrepôt |url=https://effectivestates.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/Singapore-The-Evolution-of-an-Entrepot.pdf |access-date=30 April 2022 |publisher=Institute for State Effectiveness}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title=Singapore: Its Growth as an Entrepot Port, 1819-1941* |year=1978 |publisher=Cambridge University Press|doi=10.1017/S002246340000953X |last1=Ken |first1=Wong Lin |journal=Journal of Southeast Asian Studies |volume=9 |pages=50–84 |s2cid=163088278 |doi-access=free}}</ref> by purchasing raw goods and refining them for re-export in order to sustain its high levels of [[export-oriented industrialization]], such as in the [[wafer fabrication|wafer-fabrication]] industry and in [[oil refining]].  Singapore has a strategic port which makes it more competitive than many of its neighbours in carrying out such entrepôt activities. Singapore's [[trade-to-GDP ratio]] is among the highest in the world, as of 2020 the ratio was 320%.<ref>{{cite web |title=WTO Trade Policy Review: Singapore |url=http://www.intracen.org/BB-2012-08-27-WTO-Trade-Policy-Review-Singapore |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140715013128/http://www.intracen.org/BB-2012-08-27-WTO-Trade-Policy-Review-Singapore/ |archive-date=15 July 2014 |access-date=19 June 2013 |publisher=WTO}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Trade (% of GDP) |url=http://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NE.TRD.GNFS.ZS?year_high_desc=true |publisher=World Bank}}</ref> The [[Port of Singapore]] is the [[List of world's busiest ports by cargo tonnage|sixth-busiest]] in the world by cargo tonnage and is the busiest transshipment port in the world.<ref>{{Cite web |last=madhukar |date=2022-01-16 |title=Singapore remains the world's busiest transshipment port - Maritime Gateway |url=https://www.maritimegateway.com/singapore-remains-the-worlds-busiest-transshipment-port/ |access-date=2022-05-18 |website=maritimegateway.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

Singapore is also a regional, continental, and global hub for the management and operations of various [[MNCs]] because of its location in proximity of other [[Asia-Pacific]] markets, along with its connectivity and [[infrastructure]] (including [[airline hub]]s, [[Port|maritime ports]], Gigabit [[fiber-optic communication]]s, [[Road transport#Modern roads|road transport]] and [[public transport]]) and its immigration policies in encouraging [[Human capital|global talent]]. In addition, Singapore is an international destination for various types of [[tourism]] ([[Business tourism]], [[MICE (Meetings, Incentives, Conferences, Exhibitions) tourism]], [[Medical tourism]], [[Urban tourism]]).

Singapore's economy is often referred to as a "miracle" due to its rapid transformation from a developing country to a developed, high-income economy in a relatively short period of time. This transformation took place in the second half of the 20th century under the leadership of Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew and his government.<ref>{{Cite journal |title=What is the Singapore model of economic development? |url=https://academic.oup.com/cje/article/19/6/735/1688941/What-is-the-Singapore-model-of-economic |access-date=2023-01-12 |journal=Cambridge Journal of Economics |year=1995 |doi=10.1093/oxfordjournals.cje.a035339|url-access=subscription}}</ref> One of the key factors contributing to Singapore's economic miracle was its strategic location, which made it an ideal hub for international trade and commerce.<ref>{{Cite book|editor-last=Lim |editor-first=Linda Y. C. |title=Singapore's Economic Development: Retrospection And Reflections |isbn=978-9-81472345-9 |url=https://www.vitalsource.com/products/singapore-39-s-economic-development-retrospection-lim-linda-y-c-v9789814723473 |access-date=2023-01-12 |language=en |publisher=World Scientific |year=2016}}</ref>

The country's main exports include [[electronics]], [[chemical]]s and [[Service (economics)|services]]. Singapore is the regional hub for [[wealth management]].<ref>{{cite journal|last= Aun Long|first= Jek|author2= Danny Tan|title= The growth of the private wealth management industry in Singapore and Hong Kong|journal= Capital Markets Law Journal|date= June 2010|volume= 6|issue= 1|pages= 104–126|doi= 10.1093/cmlj/kmq022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title= Wealth Management|url= https://www.ubs.com/sg/en/wealth_management.html|work= UBS|access-date= 18 April 2013|date= 3 April 2013|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20130511023641/http://www.ubs.com/sg/en/wealth_management.html|archive-date= 11 May 2013|url-status= live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title= Wealth management prospers in Singapore|url= https://www.nytimes.com/2008/12/14/business/worldbusiness/14iht-singapore.1.18654227.html?_r=0|access-date= 18 April 2013|newspaper= The New York Times|date= 14 November 2008|author= Neil Chatterjee|author2= John O'Donnell|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20141215232017/http://www.nytimes.com/2008/12/14/business/worldbusiness/14iht-singapore.1.18654227.html?_r=0|archive-date= 15 December 2014|url-status= live}}</ref> Water is [[Water supply and sanitation in Singapore|scarce in Singapore]] and a sizeable percentage of water is [[Water conflicts between Malaysia and Singapore|imported from Malaysia]].<ref>{{cite news|title= Singapore water makes global waves|url= https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/business/7371463.stm|access-date= 18 April 2013|newspaper= BBC News|date= 6 May 2008|author= Jorn Madslien|author-link= Jorn Madslien|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20130928074837/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/business/7371463.stm|archive-date= 28 September 2013|url-status= live}}</ref>

[[Small and medium-sized enterprises]] (SMEs) are the backbone of Singapore's economic landscape. In 2022 SMEs contributed 48% (S$284&nbsp;bil) of Singapore's total enterprise nominal value-added and employed 71% of Singapore's total workforce of 3.63&nbsp;million.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.singstat.gov.sg/modules/infographics/economy#enterprise|title=Singapore Economy Infographic|website=Base}}</ref>

Singapore has limited arable land, meaning that Singapore is heavily reliant on [[agrotechnology]] parks (particularly vertical [[Hydroponics|hydroponic]] farms) for [[Agriculture in Singapore|agricultural production]].<ref>{{cite web|title= Part IV Country Papers (Contd.)|url= http://www.fao.org/docrep/004/AC153E/AC153E13.htm|work= FAO Corporate Document Repository|publisher= Agriculture and Consumer Protection|access-date= 18 April 2013|author= Shim Kim Fah|year= 1990|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20130605143813/http://www.fao.org/docrep/004/AC153E/AC153E13.htm|archive-date= 5 June 2013|url-status= live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title= Agrotechnology Parks|url= http://www.ava.gov.sg/AgricultureFisheriesSector/FarmingInSingapore/AgroTechParks/|work= Agri-Food & Veterinary Authority of Singapore|publisher= Government of Singapore|access-date= 18 April 2013|date= 14 November 2012|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20130122090304/http://www.ava.gov.sg/AgricultureFisheriesSector/FarmingInSingapore/AgroTechParks|archive-date= 22 January 2013}}</ref> As a result, Singapore imports 90% of its food supply and has a wide variety of supplier countries in order to achieve its [[food security]]; Singapore is ranked as among the most food secure in the world.<ref>{{Cite web |title=SFA {{!}} The Food We Eat |url=https://www.sfa.gov.sg/food-farming/singapore-food-supply/the-food-we-eat |access-date=2022-05-18 |website=sfa.gov.sg |archive-date=18 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220518172658/https://www.sfa.gov.sg/food-farming/singapore-food-supply/the-food-we-eat }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Singapore tops 2019 Global Food Security Index |url=https://www.sfa.gov.sg/food-for-thought/article/detail/singapore-tops-2019-global-food-security-index |access-date=2022-05-18 |website=[[Singapore Food Agency]] |language=en}}</ref>

Apart from its strategic location at the cross-roads of [[trade]] between [[Eastern world|the East]] and [[Western world|the West]], Singapore has little to no [[natural resource]]s, hence [[human resources]] is a pivotal issue for the health of the Singaporean economy; the services and manufacturing sectors of the economy are heavily reliant on a highly-[[Education|educated]] and highly-[[skill]]ed '[[Professional]], [[Management|Managerial]], [[Business executive|Executive]] and [[Technician|Technical]]' (PMET) [[workforce]] composed of residents and [[expatriate]]s.<ref>{{cite web|title= Rapid Growth in Singapore's Immigrant Population Brings Policy Challenges|url= http://www.migrationinformation.org/feature/print.cfm?ID=887|work= Migration Policy Institute|access-date= 18 April 2013|author= Brenda S.A. Yeoh|author2= Weiqiang Lin|date= April 2012|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20130512234313/http://www.migrationinformation.org/feature/print.cfm?ID=887|archive-date= 12 May 2013|url-status= live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Wei |first=Aw Cheng |date=2020-02-19 |title=3 in 4 PMET jobs in growth sectors filled by Singaporeans, PRs |url=https://tnp.straitstimes.com/news/singapore/3-4-pmet-jobs-growth-sectors-filled-singaporeans-prs |access-date=2022-05-18 |website=The New Paper |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Ho |first=Grace |date=2021-07-23 |title=Professionalise all jobs, do away with PMET classification: MAS chief|work=The Straits Times |url=https://www.straitstimes.com/singapore/politics/professionalise-all-jobs-do-away-with-pmet-classification-mas-chief |access-date=2022-05-18}}</ref> The economy of Singapore ranked 2nd overall in the Scientific American Biotechnology ranking in 2014,<ref>{{cite web|url= http://www.saworldview.com/scorecard/2014-scientific-american-worldview-overall-scores/ |title= 2014 Scientific American Worldview Overall Scores: WorldVIEW |access-date= 25 March 2015 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20140713110810/http://www.saworldview.com/scorecard/2014-scientific-american-worldview-overall-scores/ |archive-date= 13 July 2014 }}</ref> with the featuring of [[Biopolis]].

To preserve its international standing and to further its economic [[prosperity]] in the 21st century, Singapore has taken measures to promote [[innovation]], to encourage [[entrepreneurship]] and to [[Retraining|retrain]] its [[workforce]].<ref>{{cite web |year=2015 |title=Singapore Ranked Best for Business |url=http://www.investasian.com/2014/11/21/singapore-ranked-best-business/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150623142733/http://www.investasian.com/2014/11/21/singapore-ranked-best-business/ |archive-date=23 June 2015 |access-date=27 May 2015 |work=InvestAsian }}</ref> The [[Ministry of Manpower (Singapore)|Ministry of Manpower]] (MoM) has the prime responsibility for setting, adjusting, and enforcing [[immigration]] rules for [[foreign worker]]s, in order to achieve the dual mandate of maximum employment of the local resident population and maximum economic growth for the nation. Approximately 29% of the total population within Singapore are non-resident foreigners, including 255,800 foreign [[domestic worker]]s (FDWs) who operate in Singapore.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Big Read in short: S'pore families' dependence on maids and the issues that need addressing |url=https://www.todayonline.com/big-read/big-read-short-spore-families-dependence-maids-and-issues-need-addressing |access-date=2022-05-18 |website=TODAY |language=en}}</ref>

== History ==
{{Main|History of Singapore}}

[[File:GDP per capita development of Singapore.jpg|thumb|right|Historical GDP per capita development]]

===British colonization===
In 1819, [[Stamford Raffles]], at the time [[Lieutenant-Governor of Bencoolen]], established a trading post in Singapore.<ref name="Lim 2015">{{Cite journal|last=Lim|first=Linda Y. C.|date=August 2015|title=Fifty Years of Development in the Singapore Economy: An Introductory Review|journal=The Singapore Economic Review|volume=60|issue=3|page=1502002|doi=10.1142/S0217590815020026|issn=0217-5908}}</ref> Raffles had been searching for a new settlement that could be used as an outpost of the British Empire. He left Calcutta and set out to explore much of South-East Asia. At the time, the Dutch Empire and British Empire were close economic rivals. Colonization enabled these empires to gain control of the vast resources of militarily weaker and economically less prosperous [[nations]]. Raffles was looking for a new settlement that could replace Malacca as a key economic advantage over the Dutch Empire. The former had been handed over to the Dutch under the [[Treaty of Vienna (1815)|Treaty of Vienna of 1815]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Stamford Raffles's career and contributions to Singapore {{!}} Infopedia|url=https://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/infopedia/articles/SIP_715_2004-12-15.html|access-date=27 March 2021|website=eresources.nlb.gov.sg}}</ref> Raffles found Singapore to be a perfect location, sitting just off the edge of the Straits of Malacca, nowadays one of the most important shipping lanes in the world. As well, the territory had key economic resources which would benefit the British. There was abundant timber and fresh water, and a natural deep water harbor which would be beneficial for the British fleet. He arrived on an island at the mouth of the Singapore River, where there was a small Malay settlement. At the time  accompanied by William Farquhar, Raffles met with [[Temenggong]] (essentially, Chief of Security, for the settlement) [[Temenggong Abdul Rahman|Abdul Rahman]] to negotiate the right to establish a trading post on the island, under the British Empire. The island was ruled nominally from [[Johor Sultanate|Johar]] on the peninsula by [[Tengku]] (essentially, Prince) [[Abdul Rahman Muazzam Shah of Johor|Rahman, Sultan of Johor]], who was heavily influenced by the Dutch and the [[Bugis]]. However, the Sultanate was weakened by factional division so that Temenggong Abdul Rahman and his officials were more loyal to Rahman's elder brother Tengku [[Hussein Shah of Johor|Hussein]] (or Tengku Long) who was living in exile in "Riau" (likely [[Riau Archipelago|the Riau Archipelago]]). With the Temenggong's help, Raffles managed to smuggle Hussein back to Singapore. He offered to recognize Hussein as the rightful Sultan of Johor and provide him with a yearly [[stipend]]; in return, Hussein would grant the British the right to establish a trading post on Singapore.{{citation needed|date=August 2021}} On 6 February 1819 Raffles succeeded in having the territory formally incorporated into the British Empire as the aforementioned trading post.{{citation needed|date=August 2021}} Much of the settlement's rapid economic growth thereafter can be credited to its natural suitability as a seaport hub.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-15971013|title=Singapore profile|date=10 May 2018|access-date=17 March 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190407044946/https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-15971013|archive-date=7 April 2019|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Trade expansion===
On 17 November 1869, the [[Suez Canal]] opened, connecting the [[Mediterranean Sea]] to the [[Red Sea]]. This allowed for a decrease in travel time, which resulted in a rise in trade volume. The nation saw a $32&nbsp;million rise just a year after its opening.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/history/events/15fcae20-2e3d-4eec-b5ab-2384f1aac2b9|title=Opening of the Suez Canal – Singapore History|website=eresources.nlb.gov.sg|access-date=17 March 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181017163842/http://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/history/events/15fcae20-2e3d-4eec-b5ab-2384f1aac2b9|archive-date=17 October 2018|url-status=live}}</ref>

Trade volume reached $105&nbsp;million [[Straits dollar]]s in 1879,<ref>{{cite book|last1=Huang|first1=Flora|last2=Yeung|first2=Horace|url=https://play.google.com/store/books/details?id=EVVSDwAAQBAJ|title=Institutions and Economic Growth in Asia: The Case of Mainland China, Hong Kong, Singapore and Malaysia|publisher=Routledge|year=2018|isbn=978-1-315-51611-0}}</ref> during which entrepot trade was the main source of income and trade alone accounted for more than one-third of GDP.{{citation needed|date=June 2021}}

=== Independence ===
In the 1950s, the region saw social unrest which resulted in colonial powers deciding to relinquish some decision making. With spurs of race riots the colonial powers sought to empower and establish a formidable local government. With most of the unrest resulting from high unemployment, the local government was directed to solve this issue.<ref name="Lim 2015" /> The [[Economic Development Board]] was formed to empower the Singapore government in establishing, developing, and financing industrial undertakings.<ref>{{cite news|date=14 January 1957|title=Aiding Industry|newspaper=[[The Straits Times]]|url=https://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/Digitised/Article/straitstimes19570114-1.2.70}}</ref>

In 1955, a Singapore local legislative Assembly with 25 out of 35 members elected was formed.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Chung|first=Ong Chit|date=1975|title=The 1959 Singapore General Election|journal=Journal of Southeast Asian Studies|volume=6|issue=1|pages=61–86|issn=0022-4634|jstor=20070113|doi=10.1017/S0022463400017112|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Upon independence from Malaysia in 1965, Singapore faced a small domestic market, and high levels of unemployment and poverty. 70 percent of Singapore's households lived in badly overcrowded conditions, and a third of its people squatted in slums on the city fringes. Unemployment averaged 14 percent, GDP per capita was US$516, and half of the population was illiterate.{{Citation needed|date=July 2023}}

===Industrialisation boom and change===
After [[Lee Kuan Yew]] was elected, he oversaw significant economic reforms to the country. Structural change and machinery propelled the economy during his tenure. Singapore was a small and densely populated nation, with very few natural resources and little space to grow outwards. Recognizing this, Lee identified that the key advantage that Singapore held was its human capital, and its ability to provide highly educated citizens capable of competing in global industry and trade. On 1 August 1961, the Singapore Government established the [[Economic Development Board]] to spearhead an investment drive, and make Singapore an attractive destination for foreign investment.<ref name="Huff 1995">{{cite journal|title=What is the Singapore model of economic development?|first=W. G.|last=Huff|url=https://academic.oup.com/cje/article-abstract/19/6/735/1688941|journal=Cambridge Journal of Economics|volume=19|issue=6|date=December 1995|pages=735–759|doi=10.1093/oxfordjournals.cje.a035339|jstor=23600207|s2cid=154620995|issn=0309-166X|publisher=Oxford University Press|url-access=subscription}}</ref> FDI inflows increased greatly over the following decades, and by 2001 foreign companies accounted for 75% of manufactured output and 85% of manufactured exports. Meanwhile, Singapore's savings and investment rates rose among the highest levels in the world, while household consumption and wage shares of GDP fell among the lowest.<ref>{{cite book|last=Sugimoto|first=Ichiro|title=Economic Growth of Singapore in the Twentieth Century|year=2011|isbn=978-981-4317-91-7|page=299|publisher=World Scientific}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=The familiar pattern of Chinese consumption growth|url=http://www.treasury.gov.au/PublicationsAndMedia/Publications/2012/Economic-Roundup-Issue-4/HTML/article3|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131203122237/http://www.treasury.gov.au/PublicationsAndMedia/Publications/2012/Economic-Roundup-Issue-4/HTML/article3|archive-date=3 December 2013|access-date=4 March 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Wage share of GDP has risen over the decades: Minister for Trade and Industry|url=http://www.straitstimes.com/microsites/parliament/story/wage-share-gdp-has-risen-over-the-decades-minister-trade-and-industry-20|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150217081105/http://www.straitstimes.com/microsites/parliament/story/wage-share-gdp-has-risen-over-the-decades-minister-trade-and-industry-20|archive-date=17 February 2015|access-date=4 March 2015}}</ref> The beginning of Lee's tenure was marked with success and from 1965 to 1973, annual growth of real GDP was 12.7%. He directed spending to repair and improve infrastructure. This effort spurred economic productivity and put in place the foundations needed to build up basic industry. As of 2019, Singapore's infrastructure is ranked the best in terms of quality, with a score of 95.4 out of 100.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Quality of infrastructure: countries with best infrastructure 2019|url=https://www.statista.com/statistics/264753/ranking-of-countries-according-to-the-general-quality-of-infrastructure/|access-date=27 March 2021|website=Statista|language=en}}</ref> The period from 1973 to 1979 marked a struggle for Singapore as they pivoted away from basic infrastructure spending and moved towards more sustainable economic progress. The 1973 oil crisis raised government awareness of issues such as economic concentration. It forced the government to hold a new forum to discuss ways of adapting the country's economy to economic change. GDP growth during this time was slightly lower than the preceding years, at 8.5% annually. However, unemployment was virtually 0%, and most of the population had experienced great strides in productivity.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Commanding Heights: Singapore Economic {{!}} on PBS|url=https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/commandingheights/lo/countries/sg/sg_economic.html|access-date=27 March 2021|website=pbs.org}}</ref> The government highlighted a focus in technology and education to be the new wave of economic gain.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.singaporeexpats.com/about-singapore/brief-history.htm|title=Brief History of Singapore, Singapore Growth & Economy • About Singapore|website=singaporeexpats.com|access-date=10 March 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190410055552/https://www.singaporeexpats.com/about-singapore/brief-history.htm|archive-date=10 April 2019}}</ref> In addition, they identified financial services as a key area in which Singapore could diversify and attract new growth. During this time, the government invested heavily in its budding financial services industry. It managed to minimize inflation and provide workers with the proper equipment and machinery to sustain growth.

===Recent history===
====Growth in the service sector====
As a result of this investment drive, Singapore's capital stock increased 33 times by 1992, and achieved a tenfold increase in the capital-labour ratio.<ref>{{cite book |last=Bercuson |first=Kenneth |title=Singapore: a Case Study in Rapid Development |year=1995 |isbn=978-1-55775-463-9 |page=5|publisher=International Monetary Fund}}</ref> Living standards steadily rose, with more families moving from a lower-income status to middle-income security with increased household incomes.

Under Lee, Singapore had both low inflation and unemployment. However, much unlike the economic policies of Greece and the rest of Europe, Singapore followed a policy of individualising the social safety net. This led to a higher than average savings rate.<ref>Driven by Growth: Political Change in the Asia-Pacific Region edited by James W. Morley</ref>

In the late 1980s, Singapore's export-driven economic model required adjustment for further development.<ref name=":8">{{Cite book |last=Lin |first=Zhongjie |title=Constructing Utopias: China's New Town Movement in the 21st Century |date=2025 |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |isbn=978-0-19-779330-5 |location=New York, NY}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=79}} The 1990s emergence of efficient manufacturing firms in southeast Asia challenged the nation with such a small labor force and land restrictions. Friedrich noted how it would be "unlikely to expand beyond the current 25% share of the economy," when regarding manufacturing firms.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Wu|first=Friedrich|date=October 1991|title=The ASEAN Economies in the 1990s and Singapore's Regional Role|journal=California Management Review|volume=34|issue=1|pages=103–114|doi=10.2307/41166686|issn=0008-1256|jstor=41166686|s2cid=155079093}}</ref> Despite struggling in the manufacturing sector Singapore thrived in global finance, trading, and was an industrial hub for international trade.<ref>{{Cite web|last1=Zarroli |first1=Jim |url=https://www.npr.org/2015/03/29/395811510/how-singapore-became-one-of-the-richest-places-on-earth|title=How Singapore Became One Of The Richest Places On Earth|website=NPR.org|date=29 March 2015 |access-date=10 March 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181203083837/https://www.npr.org/2015/03/29/395811510/how-singapore-became-one-of-the-richest-places-on-earth|archive-date=3 December 2018|url-status=live}}</ref> It positioned itself as a supplier of secondary factors, including expertise in management and industrial infrastructure, and emphasized a regionalization strategy through which it would invest in other Asian countries.<ref name=":8" />{{Reference page|page=79}} Singaporean investment in China was a particularly important element of this strategy.<ref name=":8" />{{Reference page|pages=79-80}} To advance its regionalization strategy, Singapore began its Regional Industrial Parks Program to boost Singapore's domestic economy through profits from foreign industrial parks modeled on Singapore's [[Jurong Industrial Estate]] and also to build diplomatic ties in the host countries.<ref name=":8" />{{Reference page|page=80}}

Singapore's economic strategy produced real growth averaging 8.0% from 1960 to 1999. Since the nation's independence in 1965, Singapore's GDP has amassed an average of a 9.5% increase.<ref name="Chen Shao 2017">{{Cite journal|last1=Chen|first1=Xiaoping|last2=Shao|first2=Yuchen|date=11 September 2017|title=Trade policies for a small open economy: The case of Singapore|journal=The World Economy|volume=40|issue=11|doi=10.1111/twec.12555|s2cid=158182047|issn=0378-5920|pages=2500–2511|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/twec.12555|url-access=subscription}}</ref> The economy picked up in 1999 under [[Goh Chok Tong]], the Prime Minister of Singapore, after the regional financial crisis, with a growth rate of 5.4%, followed by 9.9% for 2000. However, the economic slowdown in the United States, Japan and the [[European Union]], as well as the worldwide electronics slump, had reduced the estimated economic growth in 2001 to a negative 2.0%.

The economy expanded by 2.2% the following year, and by 1.1% in 2003 when Singapore was affected by the [[SARS]] outbreak. Subsequently, a major turnaround occurred in 2004 allowed it to make a significant recovery of 8.3% growth in Singapore, although the actual growth fell short of the target growth for the year more than half with only 2.5%. In 2005, economic growth was 6.4%; and in 2006, 7.9%.

It was apparent that Singapore would also struggle due to the [[2008 financial crisis]] given its status as a financial services hub. Some market commentators doubted the economy's ability to cope with the effects of the crisis. In the end the economy grew in 2009 by 3.1% and in 2010, the nation saw a 15.2% growth rate.<ref name="Chen Shao 2017" /><ref>{{Cite news|last=Subler|first=Jason|date=2 January 2009|title=Factories slash output, jobs around world|language=en|work=Reuters|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-financial-idUSTRE4B70ME20090102|access-date=20 September 2020}}</ref>

As of 8 June 2013, Singapore's unemployment rate is around 1.9% and the country's economy has a lowered growth rate, with a rate of 1.8% on a quarter-by-quarter basis—compared to 14.8% in 2010.

2015 and 2016 saw a downturn for the nation as GDP growth shrunk to just 2 percent. Despite growth diminishing, the nation has yet to post negative growth rates which are a positive sign. During the same period of diminishing economic growth, unemployment and inflation have also decreased.<ref name="Chen Shao 2017" />

As of 2017 Singapore's GDP reached $323.907&nbsp;billion.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NY.GDP.MKTP.CD?locations=SG|title=GDP (current US$) {{!}} Data|website=data.worldbank.org|access-date=2 May 2019}}</ref>

Singapore is expected to experience an economic slowdown in 2019, with GDP growth slowing to 1.9% from 3.1% in 2018, due to tariff hikes from the United States and China.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.straitstimes.com/business/economy/singapore-to-see-sharpest-slowdown-in-se-asia-this-year-with-19-gdp-growth-icaew|title=Singapore to see sharpest slowdown in South-east Asia this year with 1.9% GDP growth: Report|work=The Straits Times|date=4 June 2019|access-date=4 June 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190605143351/https://www.straitstimes.com/business/economy/singapore-to-see-sharpest-slowdown-in-se-asia-this-year-with-19-gdp-growth-icaew|archive-date=5 June 2019|url-status=live}}</ref>

During the initial months of the [[COVID-19 pandemic]], on 26 March 2020, Singapore's Ministry of Trade and Industry said it believed that the economy would contract by between 1% and 4% in 2020. This was after the economy shrank 2.2% in the first quarter of 2020 from the same quarter in 2019.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2020/03/26/coronavirus-singapore-releases-first-quarter-gdp-advance-estimates.html|title=Singapore expects its economy to shrink in 2020 due to the coronavirus pandemic|last=Lee|first=Yen Nee|date=26 March 2020|website=CNBC|language=en|access-date=26 March 2020}}</ref> On 26 May, MTI said that it was revising down its expectation for the Singapore economy in 2020 to shrink by 4% to 7%.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Subhani|first=Ovais|date=26 May 2020|title=S'pore heads for deeper recession: 2020 growth forecast cut to between −7 and −4% on Covid-19 impact|url=https://www.straitstimes.com/business/economy/spore-to-sink-into-deeper-recession-than-expected-2020-growth-forecast-cut-to|access-date=26 May 2020|website=The Straits Times}}</ref> Economists had to downgrade their numbers from previously, and some suggested that the economic recovery could take some time.<ref>{{Cite web|date=23 April 2020|title=Citi: Singapore economy set to shrink by 8.5% this year|url=https://www.straitstimes.com/business/economy/citi-spore-economy-set-to-shrink-by-85-this-year|access-date=15 September 2020|website=The Straits Times}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Heng|first=Janice|date=14 July 2020|title=Quick takes: Despite Singapore's Q2 entry into recession, MAS may keep policy unchanged|url=https://www.businesstimes.com.sg/government-economy/quick-takes-despite-singapores-q2-entry-into-recession-mas-may-keep-policy|access-date=11 December 2020|website=The Business Times|language=en}}</ref> In response to the economic pressure, Moody's temporarily downgraded the Singapore banking sector that year from "stable" outlook to a "negative" outlook.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Moody's cuts outlook for Singapore banks on COVID-19 fallout|url=https://www.channelnewsasia.com/news/business/coronavirus-covid-19-banks-uob-ocbc-dbs-moodys-12602064|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200404023853/https://www.channelnewsasia.com/news/business/coronavirus-covid-19-banks-uob-ocbc-dbs-moodys-12602064|archive-date=4 April 2020|access-date=2 April 2020|website=CNA|language=en}}</ref>

It was estimated by the economist Chua Hak Bin, the [[2020–21 Singapore circuit breaker measures|Singapore "circuit breaker" measures]] in response to the pandemic, beginning on 7 April could impact the economy to the tune of S$10&nbsp;billion.<ref>{{Cite news|last1=Vishnoi|first1=Abhishek|title=Singapore Partial Lockdown to Cost Economy S$10 Billion|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2020-04-09/singapore-s-partial-lockdown-seen-costing-economy-s-20-billion?srnd=markets-vp|access-date=9 April 2020|newspaper=Bloomberg.com|date=9 April 2020}}</ref> With the lockdown imposed on construction workers, there were concerns that there could be delays in construction projects of up to six months.<ref>{{Cite web|title=COVID-19: Construction projects could be delayed months, as contractors fear manpower crunch when clearing backlog|url=https://www.channelnewsasia.com/news/singapore/covid-19-construction-projects-delay-manpower-crunch-backlog-12673450|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200426070348/https://www.channelnewsasia.com/news/singapore/covid-19-construction-projects-delay-manpower-crunch-backlog-12673450|archive-date=26 April 2020|access-date=26 April 2020|website=CNA|language=en}}</ref> Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry [[Chee Hong Tat]] announced that some 3,800 companies had closed in April 2020, only slightly higher than the 3,700 reported on average for the same month in the past 5 years, though he warned that this would likely rise in the following months. Despite this only small increase in companies shutting down, the number of companies starting up had declined by about a third from the average April since 2015.<ref>{{Cite web|title=About 3,800 companies closed down in April; expect uptick in coming months: Chee Hong Tat|url=https://www.channelnewsasia.com/news/business/3800-business-closures-april-uptick-ahead-covid19-coronavirus-12802912|access-date=6 June 2020|website=CNA|language=en|archive-date=24 November 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201124130247/https://www.channelnewsasia.com/news/business/3800-business-closures-april-uptick-ahead-covid19-coronavirus-12802912}}</ref>

==State enterprise and investment==
[[File:Singapore SOE percent of GDP.png|right|thumb|400px|Ratio of credit to Singapore's State Owned Enterprises from domestic banks to the country's GDP]]
The public sector is used both as an investor and as a catalyst for economic development and innovation. The government of Singapore has two sovereign wealth funds, [[Temasek Holdings]] and [[GIC Private Limited]], which are used to manage the country's [[Reserves of the Government of Singapore|reserves]].<ref name="MOF res">{{cite web |url=http://app.mof.gov.sg/reserves_sectionone.aspx |title=What {{sic|hide=y|comprises}} the reserves and who manages them? |publisher=Singapore Ministry of Finance |access-date=22 April 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714221433/http://app.mof.gov.sg/reserves_sectionone.aspx |archive-date=14 July 2014 }}</ref> Initially the state's role was oriented more toward managing industries for economic development, but in recent decades the objectives of Singapore's sovereign wealth funds have shifted to a commercial basis.<ref name="Bureau of Economic and Business Affairs">{{cite web |url=https://2009-2017.state.gov/e/eb/rls/othr/ics/2012/191233.htm |title=2012 Investment Climate Statement&nbsp;– Singapore |author= |date=June 2012 |publisher=U.S. Department of State (Bureau of Economic and Business Affairs) |website=2009-2017.state.gov |access-date=10 March 2014}}</ref>

Government-linked corporations play a substantial role in Singapore's domestic economy. As of November 2011, the top six Singapore-listed GLCs accounted for about 17 percent of total capitalization of the Singapore Exchange (SGX). These fully and partially state-owned enterprises operate on a commercial basis and are granted no competitive advantage over privately owned enterprises. State ownership is prominent in strategic sectors of the economy, including telecommunications, media, public transportation, defence, port, airport operations as well as banking, shipping, airline, infrastructure and real estate.<ref name="Bureau of Economic and Business Affairs" />

As of 2014, Temasek holds S$69&nbsp;billion of assets in Singapore, accounting for 7% of the total capitalization of Singapore-listed companies.<ref name="Temasek highlights" /><ref name="Singapore Exchange Stat Report March 2014">{{cite report|url=http://www.sgx.com/wps/portal/sgxweb/home/marketinfo/market_statistics|title=Statistical Report, March 2014|publisher=Singapore Exchange|access-date=9 April 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150904061549/http://www.sgx.com/wps/portal/sgxweb/home/marketinfo/market_statistics|archive-date=4 September 2015}}</ref> In 2017, GSK shifted its Asian Headquarters to Singapore.<ref>{{Cite web|date=30 October 2017|title=Pharma giant GSK's regional HQ in Singapore|url=https://www.straitstimes.com/business/companies-markets/pharma-giant-gsks-regional-hq-in-singapore-will-nurture-asia-talent-for|access-date=11 July 2020|website=The Straits Times|language=en}}</ref>

==Sectors==
To maintain its competitive position despite rising wages, the government seeks to promote higher value-added activities in the manufacturing and services sectors. It also has opened, or is in the process of opening, the financial services, telecommunications, and power generation and retailing sectors up to foreign service providers and greater competition. The government has also attempted some measures including [[incomes policy|wage restraint]] measures and release of unused buildings in an effort to control rising commercial rents with the view to lowering the cost of doing business in Singapore when central business district office rents tripled in 2006.<ref name="CostOfLivingSIC2026">{{cite web |title=Cost of Living Insights for New Residents in Singapore 2026 |url=https://singaporeimmigrationconsultancy.com.sg/cost-of-living-insights-for-new-residents-in-singapore-2026/ |website=Singapore Immigration Consultancy |language=en |author= |date=15 January 2026 |access-date=22 January 2026 }}</ref>

===Banking===
{{See also|List of banks in Singapore}}

Singapore is considered a global financial hub by many leading financial analysts, economists and politicians, with Singapore banks offering world-class corporate bank account facilities. In the 2020 [[Global Financial Centres Index]], Singapore was ranked as having the sixth most competitive financial sector in the world, and the fourth most competitive in Asia.<ref name="GFCI2">{{cite web|date=September 2020|title=The Global Financial Centres Index 28|url=https://www.longfinance.net/media/documents/GFCI_28_Full_Report_2020.09.25_v1.1.pdf|access-date=4 October 2020|publisher=Long Finance}}</ref> These include multiple currencies, internet banking, telephone banking, current accounts, savings accounts, debit and credit cards, fixed term deposits and wealth management services.<ref name="Healy Consultants">{{cite web|title=Singapore Company Registration and Formation|url=https://www.hawksford.com/corporate-services/entity-formation-and-administration|publisher=Hawksford|access-date=20 April 2026|archive-url=|archive-date=}}</ref> [[DBS Bank|DBS]], [[OCBC Bank|OCBC]] and [[United Overseas Bank|UOB]] are the three major local banks of Singapore.<ref>{{cite web |title=Three Major Local Banks |url=https://www.abs.org.sg/about-us/memberbanks |website=the Association of Banks in Singapore |access-date=16 August 2024}}</ref> In 2020, [[Monetary Authority of Singapore|MAS]] granted license to [[Neobank|digital banks]] for the first time. GXS Bank and MariBank are the two largest digital banks in Singapore.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Prisca |first1=Ang |title=Singapore's two digital banks opening up to new customers, raising deposit caps to $75,000 |url=https://www.straitstimes.com/business/banking/singapore-s-two-digital-banks-opening-up-to-new-customers-raising-deposit-caps-to-75000 |access-date=27 September 2024 |work=The Straits Times |date=19 July 2023 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Huang |first1=Simon |title=No profit, no problem: Singapore's digital banks in six charts |url=https://www.businesstimes.com.sg/companies-markets/banking-finance/tech-in-asia-1/no-profit-no-problem-singapores-digital-banks-six-charts |access-date=27 September 2024 |work=The Business Times |date=3 July 2024 |language=en}}</ref>

Singapore has also attracted assets formerly held in [[Swiss banks]] for several reasons, including new taxes imposed on Swiss accounts and a weakening of Swiss [[bank secrecy]]. [[Credit Suisse]], the second largest Swiss bank, moved its head of international [[private banking]] to Singapore in 2005. For this, the country has also been dubbed the "Switzerland of Asia".<ref>{{cite web |url=https://asia.nikkei.com/Spotlight/Comment/Switzerland-of-Asia-Singapore-increases-presence-as-tech-hub |title=Switzerland of Asia: Singapore increases presence as tech hub |last=Ruhehl |first=Mercedes |date=5 November 2020 |website=asia.nikkei.com |publisher=[[The Nikkei|Nikkei]] |access-date=26 January 2021 |quote=}}</ref>

In June 2026 Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong announced that Singapore will launch a gold clearing system in a bid to secure its position as a gold reserve amidst rising interest in the precious metal. The system is set to be active by October 2026 and will partner with six banks. [[DBS Group]], one of the partner institutions, later announced it would begin offering tokenized physical gold to customers, with each token backed by a gram of gold.<ref name="GoldClearing">{{cite web |title=Singapore to establish OTC gold clearing system, introduce central bank gold-vaulting services |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/singapore-establish-otc-gold-clearing-system-introduce-central-bank-gold-2026-06-15/ |website=Reuters |language=en |author= |date=14 June 2026 |access-date=3 July 2026 }}</ref>

===Biotechnology and pharmaceutical===
Singapore has been aggressively developing its [[biotechnology]] industry. Hundreds of millions of dollars were invested into the sector to build up infrastructure, fund research and development, and to recruit top international scientists to Singapore. Leading drug makers, such as [[GlaxoSmithKline]] (GSK), [[Pfizer]] and [[Merck & Co.]], have set up plants in [[Tuas Biomedical Park]]. In 2006 GSK invested another S$300&nbsp;million to build another plant to produce [[paediatric]] [[vaccines]], its first such facility in Asia.<ref>{{cite web|title=GlaxoSmithKline Vaccine Manufacturing Facility, Tuas, Singapore|url=http://www.pharmaceutical-technology.com/projects/gsksingapore/|work=pharmaceutical-technology.com|publisher=SPG Media Limited|access-date=18 April 2013|year=2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130513043108/http://www.pharmaceutical-technology.com/projects/gsksingapore/|archive-date=13 May 2013|url-status=live}}</ref> Pharmaceuticals now account for more than 8% of the country's manufacturing production.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.mti.gov.sg/ResearchRoom/SiteAssets/Pages/Economic-Survey-of-Singapore-2012/FullReport_AES2012.pdf|title=Economic Survey of Singapore|date=2012|publisher=Singapore Ministry of Trade and Industry|website=mti.gov.sg|access-date=31 July 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150226075500/http://www.mti.gov.sg/ResearchRoom/SiteAssets/Pages/Economic-Survey-of-Singapore-2012/FullReport_AES2012.pdf|archive-date=26 February 2015}}</ref> In 2022, the biopharma industry of Singapore accounted for manufacturing output of US$18&nbsp;billion a year, a value that had tripled during two decades.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.straitstimes.com/singapore/health/pharma-giant-sanofi-breaks-ground-on-638m-vaccine-facility-in-singapore|title=Pharma giant Sanofi breaks ground on $638m vaccine facility in S'pore|author=Joyce Teo|website=straitstimes.com|date=20 April 2022|access-date=30 April 2022}}</ref>

[[Biopolis]] serves as the main research and development centre for biomedical sciences in Singapore.

===Chemical===
Singapore's chemical industry is a cornerstone of its manufacturing sector, ranking among the world's top 10 energy and chemicals hub. Centered in [[Jurong Island]], it specializes in petroleum, petrochemicals and high-value specialty chemicals, accounting for roughly 15.9% of Singapore's value-added manufacturing sector. The industry is shifting toward sustainability, decarbonization, and advanced manufacturing.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.edb.gov.sg/en/our-industries/energy-and-chemicals.html|title=Powering Global Innovation in Energy & Chemicals &#124; EDB Singapore|website=www.edb.gov.sg}}</ref>

Singapore's defence industry is a growing, technology-based sector, with its industry is led by [[ST Engineering]] and supported by the [[Defence Science and Technology Agency]] and [[DSO National Laboratories]] for development of military technologies and capabilities.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |date=2025-08-22 |title=Singapore - Aerospace and Defense |url=https://www.trade.gov/country-commercial-guides/singapore-aerospace-and-defense |access-date=2026-04-27 |website=www.trade.gov |language=en}}</ref>

===Energy===
{{Main|Energy in Singapore}}

Singapore is the pricing centre and leading oil trading hub in Asia. The oil industry makes up 5% of Singapore's GDP, with Singapore being one of the top three export refining centres in the world. In 2007, it exported 68.1&nbsp;million tonnes of oil. The oil industry has led to the promotion of the chemical industry as well as oil and gas equipment manufacturing.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.edb.gov.sg/edb/sg/en_uk/index/industry_sectors/energy/facts_and_figures.html |title=Facts and Figures |publisher=Singapore Government |date=11 November 2010 |access-date=13 July 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111104145511/http://www.edb.gov.sg/edb/sg/en_uk/index/industry_sectors/energy/facts_and_figures.html |archive-date=4 November 2011 |url-status=live}}</ref> Singapore has 70 per cent of the world market for both jack-up rigs and for the conversion of Floating Production Storage Offloading units. It has 20 per cent of the world market for ship repair, and in 2008 the marine and offshore industry employed almost 70,000 workers.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.edb.gov.sg/edb/sg/en_uk/index/industry_sectors/marine___offshore/facts_and_figures.html |title=Facts and Figures |publisher=Singapore Government |date=13 October 2009 |access-date=13 July 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120418084237/http://www.edb.gov.sg/edb/sg/en_uk/index/industry_sectors/marine___offshore/facts_and_figures.html |archive-date=18 April 2012}}</ref>

Singapore has limited potential for renewable energy mainly due to its small surface area; solar power holds the greatest potential.<ref name="Vakulchuk etal 2000">Vakulchuk, R., Chan, H.Y., Kresnawan, M.R., Merdekawati, M., Overland, I., Sagbakken, H.F., Suryadi, B., Utama, N.A. and Yurnaidi, Z. 2020. Singapore: How to Attract More Investment in Renewable Energy? ASEAN Centre for Energy (ACE) Policy Brief Series, No 11. https://www.researchgate.net/publication/341794179</ref> The government set a target of generating solar power to cover 350,000 households in 2030 that would equal to 4% of the country's electricity demand in 2020.<ref name="Vakulchuk etal 2000" /> As a financial hub, Singapore can play an important role in attracting investment in renewable energy in the entire [[ASEAN]] region.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Overland |first1=Indra |author-link1=Indra Øverland |last2=Sagbakken |first2=Haakon Fossum |last3=Chan |first3=Hoy-Yen |last4=Merdekawati |first4=Monika |last5=Suryadi |first5=Beni |last6=Utama |first6=Nuki Agya |last7=Vakulchuk |first7=Roman |title=The ASEAN climate and energy paradox |journal=Energy and Climate Change |date=December 2021 |volume=2 |article-number=100019 |doi=10.1016/j.egycc.2020.100019 |hdl=11250/2734506 |hdl-access=free}}</ref>

=== Manufacturing ===

==== Hard disk drive ====
In the 1980s, US companies began assembling [[hard disk drive|hard disk drives]] (HDD) in Singapore. They were attracted by factors including government incentives and the availability of skilled labor. By the mid 1990s, the six largest HDD companies in the world manufactured in Singapore.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Wong|first=Poh-Kam|date=1997|title=Creation Of A Regional Hub For Flexible Production: The Case Of The Hard Disk Drive Industry In Singapore|url=http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/13662719700000010|journal=Industry and Innovation|language=en|volume=4|issue=2|pages=183–205|doi=10.1080/13662719700000010|issn=1366-2716|url-access=subscription}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=186}} However, foreign firms based in Singapore began to move assembly to nearby countries with lower costs<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Athukorala|first=Prema-Chandra|last2=Ekanayake|first2=Asanthe|date=2025|title=International Production and Industrial Transformation: The Singapore Story|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/twec.13673|journal=The World Economy|language=en|volume=48|issue=4|pages=831–846|doi=10.1111/twec.13673|issn=1467-9701|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=SHAMEEN|first=ASSIF|last2=HEALY|first2=TIM|date=November 5, 1999|title=Low-Cost Competitor|url=https://www.cnn.com/ASIANOW/asiaweek/magazine/99/1105/biz.malaysia.html|access-date=2026-09-30|website=CNN ASIANOW}}</ref> in the late 1980s.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-4-431-55498-1|title=Production Networks and Enterprises in East Asia: Industry and Firm-level Analysis|date=2016|publisher=Springer Japan|isbn=978-4-431-55497-4|editor-last=Wignaraja|editor-first=Ganeshan|series=ADB Institute Series on Development Economics|location=Tokyo|language=en|doi=10.1007/978-4-431-55498-1}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=153}}

==== Semiconductor ====
The [[semiconductor]] industry in Singapore has largely produced low-end chips, for products such as electric cars or smartphones.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Mak|first=Robyn|last2=Daga|first2=Anshuman|date=June 21, 2024|title=Tiny Singapore's chip hub retains a big punch|url=https://www.reuters.com/breakingviews/tiny-singapores-chip-hub-retains-big-punch-2024-06-21/|work=[[Reuters]]}}</ref> After [[Texas Instruments]] and [[National Semiconductor]] set up semiconductor plants in Singapore for assembly and testing in 1968, other major industry players soon followed. In 1984, [[SGS-Thomson]] set up a [[wafer fabrication]] plant in Singapore, with other manufacturers following since.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Athukorala|first=Prema-Chandra|last2=Ekanayake|first2=Asanthe|date=2025|title=International Production and Industrial Transformation: The Singapore Story|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/twec.13673|journal=The World Economy|language=en|volume=48|issue=4|pages=831–846|doi=10.1111/twec.13673|issn=1467-9701|doi-access=free}}</ref> Singapore state-owned [[Temasek Holdings]] agreed to sell its 62% stake<ref name=":2" /> in Singapore-listed<ref>{{Cite news |last=Einhorn |first=Bruce |date=October 14, 2002 |title=Merrill's Marriage of Inconvenience |work=BusinessWeek |via=EBSCO}}</ref> [[Chartered Semiconductor Manufacturing|Chartered Semiconductor]], which had been the world's third-largest foundry,<ref>{{Cite news |last=Einhorn |first=Bruce |date=July 24, 2001 |title=The Chips Are Down in Singapore |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2001-07-22/the-chips-are-down-in-singapore |work=BusinessWeek |via=EBSCO}}</ref> to [[Abu Dhabi]]'s [[Mubadala Investment Company|Advanced Technology Investment Company]] in 2009.<ref name=":2">{{Cite news |last=Lee |first=Se Young |last2=Venkat |first2=P. R. |date=2009-09-08 |title=Abu Dhabi to Buy Chartered Semi, Seeking to Challenge Top Chip Firms - WSJ |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB125228002851089603 |access-date=2026-09-28 |work=Wall Street Journal |language=en-US |issn=0099-9660}}</ref>

===Real estate===
{{Further|Public housing in Singapore}}

The Singapore government also owns 90 per cent of the country's land, as well as housing in which 80 per cent of the population lives. The [[Housing and Development Board]] is Singapore's public housing authority. Singapore housing market comprises three main types: public HDB flats (subsidised high-rise), private condominiums (with shared facilities) and landed properties (houses on private land). The majority, ~77% of residents live in HDB flats, while private condominiums (17.9%) and landed properties (4.7%) make up the rest.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.peoplespolicyproject.org/2018/03/09/how-capitalist-is-singapore-really/|title=How Capitalist Is Singapore Really?|first=Matt|last=Bruenig|author-link=Matt Bruenig|date=9 March 2018 |access-date=31 July 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190429231210/https://www.peoplespolicyproject.org/2018/03/09/how-capitalist-is-singapore-really/|archive-date=29 April 2019}}</ref>

In July 2022, a report by [[Savills]] revealed that Singapore tied with New York City in recording the highest rental growth rate for luxury homes globally.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.savills.com.sg/insight-and-opinion/savills-news/207853-0/singapore-ties-with-new-york-for-highest-prime-rental-growth-in-1h-2022 |title=Singapore ties with New York for Highest Prime Rental Growth In 1H 2022 |website=savills.com.sg |date=29 July 2022 |access-date=11 August 2022}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2022-07-29/singapore-new-york-tie-for-highest-rental-growth-in-first-half#xj4y7vzkg |title=Singapore, New York Tie for Highest First Half Rental Growth |last=Mokhtar |first=Faris |date=29 July 2022 |website=Bloomberg UK |access-date=11 August 2022}}</ref>

==International trade and investment==
{{See also|Ministry of Trade and Industry (Singapore)|ASEAN Free Trade Area|Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership|Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership}}
{{Update|section|date=July 2013}}
[[File:2006Singaporean exports.PNG|thumb|450px|Singaporean exports in 2006]]
{{Export treemap Singapore}}

Singapore's total trade in 2022 amounted to $1,365.4&nbsp;[[1000000000 (number)|billion]] [[Singapore dollar|SGD]]. In 2022, Singapore's imports were $655.4&nbsp;billion [[Singapore dollar|SGD]] and exports were $710.0&nbsp;billion [[Singapore dollar|SGD]].<ref name="Singapore International Trade">{{Cite web |title=Singapore International Trade |url=http://www.singstat.gov.sg/modules/infographics/singapore-international-trade |access-date=2024-01-23 |website=Base |language=en}}</ref> [[China]] was Singapore's main import partner, as well as its largest export market in 2021.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Singapore (SGP) Exports, Imports, and Trade Partners |url=https://oec.world/en |access-date=2024-01-23 |website=The Observatory of Economic Complexity |language=en}}</ref> Singapore's major trading partners include [[Malaysia]], the [[United States]] and the [[European Union]].<ref name="Singapore International Trade" />

[[China]] is Singapore's largest trading partner, with bilateral trade totalling roughly 175&nbsp;billion Singapore dollars in 2022.<ref>{{cite web |title=Singapore International Trade |url=https://www.singstat.gov.sg/modules/infographics/singapore-international-trade |website=SingStat |access-date=27 October 2023 |language=en}}</ref> Since 2009, the value of exports exceeds imports for Singapore's trade with China. In comparison, the value of imports exceeds exports for Singapore's trade with the US since 2006.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.pmo.gov.sg/content/pmosite/mediacentre/speechesninterviews/primeminister/2009/May/speeches_by_primeministerleehsienloongandmalaysianprimeministern.html#.VDvFfPmSxXY |title=Speeches by Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong and Malaysian Prime Minister Najib Tun Razak at the official dinner at the Istana on 22 May 2009 |access-date=26 October 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141019145833/http://www.pmo.gov.sg/content/pmosite/mediacentre/speechesninterviews/primeminister/2009/May/speeches_by_primeministerleehsienloongandmalaysianprimeministern.html |archive-date=19 October 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.singstat.gov.sg/statistics/visualising_data/visualiser/trade/trade.html |title=Statistics Singapore - Trade with Major Trading Partners |access-date=13 October 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141021082312/http://www.singstat.gov.sg/statistics/visualising_data/visualiser/trade/trade.html |archive-date=21 October 2014}}</ref>

Re-exports accounted for 43% of Singapore's total sales to other countries in 2000. Singapore's principal exports are electronic components, refined petroleum, gold, computers, and packaged medications. Singapore's main imports are electronic components, refined petroleum, crude petroleum, gold, and computers.

Trade in Singapore has benefited from the extensive network of trade agreements Singapore has implementing. According to Hawksford, Singapore may benefit from preferential market access across parts of the ASEAN network, with import duties potentially reduced for certain goods and scenarios when trading with Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand, Brunei, Myanmar, Cambodia, Laos and Vietnam.

The [[Singapore Economic Development Board]] (EDB) continues to attract investment funds on a large-scale for the country despite the city's relatively high-cost operating environment. The US leads in foreign investment, accounting for 40% of new commitments to the manufacturing sector in 2000. As of 1999, cumulative investment for manufacturing and services by American companies in Singapore reached approximately $20&nbsp;billion (total assets). The bulk of US investment is in electronics manufacturing, oil refining and storage, and the chemical industry. More than 1,500 US firms operate in Singapore.

Singapore's largely corruption-free government, skilled workforce, and advanced and efficient infrastructure have attracted investments from more than 3,000 [[multinational corporation]]s (MNCs) from the United States, Japan, and Europe. Foreign firms are found in almost all sectors of the economy. MNCs account for more than two-thirds of manufacturing output and direct export sales, although certain services sectors remain dominated by government-linked corporations.

The government also has encouraged firms to invest outside Singapore, with the country's total direct investments abroad (DIA) reaching S$1,636&nbsp;billion by the end of 2024. Mainland China was the top investment destination, accounting for S$228&nbsp;billion of total DIA, followed by [[India]] (121&nbsp;billion), United Kingdom (110&nbsp;billion), [[Netherlands]] (110&nbsp;billion) and [[Indonesia]] (100&nbsp;billion).<ref>{{Cite report |url=https://www.singstat.gov.sg/-/media/files/news/advdia2024.ashx |title=Advance Estimates of Singapore's Direct Investment Abroad (Stock as at end 2024) |date=2025-11-04 |publisher=[[Singapore Department of Statistics]] |access-date=2026-01-06 |format=PDF}}</ref> The rapidly growing economy of India, especially the high technology sector, is becoming an expanding source of foreign investment for Singapore.

The United States strives to improve bilateral trade with Singapore and has signed the [[US-Singapore Free Trade Agreement]] in 2003. Singapore corporate tax is 17 per cent.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aseanbriefing.com/news/2018/08/15/corporate-taxation-singapore.html|title=Corporate Taxation in Singapore|date=15 August 2018|website=ASEAN Business News|access-date=24 February 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190407193739/https://www.aseanbriefing.com/news/2018/08/15/corporate-taxation-singapore.html|archive-date=7 April 2019}}</ref>

Singapore is the European Union's 14th largest trading partner. Singapore-EU trade is worth more than €50&nbsp;billion [[euro]]s a year. Singapore is also the EU's 5th largest [[trade in services]] partner and the EU's 6th destination for [[foreign direct investment]]. Over 10,000 EU companies have set up their hubs or offices in Singapore.<ref name="EU-Singapore agreement explained">{{Cite web |title=The EU-Singapore agreement explained |url=https://policy.trade.ec.europa.eu/eu-trade-relationships-country-and-region/countries-and-regions/singapore/eu-singapore-agreements/agreement-explained_en |access-date=2024-01-23 |website=policy.trade.ec.europa.eu |language=en}}</ref>

In 2018, the EU and Singapore signed the [[European Union–Singapore Free Trade Agreement|EUSFTA]], a [[free trade agreement]] which aims to boost and promote [[International trade|trade]] between Singapore and the EU. The agreement includes provisions on:<ref name="EU-Singapore agreement explained" />

* Eliminating [[tariff]]s on [[goods]]
* Harmonizing [[safety]], [[Product testing|testing]] and [[label]]ing standards (for [[car]]s and [[List of auto parts|vehicle parts]], [[electronics]] and [[Textile industry|textiles]])
* Preferential [[market access]] and [[equal treatment]] for [[Service (economics)|services]] (for [[telecommunications]], [[financial services]], [[transport]], etc.)
* Simplifying [[customs]] procedures and improving [[trade facilitation]]
* Improved protection of [[intellectual property]]
* Guaranteed access to [[government procurement]] contracts
* Legally-binding commitments on [[environmental protection]] and [[workers' rights]]<ref name="EU-Singapore agreement explained" /><ref name="EU-Singapore">{{Cite web |date=2023-07-20 |title=EU-Singapore |url=https://policy.trade.ec.europa.eu/eu-trade-relationships-country-and-region/countries-and-regions/singapore/eu-singapore-agreements_en |access-date=2024-01-23 |website=policy.trade.ec.europa.eu |language=en}}</ref>

In addition to the free trade agreement, the EU and Singapore signed an investment protection agreement which aims to encourage [[investment]] between Singapore and the EU. It ensures that [[government]]s in the EU and Singapore [[National treatment|treat each other's investors equally]], and replaces old-style [[Bilateral investment treaty|bilateral investment treaties]] between Singapore and individual EU countries.<ref name="EU-Singapore agreement explained" />
