== History ==

=== Maduro administration ===
In November 2016, Venezuela entered a period of [[hyperinflation]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/stevehanke/2018/08/18/venezuelas-great-bolivar-scam-nothing-but-a-face-lift/#7edf9d24c23e|title=Venezuela's Great Bolivar Scam, Nothing but a Face Lift|last1=Hanke|first1=Steve|date=18 August 2018|work=[[Forbes (magazine)|Forbes]]|access-date=19 August 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180819002426/https://www.forbes.com/sites/stevehanke/2018/08/18/venezuelas-great-bolivar-scam-nothing-but-a-face-lift/#7edf9d24c23e|archive-date=19 August 2018|url-status=live}}</ref> In December 2016, monthly inflation exceeded 50% for the 30th consecutive day, meaning the economy was officially experiencing hyperinflation, making Venezuela the 57th country to be added to the [[Hanke-Krus World Hyperinflation Table]].<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.miamiherald.com/news/nation-world/world/americas/venezuela/article120451593.html|title=Entering a 'world of economic chaos,' Venezuela struggles with hyperinflation|date=12 December 2016|access-date=2016-12-19|author=Jim Wyss|newspaper=Miami Herald|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161215112717/http://www.miamiherald.com/news/nation-world/world/americas/venezuela/article120451593.html|archive-date=15 December 2016|url-status=live}}</ref>

The inflation rate reached 4,000% in 2017.<ref name="Sequera 2018" /> The same year, a trend began in Venezuela in which [[gold farming]] in cybergames, such as ''[[RuneScape]]'', became an acquirable{{clarify|date=April 2020}} way to obtain [[hard currency]]. In many cases, they{{clarify|date=April 2020}} made more money than salaried workers in Venezuela, despite earning just a few dollars per day.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Rosati|first1=Andrew|title=Desperate Venezuelans Turn to Video Games to Survive|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2017-12-05/desperate-venezuelans-turn-to-video-games-to-survive|access-date=6 December 2017|work=[[Bloomberg.com|Bloomberg]]|date=5 December 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171206014208/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2017-12-05/desperate-venezuelans-turn-to-video-games-to-survive|archive-date=6 December 2017|url-status=live}}</ref> During the Christmas season in 2017, some shops no longer used price tags; since prices inflated so quickly, customers were required to ask staff how much each item was.<ref>{{cite news|title=Tiendas de ropa eliminan etiquetas y habladores para agilizar aumento de precios {{!}} La Region|url=http://www.diariolaregion.net/2017/12/12/tiendas-de-ropa-eliminan-etiquetas-y-habladores-para-agilizar-aumento-de-precios/|access-date=16 December 2017|work=Diario La Region|date=12 December 2017|language=es-ES|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171215211841/http://www.diariolaregion.net/2017/12/12/tiendas-de-ropa-eliminan-etiquetas-y-habladores-para-agilizar-aumento-de-precios/|archive-date=15 December 2017|url-status=live}}</ref> In early 2018, the Venezuelan government "essentially stopped" producing inflation estimates.<ref name="NYRoB-2018" />

In May 2019, the BCV released economic data for the first time since 2015. It reported that the inflation rate was 274% in 2016, 863% in 2017, and 130,060% in 2018.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.lemonde.fr/international/article/2019/05/29/venezuela-l-inflation-a-ete-de-130-060-en-2018_5469091_3210.html|title=Au Venezuela, l'inflation a été de 130 060 % en 2018|date=29 May 2019|work=Le Monde|access-date=31 May 2019|language=fr|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190530200722/https://www.lemonde.fr/international/article/2019/05/29/venezuela-l-inflation-a-ete-de-130-060-en-2018_5469091_3210.html|archive-date=30 May 2019|url-status=live}}</ref> The new report suggested a contraction of the economy by more than half in five years, described by the ''[[Financial Times]]'' as "one of the biggest contractions in Latin American history".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ft.com/content/5cb83c1c-821b-11e9-b592-5fe435b57a3b|title=Venezuela data offer rare glimpse of economic chaos|last=Long|first=Gideon|date=29 May 2019|website=Financial Times|access-date=31 May 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190530085333/https://www.ft.com/content/5cb83c1c-821b-11e9-b592-5fe435b57a3b|archive-date=30 May 2019|url-status=live}}</ref> According to undisclosed sources from [[Reuters]], the release of this data was due to pressure from [[China]], an ally of [[Nicolás Maduro]]. One of the sources claimed that this disclosure might bring Venezuela into compliance with the IMF, making it harder to support [[Juan Guaidó]] during [[2019 Venezuelan presidential crisis|the presidential crisis]].<ref name="reutersIMFdeniesBCV">{{Cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-venezuela-politics-imf-idUSKCN1T01YW|title=IMF denies pressuring Venezuela to release economic data|last1=Wroughton|first1=Lesley|date=30 May 2019|work=Reuters|access-date=31 May 2019|last2=Pons|first2=Corina|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190530193700/https://www.reuters.com/article/us-venezuela-politics-imf-idUSKCN1T01YW|archive-date=30 May 2019|url-status=live}}</ref> At the time, the IMF was not able to support the validity of the data as they had not been able to contact the authorities.<ref name="reutersIMFdeniesBCV" />

=== 2018 inflation estimate ===
In 2018, the IMF estimated that Venezuela's inflation rate would reach 1,000,000% by the end of the year.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2018/07/27/venezuelan-inflation-predicted-to-hit-1-million-percent-this-year.html|title=Venezuelan inflation predicted to hit 1 million percent this year|last=Amaro|first=Silvia|date=2018-07-27|work=[[CNBC]]|access-date=2018-07-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180728105617/https://www.cnbc.com/2018/07/27/venezuelan-inflation-predicted-to-hit-1-million-percent-this-year.html|archive-date=2018-07-28|url-status=live}}</ref> This forecast was criticized by economist [[Steve Hanke]], who claimed that the IMF had released a "bogus forecast" because "no one has ever been able to accurately forecast the course or the duration of an episode of hyperinflation. But that has not stopped the IMF from offering inflation forecasts for Venezuela that have proven to be wildly inaccurate". According to Hanke, Venezuela's inflation rate on 31 July 2018 was 33,151%, suggesting that "Venezuela is now experiencing the 23rd most severe episode of hyperinflation in history."<ref name="Hanke">{{cite web|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/stevehanke/2018/07/31/imf-produces-another-bogus-venezuela-inflation-forecast/#78430a7b7dc8|title=IMF Produces Another Bogus Venezuela Inflation Forecast|last1=Hanke|first1=Steve|date=31 July 2018|website=Forbes|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180831104955/https://www.forbes.com/sites/stevehanke/2018/07/31/imf-produces-another-bogus-venezuela-inflation-forecast/#78430a7b7dc8|archive-date=31 August 2018|url-status=live|access-date=31 August 2018}}</ref>

The IMF reported that the inflation rate for 2018 reached 929,790%, slightly below the original 1,000,000% estimate.<ref name="WSJ0519">{{Cite news|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/venezuelas-central-bank-releases-data-showing-dire-economy-11559098083|title=Venezuela's Central Bank Releases Data on Dire Economy|last=Dube|first=Ryan|date=28 May 2019|work=[[The Wall Street Journal]]|access-date=15 June 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190616034129/https://www.wsj.com/articles/venezuelas-central-bank-releases-data-showing-dire-economy-11559098083|archive-date=16 June 2019|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== 2019 inflation estimate ===
In October 2018, the IMF estimated that the inflation rate would reach 10,000,000% by the end of 2019, which was again mentioned in its April 2019 World Economic Outlook report.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://in.reuters.com/article/venezuela-economy-idINKCN1MJ1YX|title=IMF sees Venezuela inflation at 10 million percent in 2019|date=9 October 2018|work=Reuters|access-date=31 May 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190507112345/https://in.reuters.com/article/venezuela-economy-idINKCN1MJ1YX|archive-date=7 May 2019|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="IMF" />

=== 2021 inflation estimate ===
In December 2021, economists and the [[Central Bank of Venezuela]] announced that Venezuela would reach in the first quarter of 2022 more than 12 months with monthly inflation below 50% after more than four years of a hyperinflationary cycle, which would technically indicate its exit from hyperinflation, but its consequences remained by that date.<ref name="Singer 2021" />

== Causes ==
[[File:Money on the floor → economic crisis.jpg|right|thumb|300px|Venezuelan banknotes scattered in the street during the [[Venezuelan presidential crisis]]]]
A [[monetarist]] view<ref>See, for instance, Friedman, Milton. ''Inflation: Causes and Consequences''. New York: Asia Publishing House: "Inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon."</ref> is that a general increase in the prices of things is less a commentary on the worth of those things than on the worth of the money. This has objective and subjective components:
*Objectively, that the money has no firm basis to give it a value.
*Subjectively, that the people holding the money lack confidence in its ability to retain its value.

According to experts, Venezuela's economy began to experience hyperinflation during the first year of Nicolás Maduro's presidency.<ref>{{cite news|title=Venezuela joins the hyperinflation club: 54.3% in last twelve months and climbing|url=http://en.mercopress.com/2013/11/08/venezuela-joins-the-hyperinflation-club-54.3-in-last-twelve-months-and-climbing|access-date=16 October 2014|agency=MercoPress|date=8 November 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141006132535/http://en.mercopress.com/2013/11/08/venezuela-joins-the-hyperinflation-club-54.3-in-last-twelve-months-and-climbing|archive-date=6 October 2014|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Hyperinflation is forcing Venezuela to print hundreds of millions of extra banknotes|url=http://qz.com/125339/hyperinflation-is-forcing-venezuela-to-print-hundreds-of-millions-of-extra-banknotes/|website=Quartz|date=18 September 2013 |access-date=16 October 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141020132407/http://qz.com/125339/hyperinflation-is-forcing-venezuela-to-print-hundreds-of-millions-of-extra-banknotes/|archive-date=20 October 2014|url-status=live}}</ref> Potential causes of the hyperinflation include heavy money-printing and [[deficit spending]].<ref name="CNBCoct2014">{{cite news|last1=Caruso-Cabrera|first1=Michelle|title=Creating inflation is easy. Just look at Venezuela|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2014/10/13/venezuelan-economy-creating-inflation-is-easy-just-look-at-venezuela.html|access-date=11 November 2014|agency=CNBC|date=13 October 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141112051206/http://www.cnbc.com/id/102082864#.|archive-date=12 November 2014|url-status=live}}</ref> In April 2013, the month Maduro took office, the annual inflation rate was 29.4%, only 0.1% less than the rate in 1999 when Hugo Chávez took office.<ref>{{cite news|title=VenEconomy: Venezuela's Economy is an Erupting Volcano|url=http://www.laht.com/article.asp?ArticleId=774552&CategoryId=13303|access-date=20 June 2014|agency=Latin American Herald Tribune|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141020190809/http://www.laht.com/article.asp?ArticleId=774552&CategoryId=13303|archive-date=20 October 2014|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="CEPR2010">{{cite web|last1=Weisbrot|first1=Mark|last2=Ray|first2=Rebecca|last3=Sandoval|first3=Luis|title=The Chávez Administration at 10 Years: The Economy and Social Indicators|url=http://www.cepr.net/documents/publications/venezuela-2009-02.pdf|publisher=CEPR|access-date=20 June 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140312044559/http://www.cepr.net/documents/publications/venezuela-2009-02.pdf|archive-date=12 March 2014|url-status=live}}</ref> By April 2014, the annual inflation rate was 61.5%.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Dreier|first1=Hannah|title=Venezuela Takes Dramatic Step Towards Food Rationing|url=https://www.huffingtonpost.com/2014/04/01/venezuela-rationing_n_5072160.html|access-date=31 August 2014|agency=Huffington Post|date=1 April 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140904043642/http://www.huffingtonpost.com/2014/04/01/venezuela-rationing_n_5072160.html|archive-date=4 September 2014|url-status=live}}</ref> In early 2014, the BCV did not release statistics for the first time in its history, with ''[[Forbes]]'' reporting that it was a possible way to manipulate the image of economy.<ref>{{cite news|last=Kurmanaev|first=Anatoly|title=Venezuela in Data Denial After Inflation Tops 50%: Andes Credit|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/2014-01-09/venezuela-in-data-denial-after-inflation-tops-50-andes-credit.html|access-date=16 January 2014|newspaper=Bloomberg|date=9 January 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140116230150/http://www.bloomberg.com/news/2014-01-09/venezuela-in-data-denial-after-inflation-tops-50-andes-credit.html|archive-date=16 January 2014|url-status=live}}</ref> In April 2014, the IMF stated that economic activity in Venezuela was uncertain but may continue to slow, and that "loose [[macroeconomic]] policies have generated high inflation and a drain on official [[foreign exchange reserves]]". The IMF suggested that "more significant policy changes are needed to stave off a disorderly adjustment".<ref>{{cite web|title=World Economic Outlook|date=April 2014|url=http://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/weo/2014/01/pdf/text.pdf|work=Report|publisher=International Monetary Fund|access-date=9 April 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140408225045/http://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/weo/2014/01/pdf/text.pdf|archive-date=8 April 2014|url-status=live}}</ref> According to economist Steve Hanke, Venezuela's current economy, as of March 2014, had an inflation rate hovering above 300%, an official inflation rate around 60%, and a product scarcity index rising above 25% of goods.<ref>{{cite news|last=Neuman|first=William|title=Slum Dwellers in Caracas Ask, What Protests?|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/03/01/world/americas/slum-dwellers-in-caracas-ask-what-protests.html|access-date=3 March 2014|newspaper=The New York Times|date=28 February 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140302220833/http://www.nytimes.com/2014/03/01/world/americas/slum-dwellers-in-caracas-ask-what-protests.html|archive-date=2 March 2014|url-status=live}}</ref> The Venezuelan government did not report inflation data for September and October 2014.<ref>{{cite news|title=Gobierno demora nuevamente divulgación de datos de inflación|url=http://www.lapatilla.com/site/2014/11/11/gobierno-demora-nuevamente-divulgacion-de-datos-de-inflacion/|access-date=15 November 2014|agency=La Patilla|date=11 November 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141113145040/http://www.lapatilla.com/site/2014/11/11/gobierno-demora-nuevamente-divulgacion-de-datos-de-inflacion/|archive-date=13 November 2014|url-status=live}}</ref>

The growth in the BCV's [[money supply]] accelerated during the beginning of Maduro's presidency, which increased price inflation in the country.<ref>{{cite web|title=Monetary aggregates rising sharply|url=http://www.eiu.com/industry/article/711546455/monetary-aggregates-rising-sharply/2014-02-17|publisher=Economist Intelligence Unit|access-date=25 February 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140228163204/http://www.eiu.com/industry/article/711546455/monetary-aggregates-rising-sharply/2014-02-17|archive-date=28 February 2014|url-status=live}}</ref> The money supply of the bolívar fuerte in Venezuela increased 64% in 2014, three times faster than any other economy observed by Bloomberg News at the time.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/2014-12-30/venezuelan-1000-inflation-seen-by-bofa-without-weaker-bolivar.html|title=Venezuelan 1,000% Inflation Seen by BofA Without Weaker Bolivar|last1=Boyd|first1=Sebastian|date=30 December 2014|access-date=4 January 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150104114535/http://www.bloomberg.com/news/2014-12-30/venezuelan-1-000-inflation-seen-by-bofa-without-weaker-bolivar.html|archive-date=4 January 2015|url-status=live|agency=Bloomberg}}</ref> Due to the rapidly decreasing value of the bolívar fuerte, Venezuelans jokingly called it "bolívar muerto" ("dead bolívar").<ref name="REUTbolivar3000">{{cite news|title=Venezuela currency tanks 60 percent in month on black market|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-venezuela-economy-idUSKBN13N1M7?il=0|access-date=30 November 2016|work=[[Reuters]]|date=28 November 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161130090321/http://www.reuters.com/article/us-venezuela-economy-idUSKBN13N1M7?il=0|archive-date=30 November 2016|url-status=live}}</ref>

Maduro has blamed capitalist [[speculation]] for driving high inflation rates and creating widespread shortages of basic necessities. He has said he is fighting an "economic war", referring to newly enacted economic measures as "economic offensives" against political opponents, who, according to Maduro and his loyalists, are behind an international economic conspiracy.<ref>{{cite news|title=Mr. Maduro in His Labyrinth|newspaper=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/01/26/opinion/mr-maduro-in-his-labyrinth.html|access-date=26 January 2015|agency=[[The New York Times]]|date=26 January 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150126123822/http://www.nytimes.com/2015/01/26/opinion/mr-maduro-in-his-labyrinth.html|archive-date=26 January 2015|url-status=live}}<br />* {{cite news|title=Venezuela's government seizes electronic goods shops|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-latin-america-24883849|access-date=19 February news|title=Maduro anuncia que el martes arranca nueva "ofensiva económica"|url=http://www.lapatilla.com/site/2014/04/21/maduro-anuncia-que-el-martes-arranca-nueva-ofensiva-economica/|access-date=23 2014|url-status=live}}<br />* {{cite news|title=Maduro insiste con una nueva "ofensiva económica"|url=http://www.lanacion.com.ar/1684248-maduro-insiste-con-una-nueva-ofensiva-economica|access-date=1 May 2014|newspaper=La Nacion|date=23 April 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140502001154/http://www.lanacion.com.ar/1684248-maduro-insiste-con-una-nueva-ofensiva-economica|archive-date=2 May 2014|url-status=live}}<br />* {{cite web |author=Mariano Castillo and Osmary Hernandez |url=https://edition.cnn.com/2013/11/20/world/americas/venezuela-economy-decree-powers/ |title=Decree powers 2015|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Devaluation of the ''bolívar'' ===
After the [[Chávez administration]] established strict currency controls in 2003, there have been a series of five currency [[devaluation]]s, disrupting the economy.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.ft.com/content/12e9f32e-739e-11e2-9e92-00144feabdc0|title=Venezuelan devaluation sparks panic|last=Mander|first=Benedict|date=10 February 2013|work=Financial Times|access-date=11 February 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130212182006/http://www.ft.com/cms/s/0/12e9f32e-739e-11e2-9e92-00144feabdc0.html#axzz2KaYrvVGc|archive-date=12 February 2013|url-status=live}}</ref> On 8 January 2010, the government changed the official [[fixed exchange rate]] from 2.15 bolívares fuertes (Bs.F) to 2.60 bolívares (for imported healthcare goods and certain foods) and 4.30 bolívares (for imported cars, petrochemicals, and electronics).<ref>{{cite news |publisher=BBC |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/business/8449721.stm |title=Venezuela will slash value of currency, the bolivar |access-date=2010-01-09 |date=2010-01-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100109051919/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/business/8449721.stm |archive-date=2010-01-09 |url-status=live }}</ref> On 4 January 2011, the fixed exchange rate became 4.30 bolívares per US$1.00 for both sides of the economy. On 13 February 2013, the bolívar was devalued to 6.30 bolívares per USD in an attempt to counter budget deficits.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.businessweek.com/news/2013-02-10/chavez-devaluation-puts-venezuelans-to-queue-before-price-raise|title=Chavez Devaluation Puts Venezuelans to Queue on Price Raise|date=11 February 2013|work=Bloomberg|access-date=11 February 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130217113204/http://www.businessweek.com/news/2013-02-10/chavez-devaluation-puts-venezuelans-to-queue-before-price-raise|archive-date=17 February 2013|url-status=dead}}</ref> The black (or parallel) market value of the ''bolívar fuerte'' and the ''bolívar soberano'' has been significantly lower than the [[fixed exchange rate]] and other rates set by the Venezuelan government (SICAD, SIMADI, DICOM). In November 2013, it was almost one-tenth that of the official fixed exchange rate of 6.3 bolívares per [[U.S. dollar]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.latimes.com/world/worldnow/la-fg-wn-venezuela-currency-exchange-air-travel-20131112,0,7697325.story#axzz2mC4h9K5A|title=Stuck in Venezuela with those currency exchange blues|date=12 November 2013|newspaper=Los Angeles Times|access-date=7 January 2014}}</ref> On 18 February 2016, President Maduro used his newly granted economic powers to devalue the official exchange rate of the bolívar fuerte from 6.3 Bs.F per USD to 10 Bs.F per USD.<ref name="BIgasprices">{{cite news|last1=Holodny|first1=Elena|title=Venezuela raises gas prices 6,200%|url=http://www.businessinsider.com/venezuela-hiked-gas-prices-by-60-times-2016-2|access-date=18 February 2016|work=[[Business Insider]]|date=18 February 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160219095600/http://www.businessinsider.com/venezuela-hiked-gas-prices-by-60-times-2016-2|archive-date=19 February 2016|url-status=live}}</ref>

In September 2014, the unofficial exchange rate for the bolívar fuerte in [[Cúcuta]], [[Colombia]] reached 100 Bs.F per USD.<ref name=100BSF>{{cite news|title=Venezuela bolivar hits record low 100/U.S. dollar on black market|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-venezuela-currency-idUSKCN0HL2GW20140926|access-date=5 October 2014|work=Reuters|date=26 September 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141006142629/http://www.reuters.com/article/2014/09/26/us-venezuela-currency-idUSKCN0HL2GW20140926|archive-date=6 October 2014|url-status=live}}</ref> In May 2015, the bolívar fuerte lost 25% of its value in a week; the unofficial exchange rate was at 300 Bs.F per USD on 14 May and reached 400 Bs.F per USD on 21 May.<ref name=25percentDROP1>{{cite news|last1=Barnato|first1=Katy|title=Venezuelan currency tanks; inflation seen near 100%|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2015/05/14/venezuelan-currency-tanks-inflation-seen-near-100.html|access-date=24 May 2015|agency=[[CNBC]]|date=14 May 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150525023300/http://www.cnbc.com/id/102678399|archive-date=25 May 2015|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=REUT25drop>{{cite news|last1=Ellsworth|first1=Brian|title=Venezuela unofficial exchange rate weakens to 400 bolivars per dollar|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-venezuela-forex-idUSKBN0O701R20150522|access-date=24 May 2015|work=[[Reuters]]|date=21 May 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150525025051/http://www.reuters.com/article/2015/05/22/us-venezuela-forex-idUSKBN0O701R20150522|archive-date=25 May 2015|url-status=live}}</ref> In July 2015, the bolívar fuerte again dropped sharply, reaching 500 Bs.F per USD on 3 July and 600 Bs.F per USD on 9 July.<ref name=500drop>{{cite news|title=Venezuela's unofficial exchange rate weakens past 500 per dollar|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/venezuela-forex-idUSL1N0ZK00720150704|access-date=10 July 2015|work=[[Reuters]]|date=3 July 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150709205522/http://www.reuters.com/article/2015/07/04/venezuela-forex-idUSL1N0ZK00720150704|archive-date=9 July 2015|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=600drop>{{cite news|last1=Ulmer|first1=Alexandra|title=Venezuela's unofficial exchange rate tumbles to 600 bolivars per dollar|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-venezuela-forex-idUSKCN0PJ2VT20150709|access-date=10 July 2015|work=[[Reuters]]|date=9 July 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150710034035/http://www.reuters.com/article/2015/07/09/us-venezuela-forex-idUSKCN0PJ2VT20150709|archive-date=10 July 2015|url-status=live}}</ref> By February 2016, the unofficial rate reached 1,000 Bs.F per USD.{{Citation needed|date=August 2019}} In November 2016, the bolívar fuerte saw its largest-ever monthly loss of value; the exchange rate reached 2,000 Bs.F per USD on 21 November 2016 and nearly 3,000 Bs.F per USD only days after.<ref>{{cite news|title=Venezuela's Currency Just Had the Biggest Monthly Collapse Ever|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2016-11-24/venezuela-s-currency-just-had-the-biggest-monthly-collapse-ever|access-date=25 November 2016|work=Bloomberg|date=24 November 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161125044228/http://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2016-11-24/venezuela-s-currency-just-had-the-biggest-monthly-collapse-ever|archive-date=25 November 2016|url-status=live}}</ref> On 29 November 2016, the exchange rate surpassed 3,000 Bs.F per USD. In the month preceding 28 November 2016, the bolívar fuerte lost over 60% of its value.<ref name="REUTbolivar3000" />

On 26 January 2018, the government retired the protected and [[subsidized]] 10 Bs.F per USD exchange rate that was highly overvalued following rampant inflation.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-venezuela-economy/venezuela-eliminates-heavily-subsidized-dipro-forex-rate-idUSKBN1FJ040|title=Venezuela eliminates heavily subsidized DIPRO forex rate|date=30 January 2018|work=Reuters|access-date=2018-01-30|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180130025141/https://www.reuters.com/article/us-venezuela-economy/venezuela-eliminates-heavily-subsidized-dipro-forex-rate-idUSKBN1FJ040|archive-date=30 January 2018|url-status=live}}</ref> On 5 February 2018, the BCV announced a {{sic|99.|6%}} [[devaluation]], with the exchange rate going to 25,000 Bs.F per USD. This made the bolívar fuerte the second least-valued circulating currency in the world based on the official exchange rate, behind only the [[Iranian rial]]. Between September 2017 and August 2018, according to the informal exchange rate, the bolívar fuerte was the least-valued circulating currency in the world.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-venezuela-economy/venezuela-announces-99-6-percent-devaluation-of-official-forex-rate-idUSKBN1FP2WK|title=Venezuela announces 99.6 percent devaluation of official forex rate|date=5 February 2018|work=Reuters|access-date=20 August 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180809220034/https://www.reuters.com/article/us-venezuela-economy/venezuela-announces-99-6-percent-devaluation-of-official-forex-rate-idUSKBN1FP2WK|archive-date=9 August 2018|url-status=live}}</ref> The official exchange rate stood at 248,832 Bs.F per USD as of 10 August 2018, making it the least valued circulating currency in the world based on official exchange rates.<ref name="FX">{{Cite web |url=http://bcv.org.ve/ |title=Banco Central de Venezuela &#124; |access-date=2019-06-07 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190607155444/http://www.bcv.org.ve/ |archive-date=2019-06-07 |url-status=live }}</ref>{{Failed verification|date=August 2019}}

In June 2018, the government authorized a new exchange rate for buying, but not selling currency. On 13 August 2018, the rate was 4,010,000 Bs.F per USD according to ZOOM Remesas.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.casadecambiozoom.com/ |title=Casa de Cambio ZOOM |access-date=2018-06-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180623033202/https://www.casadecambiozoom.com/ |archive-date=2018-06-23 |url-status=live }}</ref>{{Failed verification|date=August 2019}}

=== Minimum wage ===
The [[minimum wage]] in Venezuela dropped significantly in dollar terms during Maduro's presidency. It decreased from about {{$|lk=on}}360 per month in 2012 to $31 per month in March 2015 based on the weakest legal exchange rate.<ref name=BLOOM6march>{{cite news|last1=Crooks|first1=Nathan|last2=Rosati|first2=Andrew|last3=Jamrisko|first3=Michelle|title=Monthly Salary of $20 Shows Why Venezuelans Wait in Food Lines|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2015-03-06/monthly-salary-of-20-shows-why-venezuelans-wait-in-food-lines|access-date=29 March 2015|agency=[[Bloomberg Business]]|date=6 March 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150321203010/http://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2015-03-06/monthly-salary-of-20-shows-why-venezuelans-wait-in-food-lines|archive-date=21 March 2015|url-status=live}}</ref> On the Venezuelan currency [[black market]], the minimum wage was only $20 per month.<ref name=BLOOM6march/>

In April 2014, President Maduro raised the minimum wage by 30%, hoping to improve citizens' purchasing power.<ref>{{cite news|title=Aumento del salario mínimo entra en vigencia este jueves|url=http://www.lapatilla.com/site/2014/04/30/aumento-del-salario-minimo-entra-en-vigencia-este-jueves/|access-date=1 May 2014|newspaper=La Patilla|date=30 April 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140501003740/http://www.lapatilla.com/site/2014/04/30/aumento-del-salario-minimo-entra-en-vigencia-este-jueves/|archive-date=1 May 2014|url-status=live}}</ref> According to ''[[El Nuevo Herald]]'', most economists said that the measure would only help temporarily due to the official inflation rate being over 59%, and that the wage increase would only make things more difficult for companies, since they already faced a shortage of currency.<ref name=ENHwageincrease>{{cite news|last=Maria Delgado|first=Antonio|title=Nicolás Maduro asesta otra estocada al sector privado en Venezuela|url=http://www.elnuevoherald.com/2014/05/01/1738143/maduro-asesta-otra-estocada-al.html|access-date=2 May 2014|newspaper=El Nuevo Herald|date=1 May 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140502130939/http://www.elnuevoherald.com/2014/05/01/1738143/maduro-asesta-otra-estocada-al.html|archive-date=2 May 2014|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Incremento salarial podría intensificar la inflación y agudizar la escasez|url=http://www.lapatilla.com/site/2014/04/30/incremento-salarial-podria-intensificar-la-inflacion-y-agudizar-la-escasez/|access-date=1 May 2014|newspaper=La Patilla|date=30 April 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140501003615/http://www.lapatilla.com/site/2014/04/30/incremento-salarial-podria-intensificar-la-inflacion-y-agudizar-la-escasez/|archive-date=1 May 2014|url-status=live}}</ref> In January 2015, the government announced that the minimum wage would be raised by 15%.<ref name=AP1may2015>{{cite news|last1=Goodman |first1=Joshua |title=Venezuela Raises Minimum Wage 30 Pct Amid Raging Inflation |url=http://hosted.ap.org/dynamic/stories/L/LT_VENEZUELA_MINIMUM_WAGE?SITE=AP |access-date=10 May 2015 |agency=[[Associated Press]] |date=1 May 2015 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150518080934/http://hosted.ap.org/dynamic/stories/L/LT_VENEZUELA_MINIMUM_WAGE?SITE=AP |archive-date=18 May 2015 }}</ref> On 1 May 2015, President Maduro announced that the minimum wage would increase by 30%, including 20% in May and 10% in July. The newly announced minimum wage was about $30 per month at the black market rate.<ref name=AP1may2015/>

In August 2018, following the release of a new currency, the minimum wage was raised from 392,646 Bs.F to 180 million Bs.F (equivalent to 1,800 bolívares soberanos, or Bs.S) per month.<ref>[https://www.businessinsider.com/venezuela-devalues-bolivar-and-pegs-it-to-cryptocurrency-2018-8?IR=T Venezuela just devalued the bolivar by 95% and pegged it to a cryptocurrency] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181118210952/https://www.businessinsider.com/venezuela-devalues-bolivar-and-pegs-it-to-cryptocurrency-2018-8?IR=T |date=2018-11-18 }} – Business Insider</ref><ref name="wp min wage">{{Cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/the_americas/venezuela-hikes-wages-ahead-of-monetary-overhaul/2018/08/17/5ab064d2-a281-11e8-a3dd-2a1991f075d5_story.htmlx`|title=Venezuela hikes wages ahead of monetary overhaul|date=2018-08-17|newspaper=Washington Post|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190607172304/https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/the_americas/venezuela-hikes-wages-ahead-of-monetary-overhaul/2018/08/17/5ab064d2-a281-11e8-a3dd-2a1991f075d5_story.htmlx%2560|archive-date=2019-06-07|url-status=dead|access-date=2018-08-24}}</ref> [[Sales tax]] was increased from 12% to 16%.<ref name="wp min wage" /> The new wage was estimated to be around $30 per month at the black market rate.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.apnews.com/7b5c293cfe164f17a0c303bae17d4db7|title=Venezuela hikes wages ahead of monetary overhaul|date=18 August 2018|work=[[Associated Press]]|access-date=11 June 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181205181742/https://www.apnews.com/7b5c293cfe164f17a0c303bae17d4db7|archive-date=5 December 2018|url-status=live}}</ref> It became effective on 1 September 2018.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.xinhuanet.com/english/2018-08/21/c_137405553.htm|title=Feature: Venezuela's new currency met with anticipation|date=21 August 2018|work=[[Xinhua]]|access-date=11 June 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180820234512/http://www.xinhuanet.com/english/2018-08/21/c_137405553.htm|archive-date=20 August 2018|url-status=dead}}</ref> The minimum wage was further increased to 4,500 Bs.S ($9.50) a month in November 2018 and then to 18,000 Bs.S ($6.52) a month in January 2019, a 300% increase.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2018-11-30/venezuela-raises-monthly-minimum-wage-for-sixth-time-in-2018|title=Venezuela Raises Monthly Minimum Wage for Sixth Time in 2018|last1=Orozco|first1=Jose|date=30 November 2018|work=[[Bloomberg News|Bloomberg]]|access-date=23 August 2019|last2=Vasquez|first2=Alex|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190809143938/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2018-11-30/venezuela-raises-monthly-minimum-wage-for-sixth-time-in-2018|archive-date=9 August 2019|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2019/01/venezuela-maduro-hikes-minimum-wage-economy-struggles-190114203539977.html|title=Venezuela's Maduro hikes minimum wage as economy struggles|date=15 January 2019|work=[[Al Jazeera English|Al Jazeera]]|access-date=23 August 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190823064205/https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2019/01/venezuela-maduro-hikes-minimum-wage-economy-struggles-190114203539977.html|archive-date=23 August 2019|url-status=live}}</ref>

By early April 2019, the 18,000 Bs.S monthly minimum wage was the equivalent of $5.50 – less than the price of a [[McDonald's]] [[Happy Meal]].<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2019-04-09/venezuela-unemployment-nears-that-of-war-ruined-bosnia-imf-says |publisher= Bloomberg |title= Venezuela unemployment nears that of war-ruined Bosnia, IMF says |author= Biller, David and Patricia Laya |date= 9 April 2019 |access-date= 9 April 2019 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20190409134653/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2019-04-09/venezuela-unemployment-nears-that-of-war-ruined-bosnia-imf-says |archive-date= 9 April 2019 |url-status= live }}</ref> Ecoanalitica estimated that prices jumped by 465% in the first two and a half months of 2019.<ref name=9Charts>{{cite news |title= Venezuela's economic collapse explained in nine charts; Venezuela's decline is now deeper than that of the Soviet Union after its breakup, and comparable only to Zimbabwe's in the late 1990s, economists say |author= Pérez, Santiago |work= Wall Street Journal |date= 25 March 2019 }}</ref> In March 2019, ''[[The Wall Street Journal]]'' stated that the "main cause of hyperinflation is the central bank printing money to fund gaping public spending deficits", reporting that a teacher could only buy a dozen eggs and two pounds of cheese with a month's wages.<ref name= 9Charts/>

On 27 April 2019, President [[Nicolás Maduro]] increased the minimum wage from 18,000 Bs.S ($3.46) to 40,000 Bs.S ($7.69), according to a presidential decree. In addition, President Maduro also announced the resumption of food vouchers worth 25,000 Bs.S ($4.80). The new wages became effective on 1 May 2019.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.novinite.com/articles/196724/The+President+of+Venezuela+Raises+the+Minimum+Wage|title=The President of Venezuela Raises the Minimum Wage|date=27 April 2019|work=novinite.com|access-date=22 August 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190514061202/https://www.novinite.com/articles/196724/The+President+of+Venezuela+Raises+the+Minimum+Wage|archive-date=14 May 2019|url-status=live}}</ref> According to a local NGO, the new minimum wage covers only one tenth of the cost of basic food products. The wage only allows Venezuelans to buy about four kilograms of beef or two McDonald's Happy Meals per month.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.businessinsider.co.za/venezuela-mcdonalds-happy-meal-more-than-months-minimum-salary-march-2019-5-2|title=Venezuela's hyperinflation is so bad that a McDonald's Happy Meal briefly cost more than a month's salary|last=Christofaro|first=Beatrice|date=14 May 2019|work=[[Business Insider]]|access-date=22 August 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190822083836/https://www.businessinsider.co.za/venezuela-mcdonalds-happy-meal-more-than-months-minimum-salary-march-2019-5-2|archive-date=22 August 2019|url-status=live}}</ref> By mid-August 2019, further inflation of the bolívar soberano had decreased the minimum wage by 65% from $8 a month to $2.80 a month<ref name="EU" /> and it had decreased further to $2 a month by late August.<ref name = "EU2" />

=== Government spending ===
{{Expand section|date=August 2019}}
In 2014, ''[[El Nuevo Herald]]'' reported that due a lack of money, [[SEBIN]] had decreased its work of monitoring of "potential external threats" and asked for [[Dirección de Inteligencia|Cuban intelligence agents]] to return to Venezuela.<ref>{{cite news|title=La crisis golpea a los servicios de inteligencia de Venezuela|url=http://www.elnuevoherald.com/2014/04/13/1724939/la-crisis-golpea-a-los-servicios.html|access-date=15 April 2014|newspaper=El Nuevo Herald|date=13 April 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140415180712/http://www.elnuevoherald.com/2014/04/13/1724939/la-crisis-golpea-a-los-servicios.html|archive-date=15 April 2014|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Inflation rate ==

=== BCV estimates ===
Under President Maduro, the inflation rate has been increasing at the highest levels, with the [[Central Bank of Venezuela|BCV]] estimating that inflation was at 56% in 2013, 69% in 2014 (highest in the world), and 181% in 2015 (highest in the world and the country's history). In 2016, Venezuela entered hyperinflation. The inflation rate reached 274% in 2016, 863% in 2017, 130,060% in 2018 and 9,586% in 2019.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-venezuela-economy-idUSKBN1ZY2YQ|title=Venezuela's inflation tumbles to 9,586% in 2019: central bank|date=2020-02-04|work=Reuters|access-date=2020-02-05|language=en}}</ref> Since 2016, the overall inflation rate has increased to 53,798,500%.<ref name="Al Dia"/>

=== National Assembly estimates ===
[[File:Venezuela hyperinflation.webp|thumb|350px|Venezuela hyperinflation May 2018 - October 2019]]
Since 2017, the opposition-led [[National Assembly (Venezuela)|National Assembly]] has been estimating the inflation rate after the BCV stopped publishing inflation rates between 2015 and 2019.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://voanews.com/americas/national-assembly-venezuelas-january-october-inflation-826-percent|title=National Assembly: Venezuela's January–October Inflation 826 Percent|date=7 November 2017|work=[[Voice of America]]|access-date=23 August 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190823105617/https://www.voanews.com/americas/national-assembly-venezuelas-january-october-inflation-826-percent|archive-date=23 August 2019|url-status=dead}}</ref> In May 2019, Venezuela's annual inflation rate dropped below 1,000,000% for the first time since 2018, with the BCV restricting the domestic money supply.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://uk.reuters.com/article/us-venezuela-economy/venezuela-inflation-falls-below-1-million-percent-in-may-for-first-time-since-2018-congress-idUKKCN1TB2GP|title=Venezuela inflation falls below 1 million percent in May for first time since 2018: congress|date=10 June 2019|work=[[Reuters]]|access-date=10 June 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190610230654/https://uk.reuters.com/article/us-venezuela-economy/venezuela-inflation-falls-below-1-million-percent-in-may-for-first-time-since-2018-congress-idUKKCN1TB2GP|archive-date=10 June 2019|url-status=dead}}</ref>

=== IMF estimates ===
In its World Economic Outlook report, the IMF has provided inflation rate estimates between 1998 and 2019. In 2018, the annual inflation rate reached 929,790% and was expected to reach 10,000,000% by the end of 2019.<ref name="WSJ0519" /> According to the October 2019 World Economic Outlook report, Venezuela's inflation rate of 500,000 is the highest in the world. In comparison, in Latin America, [[Argentina]] has an inflation rate of 43.7%.<ref name="IMF" />

===''Café Con Leche'' and Misery Indexes ===
[[Bloomberg L.P.|Bloomberg]]'s ''Café Con Leche'' Index calculated the price of a cup of coffee to have increased 718% in the 12 weeks before 18 January 2018, an annualized inflation rate of 448,000%.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2018-01-18/venezuelan-hyperinflation-explodes-soaring-over-440-000-percent|title=Venezuelan Hyperinflation Explodes, Soaring Over 440,000 Percent|date=18 January 2018|work=Bloomberg|access-date=7 March 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180317191311/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2018-01-18/venezuelan-hyperinflation-explodes-soaring-over-440-000-percent|archive-date=17 March 2018|url-status=live}}</ref>

Venezuela's [[Misery index (economics)|misery rate]] was forecasted to reach 8,000,000% in 2019, making it the world's most miserable economy. The country has topped Bloomberg's [[Misery index (economics)|Misery Index]] for the fifth consecutive year since 2013.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2019-04-17/the-world-s-most-miserable-economy-has-seven-figure-inflation|title=The World's Most Miserable Economy Has Seven-Figure Inflation|newspaper=Bloomberg.com|date=17 April 2019|publisher=Bloomberg|access-date=17 April 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190418010645/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2019-04-17/the-world-s-most-miserable-economy-has-seven-figure-inflation|archive-date=18 April 2019|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Exchange rate history ==
Under Venezuelan law, it is illegal to publish unofficial exchange rates, including the "[[Exchange rate#Parallel exchange rate|parallel exchange rate]]", in Venezuela.<ref name="NYT_Feb08">{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/02/09/world/americas/09venez.html|title=In Venezuela, Faith in Chávez Starts to Wane|author=Simon Romero|date=9 February 2008|work=New York Times|author-link=Simon Romero}}</ref> One popular website that has been publishing parallel exchange rates since 2010 is [[DolarToday]], which has also been critical of the Maduro government.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://cpj.org/blog/2013/12/venezuela-forces-isps-to-police-internet.php|title=Venezuela forces ISPs to police Internet|author=Otis, John|date=12 December 2013|publisher=[[Committee to Protect Journalists]]|access-date=15 May 2015}}</ref> These tables and graphs show the exchange rate history of both the ''bolívar fuerte'' and the ''bolívar soberano'' compared to the [[United States dollar]] (USD) between 2012 and 2021.<ref name="dolartoday">{{Cite web |url=https://dxj1e0bbbefdtsyig.woldrssl.net/custom/dolartoday.xlsx |title=DolarToday Venezuela | format=XLSX |access-date=2019-06-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190617102732/https://dxj1e0bbbefdtsyig.woldrssl.net/custom/dolartoday.xlsx |archive-date=2019-06-17 |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[File:Venezuela inflation on the black market (DolarToday) on a logarithmic scale.png|thumb|550px|The value of one U.S. dollar in Venezuelan bolívares fuertes (before 20 August 2018) and bolívares soberanos on the parallel (or black) market through time. Blue and red vertical lines represent each time the currency has lost 99% of its remaining value, which has happened five times since 2012. This graph shows that as of March 2020, the currency is worth 750 million times less<!--As of 8 March 2020--> than it was worth in August 2012. Since the beginning of [[Venezuelan presidential crisis|the presidential crisis in Venezuela]] in January 2019, the curve has been less steep than previously, meaning that the rate at which the value is lost, [[inflation]], has slowed down.]]

== Effects ==
=== Unemployment ===
Unemployment has been increasing in the years of hyperinflation with the 2019 rate seen as Venezuela's highest since the end of the [[Bosnian War]] in 1995 and the biggest contraction since 2014 start of [[Libyan Civil War]], according to the [[International Monetary Fund]] (IMF).<ref>{{cite news|author=Biller, David and Patricia Laya|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2019-04-09/venezuela-unemployment-nears-that-of-war-ruined-bosnia-imf-says|title=Venezuela unemployment nears that of war-ruined Bosnia, IMF says|date=9 April 2019|access-date=9 April 2019|publisher=Bloomberg}}</ref> In January 2016, the unemployment rate was 18.1%<ref name=imf-datamapper>{{cite web|title=Unemployment rate by World|url=http://www.imf.org/external/datamapper/LUR@WEO/OEMDC/ADVEC/WEOWORLD}}</ref> and the economy was the worst in the world according to the [[Misery index (economics)|misery index]].<ref name=economia.uol>{{cite web |title= Venezuela deve continuar como economia mais miseravel do mundo |url= https://economia.uol.com.br/noticias/bloomberg/2016/02/04/venezuela-deve-continuar-como-economia-mais-miseravel-do-mundo.htm |date= 4 February 2016 |website= economia.uol.com.br |access-date= 3 May 2017}}</ref> Venezuela has not reported official unemployment figures since April 2016, when the rate was at 7.3%.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-venezuela-economy-idUSKBN16926M|title=Job losses, low wages add to Venezuela economic hardship|author=Chinea, Eyanir|date=2 March 2017|publisher=Reuters|access-date=7 December 2018}}</ref>
 
In October 2019, the unemployment rate reached 35%.<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.bancaynegocios.com/ivan-acosta-pga-group-el-problema-no-es-solo-el-salario-sino-el-desempleo-que-ya-llega-a-35/ | title=Iván Acosta (PGA Group): el problema no es solo el salario sino el desempleo que ya llega a 35%|date= 18 October 2019| publisher=Banca y Negocios}}</ref> By the end of the year, it was estimated that it would increase to 39% to 40%, and that 60% of the economically active population belong to the informal sector, which influences the low salary that has caused many young people to emigrate to other countries.<ref>{{cite web|url= http://www.bancaynegocios.com/expertos-conozca-por-que-el-desempleo-se-puede-ubicar-sobre-40-en-2019/| title= Expertos: Conozca por qué el desempleo se puede ubicar sobre 40% en 2019|date= 20 October 2019| publisher=Banca y Negocios|language=es}}</ref>

=== Refugee and migration crisis ===
{{main|Venezuelan refugee crisis}}

Emigration in Venezuela existed in a moderate way under Maduro's predecessor [[Hugo Chávez]]. By 2015, almost 30% of the population had fled the country due to inflation, and it is at that time that the country entered hyperinflation. The [[Organization of American States]] (OAS) and [[United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees|UNHCR]] has been classified as one of the largest emigrations in the history of the [[Western Hemisphere|Western hemisphere]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.bancaynegocios.com/estos-son-los-paises-latinoamericanos-que-aceptan-pasaportes-venezolanos-vencidos/ |title=Estos son los países latinoamericanos que aceptan pasaportes venezolanos vencidos|date=25 February 2020|publisher=Banca y Negocios|language=es}}</ref>

According to the [[United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees|UNHCR]], the deterioration of the political, economic and human rights situation in Venezuela continues, making international support necessary. The latest report discloses that 4.8 million Venezuelans are registered between refugees and migrants.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://eacnur.org/blog/situacion-en-venezuela-la-diaspora-que-no-se-detiene/|title= Situación en Venezuela: la diáspora que no se detiene|date= 10 February 2020|publisher= eacnur}}{{Dead link|date=August 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.acnur.org/es-es/op/rep_am/5e4720df4/acnur-informe-mensual-sobre-las-americas-diciembre-de-2019.html#_ga=2.80877143.135759965.1582560390-1307199078.1582560390|title=Informe mensual, situación Venezuela|date=1 December 2019| publisher=UNHCR|language=es}}</ref>

== Solutions and adaptations==
=== Change of inflation rate calculations ===
In September 2014, the BCV reportedly changed its inflation rate calculation methods from the more common [[Laspeyres price index]] to the [[Price index#Fisher index and Marshall.E2.80.93Edgeworth index|Fisher price index]]. This changed the government's June inflation data from 5.7% to 4.4%, July's 5.5% rate to 4.1%, and August's 4.3% to 3.9%.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Blanco|first1=Dayrí|title=Cambio de fórmula para cálculo de inflación no modificará la realidad|url=http://www.el-carabobeno.com/portada/articulo/88721/cambio-de-frmula-para-clculo-de-inflacin-no-modificar-la-realidad-|access-date=24 September 2014|agency=El Carabobeno|date=9 September 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150923235028/http://www.el-carabobeno.com/portada/articulo/88721/cambio-de-frmula-para-clculo-de-inflacin-no-modificar-la-realidad-|archive-date=23 September 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=AVsept2014>{{cite news|title=Banco Central de Venezuela, maquilla las cifras de inflación|url=https://ahoravision.com/banco-central-de-venezuela-maquilla-las-cifras-de-inflacion/|access-date=24 September 2014|agency=AhoraVision|date=9 September 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304072405/https://ahoravision.com/banco-central-de-venezuela-maquilla-las-cifras-de-inflacion/|archive-date=4 March 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref>< It was also stated in the BCV's August report that it was an "economic war that hindered the normal course of production activities and distribution of essential goods demanded by the Venezuelan people".<ref>{{cite news|title=El último párrafo del informe del BCV que causa indignación|url=http://www.lapatilla.com/site/2014/09/09/el-ultimo-parrafo-del-informe-del-bcv-que-causa-indignacion/|access-date=24 September 2014|agency=La Patilla|date=9 September 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140913142434/http://www.lapatilla.com/site/2014/09/09/el-ultimo-parrafo-del-informe-del-bcv-que-causa-indignacion/|archive-date=13 September 2014|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Bolívar fuerte ===
[[File:Venezuelans queuing at banks in Caracas.ogv|thumb|Venezuelans lining up at the [[Banco de Venezuela]] branch in [[Chacao Municipality|Chacao]] to deposit the 100 Bs.F note after President Maduro withdrew it from circulation.]]
On 7 March 2007, the Chávez administration announced that the bolívar would be revalued at a ratio of 1,000 to 1 on 1 January 2008, and renamed it the ''bolívar fuerte'' in an effort to facilitate the ease of transaction and accounting, responding to double-digit inflation.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.republica-de-venezuela.com/about-venezuela/currency-of-venezuela.php |title=Currency of Venezuela – Venezuela's new currency the Venezuelan Bolívar fuerte |website=Republica-de-venezuela.com |access-date=2016-12-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161112064816/http://www.republica-de-venezuela.com/about-venezuela/currency-of-venezuela.php |archive-date=2016-11-12 |url-status=live }}</ref> The new name is literally translated as "strong bolívar".<ref>television advertisements [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Krn_8PSjCCg Bolivar Fuerte Bs.F] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190420043921/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Krn_8PSjCCg |date=2019-04-20 }} for the new currency repeatedly use "fuerte" as meaning "strong" such as in "Una economía fuerte" (a strong economy) and "¡Aquí hay fuerza!" (There's strength in this!)</ref><ref>{{cite news |first=Jorge |last=Rueda |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/bondsNews/idUSN0160996920080101 |title=Venezuela cuts three zeros off bolivar currency |work=Reuters |date=2008-01-01 |access-date=2008-02-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080104074358/http://www.reuters.com/article/bondsNews/idUSN0160996920080101 |archive-date=2008-01-04 |url-status=live }}</ref> It is also a reference to the ''peso fuerte'', an old coin worth 10 [[Spanish real]]es.<ref>{{cite web |author=Numismatic Catalog of Venezuela |url=https://www.numismatica.info.ve/en/coins/mv-p.htm |title=Coins in Pesos Fuerte |access-date=2008-02-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170309140238/http://www.numismatica.info.ve/en/coins/mv-p.htm |archive-date=2017-03-09 |url-status=live }}</ref> The official exchange rate is restricted to individuals by [[CADIVI]], which imposes an annual limit on the amount available for travel.

==== Introduction of higher denomination banknotes ====
Denominations of 2 and 5 Bs.F banknotes were no longer found in circulation due to the inflation in 2015, but remained legal tender. By early December 2016, the 100 Bs.F note—Venezuela's largest denomination of currency—was only worth about US$0.23 on the black market.<ref name="DW20000">{{cite news|title=Venezuela's new banknotes|url=http://www.dw.com/en/venezuelas-new-banknotes/av-36692086|access-date=9 December 2016|work=[[Deutsche Welle]]|date=8 December 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161208144803/http://www.dw.com/en/venezuelas-new-banknotes/av-36692086|archive-date=8 December 2016|url-status=live}}</ref> On 7 December 2016, a new series of notes (recolors of previous notes) in denominations of 500, 1,000, 2,000, 5,000, 10,000, and 20,000 Bs.F were unveiled to the public.<ref name="DW20000" />

On 3 November 2017, President Maduro unveiled a 100,000 Bs.F note, which was similar to the 2007-series 100 Bs.F note and the 2016-series 20,000 Bs.F note, but with the denomination spelled out in full instead of adding an additional three zeros after 100. This denomination was worth US$2.42 through black market exchange rates at the time of its release.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.businessinsider.my/venezuelas-new-note-is-worth-just-250-2017-11/?r=US&IR=T|title=Venezuela's new 100,000-bolivar note is worth less than $2.50 in US dollars|last=Perper|first=Rosie|date=6 November 2017|work=[[Business Insider]]|access-date=7 November 2017}}{{Dead link|date=August 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.dw.com/en/venezuela-introduces-100000-bolivar-bill-worth-2/a-41202082|title=Venezuela introduces 100,000 bolivar bill worth $2|date=2 November 2017|work=[[Deutsche Welle]]|access-date=7 November 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171106082631/http://www.dw.com/en/venezuela-introduces-100000-bolivar-bill-worth-2/a-41202082|archive-date=6 November 2017|url-status=live}}</ref> By July 2018, increasing hyperinflation had reduced its value by 99.9% to less than US$0.01.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.dw.com/en/inflation-hit-venezuela-to-remove-five-zeros-from-currency/a-44829497|title=Inflation-hit Venezuela to remove five zeros from currency|date=26 July 2018|work=[[Deutsche Welle]]|access-date=1 August 2018|quote=For ordinary Venezuelans, paper money is hard to get. The largest bill in the country today is the 100,000-bolivar note, equal to less than 1 cent on the commonly used black market exchange rate. A simple lunch easily costs 3 million bolivars.|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180731072748/https://www.dw.com/en/inflation-hit-venezuela-to-remove-five-zeros-from-currency/a-44829497|archive-date=31 July 2018|url-status=live}}</ref>

On 6 March 2021, the government issued three new bills, worth Bs.S 200,000, 500,000, and 1,000,000. The last is worth US$0.52.<ref>{{cite news |title=Venezuela lanzó un billete de 1 millón de bolívares que vale 52 centavos de dólar |url=https://www.infobae.com/america/venezuela/2021/03/06/venezuela-lanzo-un-billete-de-1-millon-de-bolivares-que-vale-52-centavos-de-dolar/ |access-date=March 6, 2021 |work=infobae |publisher=Infobae |date=March 6, 2021 |language=es-ES}}</ref>

==== Withdrawal of the 100 Bs.F banknote ====
{{Quote box
 |quote  = "I have given the orders to close all land, maritime and air possibilities so those bills taken out can’t be returned and they’re stuck with their fraud abroad. There has been a scam and smuggling of 100 Bs.F bills on the border with Colombia and we have tried the diplomatic way to deal with this problem with Colombia’s government; there are huge mafias. On the border with Colombia all the exchange houses are in the hands of mafias linked to the right-wing. I have taken the decision to close the border with Colombia for 72 hours."
 |author = President [[Nicolás Maduro]] announcing the withdrawal of the 100 Bs.F banknotes within for 72 hours. (11 December 2016)
 |source = 
 |width  = 30%
 |qalign = center
}}
On 11 December 2016, President Maduro, who had been [[ruling by decree]], wrote into law that 100 Bs.F notes would be pulled from circulation within 72 hours due to "mafias" allegedly storing them to drive inflation.<ref name="AFPboli">{{cite news|title=Venezuela's Maduro orders 100-unit banknotes out of circulation|url=https://sports.yahoo.com/news/venezuelas-maduro-orders-100-unit-banknotes-circulation-224549605.html|access-date=12 December 2016|work=AFP|date=11 December 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161212060910/http://sports.yahoo.com/news/venezuelas-maduro-orders-100-unit-banknotes-circulation-224549605.html|archive-date=12 December 2016|url-status=live}}</ref> With more than 6&nbsp;billion 100 Bs.F notes issued consisting of 46% of Venezuela's issued currency, Maduro allowed for Venezuelans to exchange all 100 Bs.F notes for 100 Bs.F coins or higher denomination banknotes while also blocking international travel to prevent the return of notes that were supposedly stockpiled.<ref name="AFPboli" /><ref>{{cite news|title=Venezuela pulls most common banknote from circulation to 'beat mafia'|url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2016/dec/12/venezuela-pulls-most-common-banknote-from-circulation-to-beat-mafia|access-date=12 December 2016|work=[[The Guardian]]|date=11 December 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161212043749/https://www.theguardian.com/world/2016/dec/12/venezuela-pulls-most-common-banknote-from-circulation-to-beat-mafia|archive-date=12 December 2016|url-status=live}}</ref> The government justified the move by claiming that the US was working with crime syndicates to move Venezuelan banknotes to warehouses in Europe to cause the fall of the government, and that the government was thwarting this threat by withdrawing the notes from circulation.<ref>{{cite news|title=Declaring war on common sense, Venezuela bans its own money|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/global-opinions/wp/2016/12/15/declaring-war-on-common-sense-venezuela-bans-its-own-money/|newspaper=Washington Post|date=15 December 2016|access-date=7 June 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190604114922/https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/global-opinions/wp/2016/12/15/declaring-war-on-common-sense-venezuela-bans-its-own-money/|archive-date=4 June 2019|url-status=live}}</ref> The government of India has done a similar action in November 2016, by [[2016 Indian banknote demonetisation|withdrawing the 500 and 1000 rupee notes]] from circulation that would curtail the shadow economy and reduce the use of illicit and counterfeit cash to fund illegal activity and terrorism.<ref name="India Today2">{{cite web|url=https://www.indiatoday.in/india/story/live-pm-narendra-modi-addresses-nation-350943-2016-11-08|title=Here is what PM Modi said about the new Rs 500, Rs 2000 notes and black money|date=8 November 2016|access-date=9 November 2016|work=India Today|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161108230421/http://indiatoday.intoday.in/story/live-pm-narendra-modi-addresses-nation/1/805755.html|archive-date=8 November 2016|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/india/Rs-500-and-Rs-100-notes-pulled-out-of-circulation-immediately-PM-Narendra-Modi/articleshow/55315473.cms|title=Notes out of circulation|date=8 November 2016|work=The Times of India|access-date=23 August 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180624180909/https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/india/Rs-500-and-Rs-100-notes-pulled-out-of-circulation-immediately-PM-Narendra-Modi/articleshow/55315473.cms|archive-date=24 June 2018|url-status=live}}</ref>

On 14 February 2017, [[Paraguayan]] authorities uncovered a {{Convert|30|t|lb|abbr=out|adj=on}} stash of 50 and 100 Bs.F banknotes totaling 1.5&nbsp;billion Bs.F on [[Brazil–Paraguay border|its Brazilian border]] that had not yet been circulated.<ref name="EJUlaunder">{{cite news|last1=Coutinho|first1=Leonardo|title=Veja: Venezuela y Bolivia son sospechosas de esquema estatal de lavado|url=http://eju.tv/2017/02/veja-venezuela-y-bolivia-son-sospechosas-de-esquema-estatal-de-lavado/|access-date=24 February 2017|work=Eju TV|date=23 February 2017|language=es-ES|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170224015144/http://eju.tv/2017/02/veja-venezuela-y-bolivia-son-sospechosas-de-esquema-estatal-de-lavado/|archive-date=24 February 2017|url-status=live}}</ref> According to a [[US Department of Defense]] adviser linked to [[The Pentagon]], the 1.5&nbsp;billion Bs.F was printed by Venezuela and destined for [[Bolivia]], since unlike the implied exchange rate of thousands of Bs.F per USD, the exchange rate was approximately 10 Bs.F per USD, making the value of the stash 419 times stronger, from US$358,000 to US$150&nbsp;million.<ref name="EJUlaunder" /> The adviser further stated that the Venezuelan government tried to send the newly printed notes to be exchanged by the [[Bolivian government]], so Bolivia could pay 20% of its debt to Venezuela, and so Venezuela could use the [[United States dollar|US dollars]] for its own disposal.<ref name="EJUlaunder" />

=== Petro cryptocurrency ===
{{main|Petro (cryptocurrency)}}
[[File:Petro (cryptocurrency) logo.png|thumb|150px|[[Petro (cryptocurrency)|Petro]] Logo]]
In December 2017, President Maduro announced that Venezuela would introduce a state [[cryptocurrency]] called the 'Petro' in an attempt to shore up its struggling economy. This new cryptocurrency would be backed by Venezuela's reserves of [[petroleum|oil]], [[gasoline]], [[gold]], and [[diamond]]s.<ref name="NYT">{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/12/03/world/americas/venezuela-cryptocurrency-maduro.html|title=Venezuela Plans a Cryptocurrency, Maduro Says|work=[[The New York Times]]|date=3 December 2017|access-date=3 December 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171204171215/https://www.nytimes.com/2017/12/03/world/americas/venezuela-cryptocurrency-maduro.html|archive-date=4 December 2017|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Reuters">{{cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-venezuela-economy/enter-the-petro-venezuela-to-launch-oil-backed-cryptocurrency-idUSKBN1DX0SQ|title=Enter the 'petro': Venezuela to launch oil-backed cryptocurrency|last=Ulmer|first=Alexandra|author2=Deisy Buitrago|work=[[Reuters]]|date=3 December 2017|access-date=3 December 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171203232445/https://www.reuters.com/article/us-venezuela-economy/enter-the-petro-venezuela-to-launch-oil-backed-cryptocurrency-idUSKBN1DX0SQ|archive-date=3 December 2017|url-status=live}}</ref> Maduro stated that the Petro would allow Venezuela to "advance in issues of [[monetary sovereignty]]",<ref>{{Cite news |ssrn = 3079241|title = Cryptoanarchism and Cryptocurrencies|date = 27 November 2017|last1 = Chohan|first1 = Usman W.}}</ref> and that it would make "new forms of international financing" available to the country.<ref name="NYT"/> [[Democratic Unity Roundtable|Opposition]] leaders, however, expressed doubt due to [[Economy of Venezuela#2013–present|Venezuela's economic turmoil]],<ref name="Reuters"/> pointing to the falling value of the Venezuelan bolívar, its [[fiat currency]], and $140 billion in [[Foreign Debt|foreign debt]].<ref name="BBC">{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-latin-america-42217798|title=Venezuela unveils virtual currency amid economic crisis|publisher=[[BBC]]|date=3 December 2017|access-date=3 December 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171204011023/http://www.bbc.com/news/world-latin-america-42217798|archive-date=4 December 2017|url-status=live}}</ref>

In January 2018, as a response to the petro, Venezuela's [[National Assembly (Venezuela)|National Assembly]], headed by the opposition [[Democratic Unity Roundtable]], declared the petro to be an illegal debt issuance by a government desperate for cash, and said it would not recognize it.<ref name="lesley">{{cite news| last1= Wroughton | first1=Lesley|title=U.S. warns investors over Venezuela's 'petro' cryptocurrency|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-venezuela-economy-cryptocurrency/u-s-warns-investors-over-venezuelas-petro-cryptocurrency-idUSKBN1F52AB|access-date=8 February 2018|work=Reuters|date=16 January 2018}}</ref> On the same month, Maduro announced that Venezuela would issue 100 million [[Tokenization (data security)|tokens]] of the petro,<ref>{{cite news|last1=Gupta|first1=Girish|title=Maduro says Venezuela will issue $5.9 billion in oil-backed cryptocurrency |url= https://www.reuters.com/article/us-venezuela-economy/maduro-says-venezuela-will-issue-5-9-billion-in-oil-backed-cryptocurrency-idUSKBN1EV02S|access-date=8 February 2018|work=Reuters|date=5 January 2018}}</ref> which would put the value of the entire issuance at just over $6 billion. It also established a cryptocurrency government advisory group called VIBE to act as "an institutional, political and legal base" from which to launch the petro.<ref name="NPR">{{cite news|url= https://www.npr.org/sections/thetwo-way/2017/12/04/568299704/venezuela-will-create-new-petro-cryptocurrency-president-maduro-says|title=Venezuela Will Create New 'Petro' Cryptocurrency, President Maduro Says|last=Chappell|first=Bill|work=[[National Public Radio]]|date=4 December 2017|access-date=5 December 2017}}</ref>

In March 2018, US President [[Donald Trump]] signed an [[executive order]] prohibiting transactions in any Venezuelan government-issued cryptocurrency by any US citizen or any person within the US, effective on 19 March,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/executive-order-taking-additional-steps-address-situation-venezuela/|title=Executive Order on Taking Additional Steps to Address the Situation in Venezuela|access-date=2019-06-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210120175212/https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/executive-order-taking-additional-steps-address-situation-venezuela/|archive-date=2021-01-20|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.usnews.com/news/business/articles/2018-03-19/trump-bans-us-use-of-venezuelan-cryptocurrency|title=Trump Bans US Use of Venezuelan Cryptocurrency|access-date=2019-06-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190607173324/https://www.usnews.com/news/business/articles/2018-03-19/trump-bans-us-use-of-venezuelan-cryptocurrency|archive-date=2019-06-07|url-status=live}}</ref> after claiming that the cryptocurrency was designed to obfuscate [[US sanctions]] and access international financing.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/americas/us-politics/trump-venezuela-petro-cryptocurrency-sanctions-maduro-a8264221.html|title=Donald Trump has banned all American use of Venezuelan cryptocurrencies|website=[[Independent.co.uk]]|date=19 March 2018|access-date=7 June 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190404090455/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/americas/us-politics/trump-venezuela-petro-cryptocurrency-sanctions-maduro-a8264221.html|archive-date=4 April 2019|url-status=live}}</ref>

In August 2018, the bolívar soberano had a fixed exchange rate of 3,600 Bs.S per Petro.<ref name=bloom2>{{cite news|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2018-08-20/here-s-what-maduro-has-said-of-venezuela-s-petro-cryptocurrency|title=Here's What Maduro Has Said of Venezuela's Petro Cryptocurrency – Bloomberg|newspaper=Bloomberg.com|date=20 August 2018|access-date=2019-06-22|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190622085957/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2018-08-20/here-s-what-maduro-has-said-of-venezuela-s-petro-cryptocurrency|archive-date=2019-06-22|url-status=live}}</ref> The Petro was supposedly tied to the price of a barrel of oil (about US$60 in August 2018).<ref name=bloom2 /> As of late-August 2018, there is no evidence that the Petro is being traded.<ref name="reuters petro">{{cite web |last1=Ellsworth |first1=Brian |title=Special Report: In Venezuela, new cryptocurrency is nowhere to be... |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-cryptocurrency-venezuela-specialrepor/special-report-in-venezuela-new-cryptocurrency-is-nowhere-to-be-found-idUSKCN1LF15U |website=[[Reuters]] |access-date=7 September 2018 |date=30 August 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180831000201/https://www.reuters.com/article/us-cryptocurrency-venezuela-specialrepor/special-report-in-venezuela-new-cryptocurrency-is-nowhere-to-be-found-idUSKCN1LF15U |archive-date=31 August 2018 |url-status=live }}</ref> The Petro is regarded by many as a [[Confidence trick|scam]].<ref name="reuters petro"/><ref name="wired petro scam">{{cite magazine |last1=Moskvitch |first1=Katia |title=Inside the bluster and lies of Petro, Venezuela's cryptocurrency scam |url=https://www.wired.co.uk/article/venezuela-petro-cryptocurrency-bolivar-scam |magazine=[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]] |access-date=11 October 2018 |date=22 August 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181018132135/https://www.wired.co.uk/article/venezuela-petro-cryptocurrency-bolivar-scam |archive-date=18 October 2018 |url-status=live }}</ref>
