======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Money creation
======================================================================

{{Short description|Process by which the money supply of an economic region is increased}}
{{use dmy dates|date=February 2025}}
{{About|the changes in the money supply|how money itself was first created|History of money}}
{{Banking|terms}}
{{Macroeconomics sidebar}}
'''Money creation''', or '''money issuance''', is the process by which the [[money supply]] of a country or economic region is increased. In most modern economies, both [[central bank]]s and [[commercial bank]]s create money. Central banks issue money as a liability, typically called reserve deposits, which is available only for use by central bank account holders. These account holders are generally large commercial banks and foreign central banks.<ref name=bell>{{cite web |last1=Bell |first1=Stephanie |title=The Role of the State and the Hierarchy of Money |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/5208277 |website=Research Gate |publisher=Cambridge Journal of Economics |access-date=29 December 2023}}</ref> 

Central banks can increase the quantity of reserve deposits directly by making loans to account holders, purchasing [[asset]]s from account holders, or by recording an asset (such as a deferred asset) and directly increasing liabilities. However, the majority of the money supply that the public uses for conducting [[Financial transaction|transactions]] is created by the commercial banking system in the form of commercial bank deposits. Bank loans issued by commercial banks expand the quantity of bank deposits.<ref name=bell/>

Money creation occurs when the amount of loans issued by banks increases relative to the repayment and default of existing loans. Governmental authorities, including central banks and other bank regulators, can use various policies—mainly setting short-term [[interest rate]]s—to influence the amount of bank deposits that commercial banks create.<ref name="ecb2017">{{Cite web|url=https://www.ecb.europa.eu/explainers/tell-me-more/html/what_is_money.en.html|title=What is money?|last=European Central Bank|date=20 June 2017|website=European Central Bank|language=en|access-date=8 March 2018}}</ref>

==Monetary policy==
{{Main|Monetary policy}}

The [[monetary authority]] of a nation—typically its [[central bank]]—influences the economy by creating and destroying liabilities on its balance sheet with the intent to change the supply of money available for conducting transactions and generating income. The policy that defines how the central bank changes its ledger to reduce or increase the amount of money in the economy available for banks to conduct transactions is known as monetary policy.

If the central bank is charged by law with maintaining price or employment levels in the economy, monetary policy may include reducing the money supply during times of high inflation to increase unemployment. The hope is that reducing employment will also reduce spending on goods and services that exhibit increasing prices.<ref name=Palgrave/><ref>{{cite web |title=Federal Reserve Board - Monetary Policy: What Are Its Goals? How Does It Work? |url=https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/monetary-policy-what-are-its-goals-how-does-it-work.htm |website=Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System |access-date=15 August 2023 |language=en |date=July 29, 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url= https://fixingtheeconomists.wordpress.com/2014/08/15/does-the-central-banks-control-long-term-interest-rates-a-glance-at-operation-twist/|title= Does the Central Bank Control Long-Term Interest Rates?: A Glance at Operation Twist|last= Pilkington|first= Philip|date= 15 August 2014|website= Fixing the economists|access-date=8 March 2018 }}</ref> Monetary policy directly impacts the availability and cost of commercial bank deposits in the economy,<ref name=fedmon>{{cite web |url= https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy.htm |title= Monetary Policy |publisher= Federal Reserve Board |date= 2024 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20240320175531/https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy.htm |archive-date= March 20, 2024 }}</ref> which in turn impacts investment, stock prices, [[Consumption (economics)|private consumption]], [[demand for money]], and overall economic activity.<ref name=imfmon>{{cite web |url= https://www.imf.org/en/About/Factsheets/Sheets/2023/monetary-policy-and-central-banking |title= Monetary Policy and Central Banking |publisher= International Monetary Fund |date= 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240301165840/https://www.imf.org/en/About/Factsheets/Sheets/2023/monetary-policy-and-central-banking |archive-date= March 1, 2024 }}</ref> A country's [[exchange rate]] influences the value of its [[net export]]s.

In most [[developed countries]], central banks conduct their monetary policy within an [[inflation targeting]] framework,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/fandd/basics/target.htm |title=Inflation Targeting: Holding the Line |last=Jahan |first=Sarwat |publisher=International Monetary Funds, Finance & Development |access-date=17 October 2023}}</ref> whereas the monetary policies of most [[developing countries]]' central banks target some kind of [[fixed exchange rate system]].<ref name=IMF>{{cite book |last1=Department |first1=International Monetary Fund Monetary and Capital Markets |title=Annual Report on Exchange Arrangements and Exchange Restrictions 2022 |date=26 July 2023 |publisher=International Monetary Fund |isbn=979-8-4002-3526-9 |url=https://www.elibrary.imf.org/display/book/9798400235269/9798400235269.xml?code=imf.org |access-date=17 October 2023 |language=en }}</ref> Central banks operate in practically every nation in the world, with few exceptions. There are also groups of countries for which a single entity acts as their central bank, such as the organization of states of Central Africa, which have a common central bank (the [[Bank of Central African States]]), or monetary unions, such as the [[Eurozone]]. In the Eurozone, nations retain their respective central banks yet submit to the policies of a central entity, the [[European Central Bank]].

Central banks conduct monetary policy by setting an interest rate paid on central bank deposit liabilities, directly purchasing or selling assets to change the amount of deposits on their balance sheet, or by signaling to the market through speeches and written guidance an intent to change the interest rate on deposits or to purchase or sell assets in the future.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Baker |first1=Nick |last2=Rafter |first2=Sally |title=An International Perspective on Monetary Policy Implementation Systems {{!}} Bulletin – June 2022 |url=https://www.rba.gov.au/publications/bulletin/2022/jun/an-international-perspective-on-monetary-policy-implementation-systems.html |publisher=Reserve Bank of Australia |access-date=17 October 2023 |language=en-AU |date=16 June 2022}}</ref>

Lowering interest rates by reducing the amount of interest paid on central bank liabilities or purchasing assets like bank loans and government bonds for higher prices (which results in an increase in bank reserve deposits on the central bank ledger) is called [[monetary expansion]] or [[monetary easing]]. In contrast, raising rates by paying more interest on central bank liabilities is known as [[monetary contraction]] or tightening (which results in a decrease of bank reserve deposits on the central bank ledger). An extraordinary process of monetary easing (keeping rates low) is denoted as [[quantitative easing]], which involves the central bank purchasing large amounts of assets for high prices over an extended period.

===Money supply===
{{Main|Money supply}}

[[File:Credit_Mechanics_4_mechanical_interrelationships_governing_the_credit_volume_(Table_1_by_F._Decker_&_C._Goodhart_2021).PNG|thumb|right|upright=2|In accordance with "credit mechanics," bank money expansion or destruction (or lack of change) depends on payment flows.]]
[[File:M2 Monthly Money Supply Changes.webp|thumb|M2 monthly money supply changes]]
The term "money supply" commonly denotes the total, safe, [[financial asset]]s that households and businesses can use to make payments or to hold as short-term investments.<ref name=fedms>[https://www.federalreserve.gov/faqs/money_12845.htm Money supply], [[Federal Reserve System|FRS]]</ref> The money supply is measured using so-called "[[monetary aggregates]]," which are defined based on their respective levels of [[liquidity]]. In the United States, for example:

* '''M0''': The total of all physical currency, including coinage. Using the United States dollar as an example, M0 = [[Federal Reserve note]]s + [[United States Note|US notes]] + [[Coins of the United States dollar|coins]]. It is not relevant whether the currency is held inside or outside of the private banking system as reserves.
* '''M1''': The total amount of M0 (cash/coin) outside of the private banking system{{Clarify|reason=Is this M0 different from the M0 number above? Sounds like M0 above includes reserve balances, M0 here does not?|date=December 2020}} plus the amount of [[demand deposit]]s, [[Traveler's cheque|travelers' checks]] and [[Negotiable Order of Withdrawal account|other checkable deposits]].
* '''M2''': M1 + most [[savings account]]s, [[money market account]]s, retail [[Money market fund|money market mutual funds]], and small denomination time deposits ([[Certificate of deposit|certificates of deposit]] under $100,000).

In most countries, the central bank, treasury, or other designated state authority is empowered to mint new physical currency, usually taking the form of metal coinage or paper banknotes. While the value of major currencies was once backed by the [[gold standard]], the end of the [[Bretton Woods system]] in 1971 led to all major currencies becoming [[fiat money]]—backed by a mutual agreement of value rather than a [[Commodity (type of good)|commodity]].

Various measures are taken to prevent [[Counterfeit money|counterfeiting]], including the use of [[serial number]]s on banknotes and the minting of coinage using an [[alloy]] at or above its face value. Currency may be [[Legal tender#Demonetization|demonetized]] for a variety of reasons, including [[Withdrawal of low-denomination coins|loss of value]] over time due to inflation, [[redenomination]] of its face value due to [[hyperinflation]], or its replacement as [[legal tender]] by another currency. The currency-issuing government agency typically works with commercial banks to distribute freshly minted currency and retrieve worn currency for destruction, enabling the reuse of serial numbers on new banknotes.<ref name=mankiw2012>Mankiw (2012)</ref>

In modern economies, physical currency consists of only a fraction of the [[broad money]] supply.<ref group=note>For example, in December 2010, in the United States, of the $8.853 trillion broad money supply (M2, table 1), only about 10% (or $915.7 billion, table 3) consisted of coins and paper money. See [http://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/h6/20110127/ Statistic], FRS</ref> In the United Kingdom, [[Gross (economic)|gross]] bank [[Deposit (finance)|deposit]]s outweigh the physical currency issued by the central bank by a factor of more than 30 to 1. The United States, with a currency used substantially in legal and illicit international transactions, has a lower ratio of 8 to 1.<ref name="Palgrave">{{cite book |last1=Friedman |first1=Benjamin M. |chapter=Money Supply |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/referenceworkentry/10.1057/978-1-349-95121-5_875-2 |title=The New Palgrave Dictionary of Economics |publisher=Palgrave Macmillan UK |pages=1–10 |language=en |doi=10.1057/978-1-349-95121-5_875-2 |date=2017|isbn=978-1-349-95121-5 }}</ref>

=== Debt monetization ===
{{Main|Debt monetization}}

Debt monetization is a term used to describe central bank money creation for use by government fiscal authorities, such as the U.S. Treasury. In many states, such as Great Britain, all government spending is always financed by central bank money creation.<ref name="Berkeley2020">{{cite web |last1=Berkeley |first1=Andrew |title=An Accounting Model of the UK Exchequer |url=https://gimms.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2021/02/An-Accounting-Model-of-the-UK-Exchequer-2nd-edition.pdf |website=gimms.org.uk |access-date=26 May 2024}}</ref> Debt monetization as a concept is often based on a misunderstanding of modern financial systems compared to fixed exchange rate systems like the gold standard.

Historically,  in a fixed exchange rate financial system, central bank money creation directly for government spending by the fiscal authority was prohibited by law in many countries.<ref name=ryan2015>{{Cite web|url=http://www.levyinstitute.org/publications/is-monetary-financing-inflationary-a-case-study-of-the-canadian-economy-1935-75|title=Is Monetary Financing Inflationary? A Case Study of the Canadian Economy, 1935–75|last=Ryan-Collins|first=Josh|date=25 October 2015|publisher= Levy Economics Institute|access-date=8 March 2018}}</ref> However, in modern financial systems, central banks and fiscal authorities work closely together to manage interest rates and economic stability. This involves the creation and destruction of deposits on the central bank ledger to ensure that transactions can settle so that short-term interest rates do not exceed specified targets.

In the [[Eurozone]], Article 123 of the [[Lisbon Treaty]] explicitly prohibits the [[European Central Bank]] from financing public institutions and state governments.<ref>[https://www.ecb.europa.eu/mopo/eaec/fiscal/html/index.en.html Fiscal policies], ECB</ref> In Japan, the nation's [[Bank of Japan|central bank]] "routinely" purchases approximately 70% of state debt issued each month,<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.businessinsider.com/japans-1-trillion-yen-of-debt-2013-8|title=Japan's Debt Has Officially Passed ¥1,000,000,000,000,000 — No Problem|last= Evans-Pritchard|first= Ambrose|author-link= Ambrose Evans-Pritchard|date= 10 August 2013|website= [[The Daily Telegraph]]|access-date=8 March 2018 }}</ref> and as of Oct 2018, owns approximately 440 [[trillion (short scale)|trillion]] yen (approximately $4 trillion)<ref group=note>At a $1=¥0.0094 conversion rate</ref> or over 40% of all outstanding government bonds.<ref>[https://www.boj.or.jp/en/statistics/boj/other/mei/index.htm/ Gov't Bonds], [[Bank of Japan]]</ref>
[[File:EESA128.png|thumb|Reserve Balances with [[U.S. Federal Reserve Bank|w:U.S. Federal Reserve Banks]], Weekly, 1995-2008 in Billions of Dollars]]
In the United States, the 1913 [[Federal Reserve Act]] allowed [[Federal Reserve System|federal]] banks to purchase short-term securities directly from the Treasury to facilitate its [[cash]]-management operations. The [[Banking Act of 1935]] prohibited the central bank from directly purchasing Treasury securities and permitted their purchase and sale only "in the open market". In 1942, during [[United States home front during World War II|wartime]], Congress amended the Banking Act's provisions to allow purchases of government debt by the federal banks, with the total amount they would hold not to exceed $5 billion. After the war, the exemption was renewed with time limitations until it was allowed to expire in June 1981.<ref name="garbade">{{cite web |last=Garbade |first=Kenneth D. | url=https://www.newyorkfed.org/medialibrary/media/research/staff_reports/sr684.pdf |title=Direct Purchases of U.S. Treasury Securities by Federal Reserve Banks |date=August 2014|website= FRBNY Staff Reports no. 684}}</ref> Today, primary dealers in the United States are required to purchase all Treasuries at auction, and the U.S. central bank will create any quantity of reserve deposits necessary to settle the auction transaction.

=== Open market operations ===
{{Main|Open market operation}}

Central banks can purchase or sell assets in the market, which is referred to as open market operations. When a central bank purchases assets from market participants, such as commercial banks that hold accounts at the central bank, reserve deposits are credited to the commercial banks' accounts and asset ownership is transferred to the central bank. In this way, the central bank can modulate the amount of reserve deposits in the financial system by exchanging financial assets like bonds for reserve deposits. For example, in the United States, when the Federal Reserve permanently purchases a security, the office responsible for implementing purchases and sales (The New York Fed's Open Market Trading Desk) buys eligible securities from primary dealers at prices determined in a competitive auction. The Federal Reserve pays for those securities by crediting the reserve accounts of the correspondent banks of the primary dealers. (The correspondent banks, in turn, credit the dealers' bank accounts.) In this way, the open market purchase leads to an increase in reserve balances.<ref name="USFedExplained2024">{{cite web |last1=US Federal Reserve |title=The Fed Explained |url=https://www.federalreserve.gov/aboutthefed/files/the-fed-explained.pdf |publisher=US Federal Reserve |access-date=26 May 2024}}</ref>

Conversely, sales of assets by the U.S. central bank reduce reserve balances, which reduces the amount of money available in the financial system for settling transactions between member banks. Central banks also engage in short term contracts to "sell-assets-now, repurchase-later" to manage short-term reserve deposit balances. These contracts, known as repo (repurchase) contracts, are short-term (often overnight) contracts that are continually rolled over until some desired result in the financial system is achieved. Operations conducted by central banks can address either short-term goals on the bank's agenda or long-term factors such as maintaining financial stability or maintaining a floor and/or ceiling around a targeted interest rate for reserve deposits.

=== Money multiplier ===
{{Main|Money multiplier}}
[[File:Bank of England Mc Leavy et al. (2014) Banks Money Creation Balance Sheets (failed in consistent description).png|thumb|Left: Balance Sheet Extension of giving loan bank, right side: Balance Sheet Contraction of giving loan bank by losing reserves (transferring to seller´s bank).]]
Historical explanations of money creation often focused on the concept of a money multiplier, where reserve deposits or an underlying commodity such as gold were multiplied by bank lending of those deposits or gold balances to a maximum limit defined by the reserve requirement for money lenders. Thus, the total money supply was a function of the reserve requirement. Many states today, however, have no reserve requirement. The money multiplier has thus largely been abandoned as an explanatory tool for the money creation process.

When commercial banks lend money today, they expand the amount of bank deposits in the economy.<ref name=mcleay>{{cite web |url= https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/-/media/boe/files/quarterly-bulletin/2014/money-creation-in-the-modern-economy.pdf|title= Money creation in the modern economy|last1= McLeay|first1= Michael|last2= Radia |first2= Amar|last3= Thomas |first3= Ryland|date= 2014|website= Quarterly Bulletin|publisher= [[Bank of England]]|access-date=8 March 2018 }}</ref> The banking system can expand the money supply of a country far beyond the amount of reserve deposits created by the central bank. This means that, contrary to popular belief, most money is not created by central banks.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Revill |first=John |date=June 11, 2018 |title=Swiss voters reject campaign to radically alter banking system |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/idUSKBN1J60C0/ |access-date=July 6, 2024 |work=[[Reuters]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Werner |first=Richard |date=March 14, 2023 |title=Why central banks are too powerful and have created our inflation crisis – by the banking expert who pioneered quantitative easing |url=https://theconversation.com/why-central-banks-are-too-powerful-and-have-created-our-inflation-crisis-by-the-banking-expert-who-pioneered-quantitative-easing-201158 |access-date=July 6, 2024 |work=[[The Conversation (website)|The Conversation]]}}</ref> Some argue that banks are limited in the total amount they can lend by their [[capital adequacy ratio]]s and, in countries that impose [[required reserve ratio]]s, by required reserves.

Bank capital, used for calculating the capital adequacy ratio, consists of assets on the bank balance sheet in excess of liabilities, with values further refined by regulation such as the international regulatory framework for banks, Basel III. Banks create capital by creating loans (assets) and destroying bank liabilities, which occurs when loans are repaid. This process increases bank equity, enabling banks to create commercial bank deposit liabilities (money) for their own use. In this way, banks create and manage their own capital levels. Because accounting conventions define the value of any given asset or liability, bank capital is a subjective measure that many argue is open to manipulation and may be a poor method for regulating money creation.

Reserve requirements oblige commercial banks to keep a minimum, predetermined percentage of their deposits in an account at the central bank. Countries with no reserve requirement include the United States, Great Britain, Australia, Canada, and New Zealand, which means no minimum reserve requirement is imposed on banks. The constraining factor on bank lending recognized today is largely the number of available borrowers willing to create loan contracts.

==Degree of control==
While central banks can directly control the issuance of physical currency, the question of to what extent they can control broad monetary aggregates like [[M2 (economics)|M2]] by also indirectly controlling the money creation of commercial banks is more controversial.<ref name=Abel>{{cite journal |last1=Ábel |first1=István |last2=Lehmann |first2=Kristóf |last3=Tapaszti |first3=Attila |title=The controversial treatment of money and banks in macroeconomics |journal=Financial and Economic Review |date=June 2016 |volume=15 |issue=2 |pages=33–58 |url=https://en-hitelintezetiszemle.mnb.hu/letoltes/istvan-abel-kristof-lehmann-attila-tapaszti-en.pdf |access-date=17 October 2023}}</ref> According to the [[money multiplier]] theory, which is often cited in macroeconomics textbooks, the central bank controls the money multiplier because it can impose [[reserve requirement]]s and consequently, via this mechanism, also governs the amount of money created by commercial banks.<ref name=Abel/><ref>{{cite web |last1=Ihrig |first1=Jane |last2=Weinbach |first2=Gretchen C. |last3=Wolla |first3=Scott A. |title=Teaching the Linkage Between Banks and the Fed: R.I.P. Money Multiplier |url=https://research.stlouisfed.org/publications/page1-econ/2021/09/17/teaching-the-linkage-between-banks-and-the-fed-r-i-p-money-multiplier |website=research.stlouisfed.org |access-date=18 October 2023 |language=en |date=September 2021}}</ref> Most central banks in developed countries, however, have ceased to rely on this theory and have stopped shaping their monetary policy through required reserves.<ref name=Abel/>

[[Benjamin M. Friedman|Benjamin Friedman]] explains in his chapter on the money supply in ''[[The New Palgrave Dictionary of Economics]]'' that the money multiplier representation is a shorthand simplification of a more complex equilibrium of supply and demand in the markets for both reserves ([[outside money]]) and [[inside money]]. Friedman adds that the simplification will work well or badly "depending on the strength of the relevant interest elasticities and the extent of variation in interest rates and the many other factors involved".<ref name="Palgrave"/> [[David Romer]] notes in his graduate textbook ''Advanced Macroeconomics'' that it is difficult for central banks to control broad monetary aggregates like M2.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Romer |first1=David |title=Advanced macroeconomics |date=2019 |publisher=McGraw-Hill |location=New York, NY |isbn=978-1-260-18521-8 |edition=Fifth |quote=The measures of the money stock that the central bank can control tightly, such as [[high-powered money]], are not closely linked to [[aggregate demand]]. And the measures of the money stock that are sometimes closely linked with aggregate demand, such as ''M2'', are difficult for the central bank to control.}}</ref>{{rp|607–608}}

[[Monetarist]] theory, which was prominent during the 1970s and 1980s, argued that the central bank should concentrate on controlling the money supply through its monetary operations.<ref name="jahan2014">{{cite web |url=http://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/fandd/2014/03/pdf/basics.pdf|title=What Is Monetarism? |last1= Jahan|first1=Sarwat |last2= Papageorgiou|first2= Chris|date= March 2014|website= Finance & Development|publisher= [[IMF]]|access-date=8 March 2018 }}</ref> The strategy did not work well for the central banks like the US Federal Reserve that tried it, however, and it was abandoned after some years. Central banks then turned to steering interest rates to obtain their monetary policy goals rather than holding the quantity of base money fixed in order to steer money growth.<ref name=Blanchard>{{cite book |last1=Blanchard |first1=Olivier |last2=Amighini |first2=Alessia |last3=Giavazzi |first3=Francesco |title=Macroeconomics: a European perspective |date=2017 |publisher=Pearson |isbn=978-1-292-08567-8 |edition=3rd}}</ref>{{rp|464–465}} Interest rates influence commercial bank issuance of credit indirectly, so the ceiling implied by the money multiplier does not impose a limit on money creation in practice.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hubbard & O'Brien |title=Economics |chapter=Chapter 25, Monetary Policy |page=943}}</ref> By setting interest rates, central-bank operations will affect, but not control, the money supply.<ref name="mcleay" /><ref group=note>"Another common misconception is that the central bank determines the quantity of loans and deposits in the economy by controlling the quantity of central bank money. ... Rather than controlling the quantity of reserves, central banks today typically implement monetary policy by setting the price of reserves — that is, interest rates." McLeay (2014)</ref>

== Credit theory of money ==
{{Main|Credit theory of money}}

The [[fractional-reserve banking|fractional reserve]] theory of money creation, where the [[money supply]] is limited by the [[money multiplier]], has been abandoned since the [[2008 financial crisis]]. It has been observed that [[bank reserves]] are not a limiting factor because the [[central bank]]s supply more reserves than necessary (excess reserves).<ref name="SP2013">[[Standard & Poor's]] (13 August 2013) "[https://www.kreditmagazin.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/02/S_and_P__Repeat_After_Me_8_14_13.pdf Repeat after me: Banks cannot and do not lend out reserves]", Ratings Direct</ref> Economists and bankers now understand that the amount of money in circulation is limited only by the demand for loans.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Benes |first1=Jaromir |last2=Kumhof |first2=Michael |title=The Chicago Plan Revisited |journal=IMF Working Paper |date=2012 |volume=202 |url=https://www.imf.org/en/Publications/WP/Issues/2016/12/31/The-Chicago-Plan-Revisited-26178}}</ref><ref name="kumhof2016">{{cite journal |last1=Kumhof |first1=Michael |last2=Jakab |first2=Zoltán| title=The Truth about Banks |journal=Finance & Development |date=2016 |volume=53 |issue=1 |pages=50–53 |url=http://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/fandd/2016/03/kumhof.htm}}</ref><ref name="mcleay" />

The [[credit theory of money]], initiated by [[Joseph Schumpeter]], asserts the central role of banks as creators and allocators of the money supply and distinguishes between "productive credit creation" (allowing non-inflationary [[economic growth]] even at [[full employment]], in the presence of technological progress) and "unproductive credit creation" (resulting in [[inflation]] of either the [[consumer price inflation|consumer-]] or [[asset price inflation|asset-price]] variety).<ref>{{cite book |last= Schumpeter|first= Joseph A.|date= 1996|orig-year=1954|title= History of Economic Analysis|publisher= Oxford University Press|isbn= 978-0195105599|author-link=Joseph A. Schumpeter}}</ref>

The model of bank lending stimulated through central-bank operations (such as "monetary easing") has been rejected by [[Neo-Keynesian economics|Neo-Keynesian]]<ref>{{cite book|last= Samuelson|first= Paul|date= 1997|orig-year= 1948|title= Economics|url= https://archive.org/details/economicsintrodu0000samu|publisher= McGraw-Hill Education|isbn= 978-0070747418|author-link= Paul Samuelson|url-access= registration}}</ref> and [[Post-Keynesian economics|Post-Keynesian]] analysis<ref name=kelton>{{cite web|last=Kelton, ''née'' Bell|first=Stephanie |url=https://ideas.repec.org/p/wpa/wuwpma/9805014.html |title=The Hierarchy of Money|date=1998 |publisher=[[The Jerome Levy Economics Institute]]|ssrn=96845}}</ref><ref name="mitch2009">{{cite web |url=http://bilbo.economicoutlook.net/blog/?p=1623|title= Money multiplier and other myths|last= Mitchell|first= William|author-link=Bill Mitchell (economist)|date= 21 April 2009|access-date=8 March 2018}}</ref> as well as central banks.<ref name="tucker2007">{{cite web |last=Tucker|first=Paul|url=https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/-/media/boe/files/speech/2007/money-and-credit-banking-and-the-macroeconomy.pdf|title=Money and credit: Banking and the Macroeconomy|date=2007 |publisher=Bank of England }}</ref><ref name=Disyatat>{{Cite web|url=http://www.bis.org/publ/work297.pdf|title=The bank lending channel revisited|last=Disyatat|first=Piti|date=February 2010|publisher=[[Bank of International Settlements]]|website=BIS Working Papers|language=en|access-date=8 March 2018}}</ref><ref group=note>"In reality, neither are[bank] reserves a binding constraint on lending, nor does the central bank fix the amount of reserves that are available. ... Banks first decide how much to lend depending on the profitable lending opportunities available to them — which will, crucially, depend on the interest rate set by the [central bank]." McLeay et al. (2014)</ref>
The major argument offered by dissident analysis is that any bank balance-sheet expansion (e.g., through a new loan) that leaves the bank short of the required reserves may affect the return it can expect on the loan because of the extra cost the bank will undertake to return within the ratio limits–but this does not and "will never impede the bank's capacity to give the loan in the first place". Banks first lend and ''then'' cover their reserve ratios: The decision whether or not to lend is generally independent of their reserves with the central bank or their deposits from customers; banks are not lending out deposits or reserves, anyway. Banks lend on the basis of lending criteria, such as the status of the customer's business, the loan's prospects, and/or the overall economic situation.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Money and Inflation|last=Wray|first=L. Randall|author-link=L. Randall Wray |url=https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1010331|date=1 September 2000|publisher=[[University of Missouri-Kansas City]]|language=en|ssrn = 1010331}}</ref><ref>BoE (2019): [https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/explainers/how-is-money-created How is money created]</ref><ref>Frank Decker, Charles A.E. Goodhart: ''Wilhelm Lautenbach’s credit-mechanics – a precursor to the current money supply debate'', Taylor & Francis, 2021, DOI=10.1080/09672567.2021.1963796.</ref>

'''Sterling''' <!--"Sterling" is the official name of this currency. The pound is just its primary unit today, in antiquity it was the penny.-->([[pound sign|symbol]]: '''£'''; [[ISO 4217|code]]: '''GBP''') is the [[currency]] of the [[United Kingdom]] and nine of its [[Dependent territories of the United Kingdom|dependent territories]]<ref>{{cite book |title=A Dictionary of Economics |edition=5 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=9780198759430 |url=https://global.oup.com/academic/product/a-dictionary--of-economics-9780198759430?lang=en&cc=gb |first1=Nigar |last1=Hashimzade |first2=Gareth |last2=Myles |first3=John |last3=Black |quote='''Sterling''': The UK currency. The name originated from the pound Easterling, formerly used in trade with the Baltic. |date=2017 |archive-date=20 September 2022 |access-date=23 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220920192530/https://global.oup.com/academic/product/a-dictionary--of-economics-9780198759430?lang=en&cc=gb |url-status=live }}</ref> and formerly of the [[Kingdom of England]]. The '''pound''' is the base [[unit of account|unit]] of sterling,<ref name="Can Ox D" />{{efn|Historically, 'sterling' was the name of the currency and the pound (or, for centuries, the silver penny) were its [[units of account]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Pounds, shillings and pence |url=https://www.royalmintmuseum.org.uk/journal/history/pounds-shillings-and-pence/ |website=Royal Mint |access-date=16 October 2024 |archive-date=5 January 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210105150045/https://www.royalmintmuseum.org.uk/journal/history/pounds-shillings-and-pence/ |url-status=live }}</ref> In modern usage, the name "pound sterling" is used for both sterling and its pound base unit.<ref>{{cite web |title=UK Notes and Coins |url=https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/banknotes/uk-notes-and-coins |website=Bank of England |access-date=16 October 2024 |archive-date=20 July 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180720003937/https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/banknotes/uk-notes-and-coins |url-status=live }} "The pound sterling is the official currency in the United Kingdom."</ref>}} and the word ''[[Pound (currency)|pound]]'' is also used to refer to the British currency generally,<ref name="HbIFT">{{cite book |title=The Handbook of International Financial Terms |first1=Peter |last1=Moles |first2=Nicholas |last2=Terry |isbn=9780198294818 |date=1999 |url=https://global.oup.com/academic/product/the-handbook-of-international-financial-terms-9780198294818 |quote='''Sterling (UK).''': The name given to the currency of the United Kingdom (cf. [[Cable (foreign exchange)|cable]]). Also called pound sterling or pounds. |archive-date=3 December 2024 |access-date=23 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241203052737/https://global.oup.com/academic/product/the-handbook-of-international-financial-terms-9780198294818 |url-status=live }}</ref> often qualified in international contexts as the '''British pound''' or '''pound sterling'''.<ref name="Can Ox D">{{cite encyclopedia | dictionary=Canadian Oxford Dictionary |edition=2 | title=Pound |quote='''Pound''':2. (in full '''pound sterling''') (pl. same or '''pounds''') the chief monetary unit of the UK and several other countries. |editor-first=Katherine |editor-last=Barber |isbn=9780195418163 |date=2004|publisher=Oxford University Press }}</ref> [[Decimal Day|Since 1971]], each pound has been divided into 100 [[penny|pence]] (singular is 'penny').

Sterling is the world's oldest currency in continuous use since its inception.<ref name="Rendall">{{Cite news |last=Rendall |first=Alasdair |date=12 November 2007 |title=Economic terms explained |work=BBC News |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/programmes/bbc_parliament/7090665.stm |access-date=14 February 2014 |archive-date=3 May 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080503031518/http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/programmes/bbc_parliament/7090665.stm |url-status=live }}</ref> In 2025, it was the fourth-most-traded currency in the [[foreign exchange market]], after the [[United States dollar]], the [[euro]], and the [[Japanese yen]].<ref>{{cite web |date=1 April 2025 |title=Triennial Central Bank Survey |url=https://www.bis.org/publications/triennial-survey/rpfx25-fx-annex-2606.pdf |access-date=11 September 2026 |publisher=[[Bank for International Settlements|BIS]] |archive-date=11 September 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260911044251/https://www.bis.org/publications/triennial-survey/rpfx25-fx-annex-2606.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> Together with those three currencies and the [[renminbi]], it forms the [[basket of currencies]] that [[special drawing rights#Value definition|calculate the value]] of [[IMF]] [[special drawing rights]]. As of early 2026, sterling is also the fourth <!-- Citation lists first by the five IMF basket currencies and then by alphabetical, as the source explicitly points out, with the GBP amount clearly FOURTH--> most-held [[reserve currency]] in [[Foreign exchange reserves|global reserves]].<ref name="IMFCOFER">{{cite web |date=1 July 2026 |title=IMF Data Brief: Currency Composition of Official Foreign Exchange Reserves |url=https://data.imf.org/en/news/imf%20data%20brief%20july%201 |access-date=11 September 2026 |publisher=[[International Monetary Fund]] |archive-date=3 September 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260903212143/https://data.imf.org/en/news/imf%20data%20brief%20july%201 |url-status=live }}</ref>

The [[Bank of England]] is the [[central bank]] for sterling, issuing its [[Bank of England note issues|own banknotes]] (as used in England and Wales) and regulating issuance of banknotes [[Banknotes of Scotland|by private banks in Scotland]], such as the [[Bank of Scotland]] and [[Clydesdale Bank]], and [[Banknotes of Northern Ireland|in Northern Ireland]], such as by [[Danske Bank (Northern Ireland)|Danske Bank]]. Sterling banknotes issued by other jurisdictions are not regulated by the Bank of England; their governments [[currency board|guarantee convertibility at par]]. Historically, sterling was also used to varying degrees by the colonies and territories of the [[British Empire]].

==Names==
===Etymology===
[[File:William I silver penny c 1075 moneyer Oswold at the mint of Lewes.jpg|thumb|Penny of [[William the Conqueror|William I]], showing the king's head between two stars]]
<span class="anchor" id="Penny sterling"></span> The basic unit of currency in medieval England was the [[Penny (English coin)|silver penny]] or sterling, weighing about {{frac|240}} of a [[tower pound]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Zupko |first=Ronald Edward |url=http://archive.org/details/britishweightsme0000zupk |title=British weights & measures : a history from antiquity to the seventeenth century |date=1977 |publication-place=Madison|publisher=University of Wisconsin Press |others=Internet Archive |isbn=978-0-299-07340-4 |pages=11}}</ref>{{efn|"Anglo-Saxon [[King Offa]] is credited with introducing the system of money to central and southern England in the latter half of the eighth century, overseeing the minting of the earliest English silver pennies{{snd}}emblazoned with his name. In practice they varied considerably in weight and 240 of them seldom added up to a pound".<ref>{{cite web |title=A short history of the pound |publisher=BBC |first=Ed |last=Lowther |date=14 February 2014 |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-26169070 |quote= |access-date=22 July 2021 |archive-date=21 July 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210721233848/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-26169070 |url-status=live }}</ref>{{snd}} Ed Lowther, BBC}} Two hundred and forty of these coins made a "pound of sterlings". This term (shortened to "pound sterling" in later usage) continued to be used in accounting even after the sterling had ceased to circulate. The earliest known instances of the term occur in [[Orderic Vitalis]]'s 12th-century ''Historia Ecclesiastica'', which makes mention of ''librae sterilensium''.<ref name=oed>{{cite OED|sterling|7669969387}}</ref>{{efn|For example, Vitalis records that sometime after 1078, the Archbishop of Canterbury sent "XL libras sterilensium" [forty pounds of sterlings] to Abbot Mainier of St Avroult.<ref>{{cite book |title= The ecclesiastical history of England and Normandy |page=[https://archive.org/details/ordericivitalish02ordeuoft/page/128/mode/2up 128, 129] |first=Orderic |last=Vitalis |author-link=Orderic Vitalis |quote={{lang|la|Lanfrancus enim archiepiscopus, dum dedicationi Cadomensis ecclesiae (3) anno scilicet duodecimo post Anglicum bellum interfuit, Mainerio abbati XLIV libras Anglicae monetae et duos auri marcos erogavit, et postmodum de Cantia per domnum Rogeriumde Sappo, qui sibi pro scientia litterarum notus et amicus erat, XL libras sterilensium misit. His igitur datis ecclesiae turris erecta est, et monachile dormitorium constructum est}} |trans-quote=Among others, Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, when he assisted at the consecration of the church of Caen, in the twelfth year after the war with England, remitted to abbot Mainier twenty-four pounds of English money and two marks of gold, and he afterwards sent over from Canterbury forty pounds sterling; by the hands of the lord Roger de Sap, who was known and esteemed by him for his learning. With these donations the abbey tower was carried up, and the dormitory for the monks built. |language=la}} (translation source [https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=hvd.32044069750123&seq=489&q1=sterling Vol 1, p 468 &lsqb;#490&rsqb;]. Chapter XII: A.D. 1066)</ref> }}

The origin of the word ''sterling'' itself is unclear. It first appears in the 11th and 12th centuries, suggesting that it was coined to describe the new, heavier penny introduced by the [[Anglo-Normans|Normans]]. According to the ''[[Oxford English Dictionary]]'', the most plausible theory is that it represents [[Old English]] *{{Lang|ang|steorling}}, meaning "coin with a star" (a pair of stars having appeared on certain Norman pennies).<ref name=oed/> The numismatist [[Philip Grierson]] rejects this, however, noting that the starred penny was only minted between 1077 and 1080 and formed a tiny fraction of the total coinage issued by the Normans. Grierson suggests instead that the first element is *{{Lang|ang|stēre}}, meaning "stout" or "strong". In support of this theory, he notes that the Roman [[solidus]] had a name with a very similar meaning and was also introduced to replace a lighter coin.<ref name=grierson>{{cite book|title=Anglo-Saxon Coins|date=1961|editor-last=Dolley|editor-first=R. H. M.|location=London|publisher=Methuen & Co.|chapter=Sterling|last=Grierson|first=P.|pages=266–283|chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/anglosaxoncoins0000rhmd/page/266}}</ref>

An old theory that the sterling was so named because it was introduced to England by [[wikt:Easterling|Easterlings]], i.e. [[Hanseatic]] merchants, is untenable on historical and phonological grounds.<ref name=grierson/>

===Symbol===
{{main|Pound sign}}
The [[currency sign]] for the pound unit of sterling is {{char|£}}, which (depending on typeface) may be drawn [[pound sign#Double bar style|with one or two bars]]:<ref name="BoE-FoI">{{cite web |title=History of the use of the single crossbar pound sign on Bank of England's banknotes |url=https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/freedom-of-information/2022/history-of-the-use-of-the-single-crossbar-pound-sign-on-banknotes |publisher=Bank of England |access-date=13 April 2022 |archive-date=25 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220325080653/https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/freedom-of-information/2022/history-of-the-use-of-the-single-crossbar-pound-sign-on-banknotes |url-status=live }}</ref> the Bank of England has exclusively used the single bar variant since 1975.<ref name="BoEoldnotes">{{cite web |title=Withdrawn banknotes |url=https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/banknotes/withdrawn-banknotes |access-date=13 September 2019 |publisher=[[Bank of England]] |archive-date=15 January 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190115092327/https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/banknotes/withdrawn-banknotes |url-status=live }} ("£1 1st Series Treasury Issue" to "£5 Series B")</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Current banknotes |url=https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/banknotes/current-banknotes |access-date=8 November 2019 |publisher=[[Bank of England]] |archive-date=4 December 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191204081441/https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/banknotes/current-banknotes |url-status=live }}</ref> Historically, a simple capital {{char|L}} (in the historic [[black-letter]] typeface, <math>\mathfrak{L}</math>) placed before the numerals, or an italic <span style="border:1px solid #ddd; background:#fdfdfd; padding:1px; font-family:serif;">''l.''</span> after them, was used in newspapers, books and letters.<ref>For example,{{cite web |last=Samuel Pepys |date=2 January 1660 |title=Diary of Samuel Pepys/1660/January |url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Diary_of_Samuel_Pepys/1660/January |access-date=23 September 2019 |archive-date=23 September 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190923210619/https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Diary_of_Samuel_Pepys/1660/January |url-status=live |quote=Then I went to Mr. Crew's and borrowed L10 of Mr. Andrewes for my own use, and so went to my office, where there was nothing to do}}</ref> The [[Royal Mint]] was still using this style of notation as late as 1939.<ref>{{cite web |last=His Majesty's Stationery Office |date=10 July 1939 |title=Royal Mint Annual Report 1938 Volume No.69 |url=https://library.royalmintmuseum.org.uk/archive/royal-mint-annual-reports/royal-mint-annual-report-1938-volume-no69/1798041 |access-date=30 June 2022 |quote=Some 58,000,000<span style="font-family: serif;">''l''</span> of silver coin of the old fineness, comprising over a thousand million pieces, have already been withdrawn from circulation. |archive-date=17 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220817181544/https://library.royalmintmuseum.org.uk/archive/royal-mint-annual-reports/royal-mint-annual-report-1938-volume-no69/1798041 |url-status=live }}</ref>  Use of the letter {{angbr|L}} for pound derives from medieval Latin documents: "L" was the abbreviation for {{lang|la|[[Roman units of weight|libra]]}}, the [[Roman pound]] (weight), which in time became an [[Kingdom of England|English]] unit of weight defined as the [[tower pound]]. A "pound sterling" was literally a tower pound (weight) of [[sterling silver]].<ref name="ViewOfCoinage">{{Cite book |last=Thomas Snelling |url=https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_12AGAAAAQAAJ |title=A View of the Silver Coin and Coinage of England from the Norman Conquest to the Present Time |date=1762 |publisher=T. Snelling |page=ii |access-date=19 September 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=A brief history of the pound |url=http://www.dozenalsociety.org.uk/history/poundhist.html |access-date=14 January 2011 |publisher=The Dozenal Society of Great Britain |archive-date=12 November 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201112000041/http://www.dozenalsociety.org.uk/history/poundhist.html |url-status=live }}</ref> In the British pre-decimal ([[duodecimal]]) currency system, the term [[£sd]] (or Lsd) for pounds, [[shilling]]s and [[pence]] referred to the Roman {{lang|la|libra}}, ''[[solidus (coin)|solidus]]'', and ''[[denarius]]''.<ref name="britannica1">{{Cite encyclopedia |date=13 August 2013 |title=Pound sterling (money) |url=http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/473092/pound-sterling |access-date=19 February 2014 |encyclopedia=Encyclopædia Britannica |quote=Silver coins known as 'sterlings' were issued in the Saxon kingdoms, 240 of them being minted from a pound of silver... Hence, large payments came to be reckoned in 'pounds of sterlings', a phrase later shortened... |archive-date=3 December 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131203201915/http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/473092/pound-sterling |url-status=live }}</ref>

Notable style guides recommend that the pound sign be used without any abbreviation or qualification to indicate sterling (e.g., £12,000).<ref>{{cite web |title = ILO House style manual |publisher = [[International Labour Organization]] |url = https://www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/---ed_norm/---relconf/documents/meetingdocument/wcms_742229.pdf |access-date = 25 June 2022 |archive-date = 17 May 2022 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20220517223204/http://www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/---ed_norm/---relconf/documents/meetingdocument/wcms_742229.pdf |url-status = live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=WHO style guide |publisher=[[World Health Organization]] |url=https://www.unaids.org/sites/default/files/sg13_web_v4%20pdf%20-%20adobe%20reader.pdf |access-date=25 June 2022 |archive-date=14 September 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210914013949/https://www.unaids.org/sites/default/files/sg13_web_v4%20pdf%20-%20adobe%20reader.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Style guide for authors and editors |publisher=[[Bloomsbury Academic]] |url=https://media.bloomsbury.com/rep/files/ba-house-style-for-authors-and-editorssept16.pdf |access-date=25 June 2022 |archive-date=26 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210626002418/https://media.bloomsbury.com/rep/files/ba-house-style-for-authors-and-editorssept16.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> The [[ISO 4217]] code "GBP" (e.g., GBP&nbsp;12,000) may also be seen should disambiguation become necessary.

===Currency code===
The [[ISO 4217]] currency code for sterling is "GBP",<ref>{{cite web |title=Maintenance Agency {{!}} ISO 4217 – Currency Code Maintenance: Get the Correct Currency Code {{!}} List One |url=https://www.six-group.com/en/products-services/financial-information/data-standards.html#scrollTo=maintenance-agency |publisher=SIX Group |access-date=1 August 2023 |archive-date=28 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220128070036/https://www.six-group.com/en/products-services/financial-information/data-standards.html#scrollTo=maintenance-agency |url-status=live }} (The official list of ISO 4217 alphabetic and numeric codes)</ref> formed from the [[ISO 3166-1 alpha-2]] code for the United Kingdom ("GB") and the first letter of "pound".<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.iso.org/iso-4217-currency-codes.html |url-access= |title=ISO 4217 - Currency Codes |author=Staff writer |year=2015 |website=www.iso.org |agency=International Organisation for Standardisation |access-date=27 June 2022 |quote=The alphabetic code is based on another ISO standard, ISO&nbsp;3166, which lists the codes for country names. The first two letters of the ISO&nbsp;4217 three-letter code are the same as the code for the country name, and, where possible, the third letter corresponds to the first letter of the currency name. |archive-date=15 February 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170215140249/http://www.iso.org/iso/home/standards/currency_codes.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> <!--The terms "Great British Pound" and "Great Britain Pound" are erroneous backronyms with no status. Please do not bother to add either as it will be deleted. -->
In historical sources and some specialist banking uses, the abbreviation '''stg''' (in various styles) has been used to indicate sterling.<ref name="Leach">{{cite book |title=Leach's Tax Dictionary |page=838 |isbn=9781913507190 |location=London |publisher=Spiramus Press Ltd |year=2021 |first=Robert |last=Leach |chapter=Section 2: Abbreviations |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=C_AhEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA838 |access-date=22 June 2022 |archive-date=17 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220817181528/https://www.google.co.uk/books/edition/Leach_s_Tax_Dictionary/C_AhEAAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&pg=PA838 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.swift.com/sites/default/files/files/chaps-getting-started-guide_v1_0.pdf|title=CHAPS ISO 20022 over SWIFT|publisher=[[SWIFT]]|date=2021|access-date=27 July 2023|archive-date=24 November 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211124114415/https://www.swift.com/sites/default/files/files/chaps-getting-started-guide_v1_0.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> Many stocks on the [[London Stock Exchange]] are quoted in '''penny sterling''', using the unofficial code "GBX".<ref>{{Cite web |title=What does GBX mean when buying stocks on the London Stock Exchange? |url=https://www.degiro.cz/helpdesk/orders/what-does-gbx-mean-when-buying-stocks-london-stock-exchange |access-date=2023-12-08 |website=[[DEGIRO]] |archive-date=18 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220818082300/https://www.degiro.cz/helpdesk/orders/what-does-gbx-mean-when-buying-stocks-london-stock-exchange |url-status=dead }}</ref>

===Cable===
{{Main|Cable (foreign exchange)}}
The exchange rate of sterling against the [[US dollar]] is referred to as "cable" in the wholesale [[foreign exchange market]]s.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.ft.com/content/47c32ec4-6a34-11e4-8fca-00144feabdc0 |title=Traders' forex chatroom banter exposed |newspaper=[[Financial Times]] |first1=Claer |last1=Barrett |first2=John |last2=Aglionby |date=12 November 2014 |quote=A trader from HSBC visits multiple chatrooms in an attempt to manipulate the 4pm WMR fix, declaring he is a net seller in "cable" (a slang term for GBP/USD currency pairing) |access-date=18 February 2022 |archive-date=18 February 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220218141204/https://www.ft.com/content/47c32ec4-6a34-11e4-8fca-00144feabdc0 |url-status=live }}</ref> The origins of this term are attributed to the fact that from the mid-19th century, the sterling/dollar exchange rate was transmitted via transatlantic cable.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1931/09/22/archives/sterling-cable-rates-319-to-7-since-1914-top-reached-when-war.html|title=STERLING CABLE RATES $3.19 TO $7 SINCE 1914; Top Reached When War Started and Bottom on Feb. 3, 1920, as Support Stopped|date=22 September 1931|newspaper=[[New York Times]]|access-date=18 February 2022|archive-date=5 January 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220105215929/https://www.nytimes.com/1931/09/22/archives/sterling-cable-rates-319-to-7-since-1914-top-reached-when-war.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Slang terms <span class="anchor" id="quid (slang)"></span>===
Historically almost every British coin had a widely recognised nickname, such as "tanner" for the [[Sixpence (British coin)|sixpence]] and "bob" for the [[Shilling (British coin)|shilling]].<ref name=UON>{{cite web |url=https://www.nottingham.ac.uk/manuscriptsandspecialcollections/researchguidance/weightsandmeasures/money.aspx |title=University of Nottingham ''Manuscripts and Special Collections'' 'Research Guidance' Weights and Measures § Money |access-date=12 March 2014 |archive-date=12 March 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140312080731/http://www.nottingham.ac.uk/manuscriptsandspecialcollections/researchguidance/weightsandmeasures/money.aspx |url-status=live }}</ref> Since decimalisation these have mostly fallen out of use except as parts of proverbs.

A common<ref name="slang">{{Cite web |url=https://www.sunnyavenue.co.uk/insight/why-is-it-called-a-quid-history-of-the-quid |title=Why is it called a quid? History of the Quid |date=2023-08-30 |access-date=2024-01-18 |website=Sunny Avenue |last=Crispe |first=Stuart |archive-date=18 January 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240118081529/https://www.sunnyavenue.co.uk/insight/why-is-it-called-a-quid-history-of-the-quid |url-status=live }}</ref> slang term for the pound unit is "'''quid'''" (singular and plural, except in the common phrase "quids in").<ref>{{cite web |title=Quid {{!}} Definition of Quid by Oxford Dictionary on Lexico.com also meaning of Quid |url=https://www.lexico.com/definition/quid |access-date=11 June 2020 |website=Lexico Dictionaries {{!}} English |language=en |archive-date=11 June 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200611103435/https://www.lexico.com/definition/quid |url-status=dead }}</ref> Its origin is unknown: possible derivations include {{lang|it|[[Italian scudo|scudo]]}}, the name for a number of currency units used in Italy until the 19th century, introduced by Italian immigrants;{{citation needed|date=October 2024}} or from Latin {{lang|la|quid}} via the common phrase ''[[quid pro quo]]'', literally, "what for what", or, figuratively, "An equal exchange or substitution".<ref>The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language, Third Edition. Houghton Mifflin. 20 August 1993.</ref> The term "nicker" (also both singular and plural) may also refer to the pound.<ref name=slang />

==Crown Dependencies and British Overseas Territories==
The currency of all the [[Crown Dependencies]] ([[Bailiwick of Guernsey|Guernsey]], [[Jersey]], [[Isle of Man]]) and a third of [[British Overseas Territories]] ([[British Antarctic Territory]];<ref>{{cite web |title=British Antarctic Territory Currency Ordinance 1990 |url=https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/478254/The_Currency_Ordinance_1990.odt |access-date=13 June 2019 |archive-date=12 April 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210412083004/https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/478254/The_Currency_Ordinance_1990.odt |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=25 March 2010 |title=Foreign and Commonwealth Office country profiles: British Antarctic Territory |url=http://www.fco.gov.uk/en/about-the-fco/country-profiles/south-america/british-antarctic-territory |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090420013058/http://www.fco.gov.uk/en/about-the-fco/country-profiles/south-america/british-antarctic-territory/ |archive-date=20 April 2009 |access-date=17 April 2010 |publisher=British Foreign & Commonwealth Office}}</ref> [[Falkland Islands]] and [[South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands]]; [[Gibraltar]]; and [[Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha]])<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.gov.uk/foreign-travel-advice/st-helena-ascension-and-tristan-da-cunha/money | title=Money - St Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha travel advice | access-date=28 January 2024 | archive-date=13 August 2013 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130813153333/https://www.gov.uk/foreign-travel-advice/st-helena-ascension-and-tristan-da-cunha/money | url-status=live }}</ref> is either sterling or [[currency peg|pegged]] to sterling at par.

The other British Overseas Territories have a local currency that is [[currency peg|pegged]] to the [[U.S. dollar]] or the [[New Zealand dollar]]. The [[Sovereign Base Areas of Akrotiri and Dhekelia]] (in [[Cyprus]]) use the euro.

==Subdivisions and other units==
===Decimal coinage===

Since [[decimalisation]] on [[Decimal Day]] in 1971, the pound has been divided into 100 pence (denoted on coinage, until 1981, as "new pence"). The symbol for the penny is "p"; hence an amount such as 50p (£0.50) properly pronounced "fifty pence" is often pronounced "fifty pee" /fɪfti piː/. The old sign ''d'' was not reused for the ''new penny'' in order to avoid confusion between the two units. A decimal [[Halfpenny (British decimal coin)|halfpenny]] ({{sfrac|2}}p, worth 1.2 old pennies) was issued until 1984 but was [[Withdrawal of low-denomination coins|withdrawn due to inflation]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> |date=2008 |title=1984: Halfpenny coin to meet its maker |work=BBC News |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/onthisday/hi/dates/stories/february/1/newsid_2828000/2828819.stm |access-date=14 February 2014 |archive-date=18 February 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150218211548/http://news.bbc.co.uk/onthisday/hi/dates/stories/february/1/newsid_2828000/2828819.stm |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Pre-decimal===
{{further|Coins of the pound sterling|List of British banknotes and coins}}

Before [[£sd#Decimalisation|decimalisation in 1971]], the pound was divided into 20 [[British shilling coin|shillings]], and each shilling into 12 [[Old penny sterling|pence]], making 240 pence to the pound. The symbol for the shilling was "''s''."{{snd}} not from the first letter of "shilling", but from the Latin ''[[solidus (coin)|solidus]]''. The symbol for the penny was "''d''.", from the French ''denier'', from the Latin ''[[denarius]]'' (the solidus and denarius were Roman coins). A mixed sum of shillings and pence, such as 3 shillings and 6 pence, was written as "3/6" or "3''s''. 6''d''." and spoken as "three and six" or "three and sixpence" except for "1/1", "2/1" etc., which were spoken as "one and a penny", "two and a penny", etc. Five shillings, for example, was written as "5''s''." or, more commonly, "5/–" (five shillings, no pence).
Various coin denominations had, and in some cases continue to have, special names, such as [[florin (British coin)|florin]] (2/–), [[crown (British coin)|crown]] (5/–), [[farthing (British coin)|farthing]] ({{frac|1|4}}''d''), [[sovereign (British coin)|sovereign]] (£1) and [[guinea (British coin)|guinea]] (21s, 21/–, £1–1–0 or £1.05 in decimal notation). <!-- half-crown, half-penny and half-farthing are not "special names". -->

By the 1950s, the coins of kings [[George&nbsp;III]], [[George&nbsp;IV]] and [[William&nbsp;IV]] had disappeared from circulation, but coins (at least the penny) bearing the head of every British monarch from [[Queen Victoria]] onwards could be found in circulation. Silver coins were replaced by those in [[cupro-nickel]] in 1947, and by the 1960s the silver coins were rarely seen. Silver/cupro-nickel sixpences, shillings (from any period after 1816) and [[Florin (British coin)|florin]]s (2 shillings) remained legal tender after decimalisation (as 2½p, 5p and 10p respectively) until 1980, 1990 and 1993 respectively, but are now officially demonetised.<ref>{{cite web|title=Shilling|url=https://www.royalmintmuseum.org.uk/journal/curators-corner/shilling/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210921210542/https://www.royalmintmuseum.org.uk/journal/curators-corner/shilling/|archive-date=21 September 2021|access-date=23 September 2021|website=The Royal Mint Museum}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Florin |url=http://www.royalmintmuseum.org.uk/coins/british-coinage/old-denominations/florin/index.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150227195515/http://www.royalmintmuseum.org.uk/coins/british-coinage/old-denominations/florin/index.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=27 February 2015 |access-date=11 September 2019 |website=The Royal Mint Museum}}</ref>

==History (600–1945)==
{{anchor|History}} <!-- previous section title-->
The pound sterling emerged after the adoption of the [[French livre|Carolingian monetary system]] in England {{circa|800}}.
